World.title: Government demands integrity in 2026 FISP implementation
World.content:
Government has called on all stakeholders in the agricultural sector to uphold integrity, professionalism and collaboration to ensure the successful implementation of the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP) during the 2026/2027 farming season.

Northwestern Province Permanent Secretary Colonel Grandson Katambi (rtd) says the success of FISP depends on the collective commitment of farmers, agro-dealers, seed suppliers, financial institutions, extension officers and other implementing partners.

Speaking in a speech read on his behalf by his Deputy Permanent Secretary Luckson Mulumbi while addressing participants during the FISP sensitisation and training meeting for agro-dealers in Solwezi, Col Katambi retired said government remains committed to transforming Zambia’s agriculture sector into a productive, competitive, climate-smart and resilient industry capable of driving economic growth and improving livelihoods.

He said the government is targeting annual production of 10 million metric tonnes of maize, three million metric tonnes of soybeans and one million metric tonnes of wheat by 2031.

Col Katambi retired disclosed that North-Western Province is projected to produce 340,000 metric tonnes of maize during the current season, representing a 10 percent increase over the previous harvest.

He attributed the projected increase to improved farmer support programmes, favourable collaboration among stakeholders and the hard work of farmers.

The Permanent Secretary said sustaining the growth will require increased investment in irrigation, agricultural mechanisation, climate-smart farming practices and access to quality farming inputs.

He further warned that weather forecasts indicate a high likelihood of El Niño conditions during the 2026/2027 farming season and urged farmers to adopt drought mitigation measures.

Col Katambi retired said the government has drawn lessons from the 2023/2024 El Niño-induced drought and has strengthened preparedness through the Agriculture and Food Security Cluster Response Framework.

He said the government has intensified interventions such as irrigation development, conservation agriculture, promotion of drought-tolerant and early-maturing crop varieties, water harvesting technologies and strengthened extension services to cushion farmers against climate-related shocks.

Col Katambi retired also noted that the government’s transition to the 100 percent electronic voucher (e-Voucher) FISP system during the 2025/2026 farming season has enhanced transparency, improved beneficiary targeting, reduced inefficiencies in input distribution and empowered farmers with greater choice in accessing agricultural inputs.

He, however, cautioned agro-dealers to uphold professionalism and ensure farmers receive genuine inputs from approved suppliers, warning that the government will not tolerate malpractice that undermines the objectives of the programme.

‘‘I further urge all seed companies to invest in research and supply climate-smart seed varieties suitable for Zambia’s changing weather patterns. I am also calling on extension officers to continue providing farmers with technical guidance on good agronomic practices and effective utilisation of inputs,’’ Katambi said.

He warned individuals involved in the sale of counterfeit, expired or substandard agricultural inputs that stern action will be taken against anyone found compromising the integrity of the agricultural input supply chain.

Meanwhile, Ministry of Agriculture, Chief Agricultural Economist Nicholus Mainza said the team was in the province for two days working visit to orient and sensitise the Agro dealers on the implementation of the E-voucher for the 2026/2027 farming season.

Dr Mainza said the orientation will also include ethical values for extension officers as they offer a service to farmers and the general public at large.

Dr Mainza disclosed that fake seed, fertiliser and crop protection chemicals threaten national food security and farmer productivity and called on stakeholders to report any irregularities to relevant authorities.

He reaffirmed the government’s commitment to supporting farmers, safeguarding food security and creating an enabling environment where agriculture becomes a viable and profitable business for all Zambians.

World.title: Madagascar: One of the Most Important Places for Life on Earth - Madagascar
World.content:
guest column

Antananarivo — Has a chance to lead the world in conservation, and species protection, and we must not waste It.

Over 150,000 of the island's species exist nowhere else, including its famous lemurs. Its forests hold species still to be described for science. If Madagascar succeeds in protecting nature, the world keeps a living library of evolution, culture and possibility. If it fails, we lose ecological treasures forever.

If the effort to preserve a living library of evolution fails, we lose ecological treasures forever.

For years, those of us who care about Madagascar have known two things: 1) the country is almost unimaginably rich in biodiversity, and 2) conservation efforts have been beset by delay and instability.

That is why this moment matters. Madagascar has a real opportunity to reclaim its role as a global conservation leader. We should not downplay that. We should recognize it, support it and move quickly.

In the early 2000s, Madagascar seemed poised to show the world that conservation could protect natural heritage while improving the lives of people who depend on it. The government made an ambitious commitment to safeguard 10 percent of its land and territorial waters.

Protect natural heritage while improving lives.

There were challenges, of course. Conservation is never simple, especially in a country where rural communities under economic hardship rely on forests as their main source of fuel, food, land and income. But there was momentum, and there was a sense among conservationists that Madagascar could lead.

Then came political crisis. In 2009, the government was swept from power, and conservation entered a long and damaging period of uncertainty. Illegal rosewood harvesting surged. Deforestation climbed. Projects stalled. The trust and continuity between government and communities required for lasting protection were shaken.

Madagascar's parks and protected areas were caught in that instability. Local communities, conservation organizations and committed individuals in government continued to work, often with extraordinary persistence, but national progress was harder than it should have been.

Finally, a new administration made a clear commitment to 30x30, the global goal to protect 30 percent of land and sea by 2030, and this pledge has endured a transition to the current administration. In its first months, the administration moved quickly to unlock long-stalled protected area designations, including 21 new temporary protected areas covering over three million acres. In March 2026, 50 scientists, most of them Malagasy, from seven specialized fields completed the first full reprioritization of the country's conservation map since 1995, identifying roughly 44 million acres of priority land.

Rainforest Trust Ivohiboro, an isolated sub-humid mountain forest in Madagascar.

This effor is rooted in Madagascar's own institutions, science and communities.

Long-delayed designations are now moving because this effort is rooted in Madagascar's own institutions, science and communities — strong enough to carry forward no matter who governs. For a country of such global biological importance, this is not a bureaucratic footnote. It is a turning point.

Protected areas only endure when they are more than lines on a map. They need legal recognition, long-term financing, effective management and above all local support. They need to create tangible benefits for communities: secure rights, sustainable livelihoods, better fisheries, climate resilience, employment, education and pride. Protection endures when communities are recognized as both stewards and beneficiaries.

Madagascar has a plan. It has political will. It has local conservation leaders who have continued the work through years of difficulty. It has communities already proving that protection and prosperity can move together.

Madagascar needs partnerships at the scale of this opportunity.

What Madagascar needs now is partnership at the scale of this opportunity.

That means funding the full life cycle of conservation: designation, management, enforcement, restoration, monitoring and community livelihoods. It means investing in Malagasy institutions and local organizations, not just international intermediaries. It means moving quickly enough to overcome the pace of forest loss, but carefully enough to ensure that protection is durable, equitable and trusted.

Madagascar once inspired the world with its conservation ambition. Then it endured years in which that promise was delayed and, in many places, undermined. Now the country has a chance to lead again by building a 30x30 strategy grounded in science, community prosperity and national leadership.

There are moments when political will, community leadership and scientific urgency align. When they do, the conservation community has to be ready. This is one of those moments.

We should meet Madagascar's leadership with investment. We should meet it with trust. And we should meet it now.

Because if Madagascar succeeds, it will prove that even after years of setbacks, a country can choose a different future.

Liva Raharijaona is 30x30 Coordinator at Madagascar's Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development. James Deutsch is CEO of Rainforest Trust

World.title: Africa: A Senegalese Factory Proves Africa Can Spin Its Own Cotton - Can It Find the Money to Keep Going?
World.content:
Domitexka's mill in Kaolack has the markets, the know-how and the partnerships to compete globally. What it still needs — like nearly every manufacturer on the continent — is patient capital.

The thread comes off the spool white, clean and taut. Inside the Domitexka workshop in Kaolack, the machines are running: raw Senegalese cotton goes in one end, spun yarn comes out the other. That, in substance, is the point Mass Thiam is trying to prove — that Senegal, and Africa more broadly, can do this.

What has proven harder to overcome is what happens when the financing runs out. Industrial machinery slows to a crawl without capital behind it, and across Africa, financing suited to manufacturers' needs remains scarce.

Domitexka Saloum, an industrial spinning mill in Kaolack, sits at the heart of one of West Africa's cotton belts. It once ran for years before an abrupt shutdown, starved of capital. Serigne Mboup — chief executive of Groupe CCBM, president of the Kaolack Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Agriculture, and the city's mayor — owns the mill and is the project's promoter. Thiam joined as general administrator, tasked with turning that ambition into a functioning business. He has spent his tenure fighting on two fronts: rebuilding the plant, and persuading financiers it has a future.

That second fight extends well beyond Domitexka. It is the fight of an entire industry.

The Number That Says It All: 5 Percent

Senegal processes only about 5 percent of the cotton it harvests. The rest leaves the country raw, crosses an ocean, becomes yarn and then fabric and then clothing — and sometimes returns, to stalls in Dakar's Sandaga market, priced ten, twenty, even thirty times higher than the raw fiber that left.

Thiam cites the figure often, and not as a statistic. "Senegal processes less than five percent of its cotton," he said — a scandal, in his telling, measured precisely against what it costs the country.

The global backdrop has rarely looked more favorable. Asian supply chains have been under strain since the pandemic, and production costs are climbing in Bangladesh, Vietnam and China. New European rules — the end, as of July 1, of the customs exemption for parcels under 150 euros, plus a coming Digital Product Passport and an EU ecodesign regulation — are pushing brands toward textiles that are traceable, nearby and clean. Africa fits that brief.

Domitexka Farmers gathered around a large cotton crop in a field.

"We see a factory with potential in a world that's shifting," Thiam said. "But the traditional banker mainly sees an industrial company that has struggled in the past."

That gap — between what the plant can produce and what a bank is willing to fund — is the crux of the problem.

"We see a factory with potential in a world that's shifting. But the traditional banker mainly sees an industrial company that has struggled in the past." — Mass Thiam, General Administrator, Domitexka Saloum

Manufacturing Runs Long. Bank Loans Run Short.

Textile manufacturing is a capital-heavy business. Carding machines, spinning frames and looms cost heavily upfront and depreciate over ten to fifteen years. Scaling up, hiring, training a workforce and winning export contracts all take time.

Commercial banks think on a shorter clock — three years, five at the outside. From Kaolack to Lagos, Bamako to Abidjan, manufacturers hear the same answer: the project runs too long, the sector is too risky, the collateral falls short.

"The maturities we need are seven to twelve years," Thiam said — roughly the time an African spinning mill needs to pay off its investments, stabilize its balance sheet, reach full capacity and start turning a net profit.

The math compounds from there. Gross margins in the industry run 25 to 35 percent, but local bank interest rates as high as 12 percent eat deeply into that cushion, and collateral requirements often exceed the loan itself. It is a combination that kills off industrial projects across the continent before they get the chance to prove themselves.

Domitexka Bobbins of cotton yarn in a spinning mill. This stage of processing marks the transition from raw cotton to a product with higher added value, which is essential to the development of a competitive textile industry in Africa.

"The financing problem has always been there, it's still there, and it will probably still be there for several more months," Thiam said — less a complaint than a plain reading of the numbers.

THE ARITHMETIC OF AFRICA'S COTTON PARADOX

Africa grows roughly 10% of the world's cotton, including much of its longest, finest fiber

Less than 5% of that cotton is processed on the continent before export

Finished garments sell for 30 to 50 times the price of the raw fiber

Gross margins in African textile manufacturing: 25% – 35%

Local bank lending rates facing manufacturers: up to 12%

Loan maturities Domitexka says the industry needs: 7 – 12 years

Domitexka's fundraising target: €50 million over 10 years

A Working Mill, Not a Pitch Deck

What sets Domitexka apart is that its story isn't hypothetical. The mill is operating — cotton in, yarn out.

Thiam inherited a foundation that predates him: a €5.7 million grant from KfW, Germany's development bank, awarded under its Invest for Employment initiative on the strength of Mboup's original project. That grant funded the restart of production and let Thiam demonstrate the mill could actually run.

Domitexka has since built a strategic partnership with Aïssa Dione Tissus, one of West Africa's most respected textile houses — a commercial, capital and creative alliance that points toward a fully integrated supply chain: Senegalese cotton spun into Senegalese thread woven into Senegalese fabric, without the material ever leaving the continent. Separately, the company is in talks with the International Finance Corporation, the World Bank's private-lending arm, about backing its next phase of growth.

"Right now, we're in an initial relaunch phase," Thiam said. "But tomorrow, we want to build new production lines. Our goal is to raise close to fifty million euros to improve our productivity and reposition the West African textile industry on the international stage."

The plan is specific: modernize equipment, bring in new investors to strengthen governance, form technical partnerships to lift productivity, and meet the traceability standards European and American buyers now demand.

Domitexka After harvesting and ginning, the cotton is spun into long, continuous fibers for weaving. Strengthening these industrial capabilities in Africa would make it possible to retain a larger share of the value generated by the sector.

"Our goal is to raise close to fifty million euros to improve our productivity and reposition the West African textile industry on the international stage." — Mass Thiam

Looking to Asia's Playbook

Thiam returns often to a comparison: Bangladesh in the 1980s, Vietnam in the 1990s, Turkey, which built a textile export industry now worth more than $20 billion a year over two decades.

None of those countries started with structural advantages greater than Africa's today, he argues. What they had was what he calls "patient capital" — long-term financing, manageable interest rates, and institutions willing to underwrite manufacturing's slow-build economics.

"Africa doesn't lack potential — it lacks capital," Thiam said.

The claim holds up. West Africa grows some of the finest cotton in the world: long, clean, hand-picked fiber that commands a premium internationally. Mali's Better Cotton-certified output climbed from 34,000 tonnes in 2014 to more than 180,000 tonnes in 2025. Burkina Faso just logged its best harvest in years. The raw material is there. The labour is there. The market is shifting toward Africa, slowly but steadily.

What's missing is the financial bridge between the fiber and the finished garment.

"Africa doesn't lack potential — it lacks capital." — Mass Thiam, General Administrator, Domitexka Saloum

What Lenders Need to Rethink

Thiam isn't just airing grievances — he has a specific ask, backed by figures he has clearly rehearsed.

He wants financial instruments built for how manufacturing actually works: loans of seven to twelve years; interest rates that leave room for margin; pooled guarantee mechanisms that don't freeze up a company's balance sheet; equity investments that strengthen a firm's capital base without stripping founders of control; industrial bonds; dedicated funds.

MinistÃ¨re de l'Industrie et du Commerce From field to fabric: These fabrics illustrate the potential of textile industrialization in Africa. Each roll demonstrates the value created when cotton is processed locally rather than exported in its raw state.

"We need more optimized financing tools — bonds, equity stakes, or any other instrument that can bring in resources without weakening companies' balance sheets," he said.

It is not an appeal for charity, he argues, but for consistency. Development banks and private lenders routinely name African industrialization a priority in annual reports, ribbon-cutting speeches and summit declarations. Domitexka's case is a test of whether they will back that rhetoric with products manufacturers can actually use.

The regulatory tailwinds are real. The EU has scrapped its duty-free threshold for small parcels. Its ESPR sustainability rules will apply to the entire textile sector by 2027. A Digital Product Passport, due by 2030, will make every garment's origin, composition and environmental footprint traceable to the buyer. Together, the rules favor cotton that is non-GMO, hand-picked, certified and traceable — attributes West African producers already have.

The opportunity won't last indefinitely, though. Ethiopia, Morocco and Tanzania are all investing in their own textile infrastructure, and competition for European brands looking to diversify away from Asia is intensifying.

A Test Case for the Continent

Domitexka's story points to a larger pattern. For decades, Africa has exported what it produces and imported what it consumes: cotton leaves raw and returns as clothing; cocoa leaves as beans and returns as chocolate bars; crude oil leaves the ground and returns as refined fuel. The arrangement carries real economic, social and political costs, keeping the continent a supplier of raw materials rather than a creator of finished value.

Changing that won't happen through declarations at summits. It will happen mill by mill, spool by spool — when entrepreneurs like Thiam find, at a development bank's counter or in an investment fund's office, financing built to last the decade their industry actually needs.

In Kaolack, Domitexka's machines are running. The thread is white. It is waiting on the money.

World.title: Namibia: Windhoek Residents Brace for Higher Tariffs
World.content:
Thousands of Windhoek households are facing another financial blow after the City of Windhoek (CoW) confirmed last week an average 4% increase in municipal tariffs. Although minimal on paper, the increase means a larger share of household and business income will now be spent on basic services, risking weaker consumer spending, slower economic activity, and making it even harder for unemployed Namibians and young families to establish themselves.

While the city cites the measure as being necessitated by inflation, there is no doubt the single digit increase will add notable pressure to already constrained family budgets, which are reeling from higher borrowing costs, rising inflation and stubbornly high unemployment.

The CoW increases, which took effect retrospectively from 1 July 2026 and will first appear on municipal accounts on 31 July, apply to water, property rates and taxes, sewerage, waste management, refuse removal and fire brigade levies.

The CoW Council stated that the revised tariffs were approved under a Council Resolution and subsequently gazetted. According to the municipality, the increase is necessary to enable the city to continue maintaining essential infrastructure and delivering critical municipal services.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"We thank you for your continued support and understanding as we work together to build a sustainable Windhoek," the municipality stated.

However, while a 4% increase may appear modest on paper, economists warn that its cumulative effect could significantly deepen the financial strain on households already battling one of the country's toughest cost-of-living environments in years, thereby adding pressure to residents already stretched to breaking point.

Economist Abraham Eita believes the latest tariff adjustment cannot be viewed in isolation.

"The problem is not created by one factor only. It is the result of several pressures happening at the same time," he said.

In a recent opinion, Eita's warning comes as many homeowners are already paying more on mortgage repayments following recent interest rate increases, while inflation continues to erode household purchasing power.

Domestic inflation is currently hovering around 4.4%, while many workers have seen little or no corresponding increase in their salaries. For low-income earners, the mathematics are becoming increasingly unforgiving.

Namibia's minimum wage is approximately N$4 000 per month; however, transport costs alone can easily consume from N$700 to N$1000 monthly. Daily living expenses in Windhoek are estimated at between N$200 and N$450, meaning even the lower estimate amounts to roughly N$6 000 per month, which is well above the minimum wage before rent, school fees, medical expenses, or municipal accounts are considered.

"A 4% tariff increase may seem small on paper, but for a low-income household it can mean choosing between paying a municipal bill, buying enough food, or paying for transport to work," Eita explained, adding: "In economics, percentages can sometimes hide pain."

Meanwhile, Namibia continues to grapple with an unemployment rate of over 36%, with only about 867 000 people participating in the labour force out of a population exceeding three million. As a result, many households rely on a single income earner, informal trading or financial support from relatives.

As disposable income shrinks, economists warn that the impact extends beyond individual families. Higher municipal bills leave consumers with less money to spend in shops, restaurants and on discretionary purchases, putting further pressure on already struggling businesses.

"Families will now spend most of their income on survival... They will have little left to save, invest, educate their children properly or support small businesses. Businesses will also suffer because customers have less spending power," Eita stated.

Justifying the increase, the CoW argues that tariff adjustments are unavoidable if it is to maintain ageing infrastructure, expand services and ensure reliable water, sanitation and waste management.

However, the question increasingly asked by residents is whether consumers are receiving sufficient value for the steadily rising costs they are expected to absorb.

Municipal tariffs have risen regularly over the past decade as the CoW has sought to keep pace with escalating operating costs, bulk water and electricity price increases, infrastructure maintenance requirements and urban expansion. In recent years, annual adjustments have generally ranged from inflationary increases to above-inflation adjustments for specific services, steadily pushing up the fixed monthly cost of living for Windhoek households and businesses alike.

Critics argue that while residents are repeatedly being asked to pay more, the City itself has come under scrutiny over the remuneration packages paid to some of its senior executives. In recent years, public debate has intensified following disclosures that top municipal executives receive annual remuneration amounting to several million Namibian dollars when salaries, housing, vehicles and other employment benefits are considered. These exorbitant remuneration packages have repeatedly drawn criticism from residents and ratepayer groups, particularly as households have simultaneously faced tariff increases, weak economic growth and deteriorating disposable incomes.

Close 

The contrast has fuelled growing calls for restraint in executive remuneration, stronger financial accountability, and clearer evidence that additional revenue collected through tariffs is translating into tangible improvements in service delivery. Economists like Eita believe public acceptance of future increases will depend heavily on transparency.

"The City of Windhoek should communicate clearly how additional revenue will improve water supply, waste management, sanitation and emergency services," he said.

"People are more likely to accept higher charges when they can see better value."

He also cautioned that policymakers need to consider the cumulative burden being placed on consumers.

"When interest rates, municipal bills, food prices and transport costs rise together, the combined effect becomes too heavy for ordinary residents," Eita added.

World.title: South Africa: Ambassador Meyer Wants Trump Afrikaner Refugee Plan Stopped
World.content:
Roelf Meyer, South Africa's new ambassador to the U.S.

Donald Trump matters a lot to Mzansi and the rest of the world right now. Trump is changing the way America works - and how the world's most powerful country deals with the rest of the world.

We'll track what he does and connect the dots to your daily life.

Roelf Meyer wants Trump Afrikaner refugee plan stopped

South Africa's ambassador to the United States, Roelf Meyer, says he wants Donald Trump's Afrikaner refugee plan stopped.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Meyer said he is trying to get Trump's order cancelled. He said this would be difficult because Trump and the White House support it, Newsday reported.

Trump signed the order in February 2025. It allows Afrikaners who say they are being treated badly in South Africa to move to the US as refugees.

Trump has said South Africa is taking land and treating some people unfairly. The South African government says these claims are not true.

The first group of 59 Afrikaners arrived in the US in May 2025. Since then, many more people have applied.

Critics say white South Africans are still among the richest and most protected people in the country. They also say crime affects people of all races.

The Trump government says the plan will continue. The White House says Afrikaners are being attacked and forced off their land.

Meyer said it would be hard to change Trump's mind, but he would keep trying.

Trump says Iran strikes honour three dead US soldiers

US President Donald Trump says the latest American strikes hit Iran very hard.

He said the attacks were carried out in honour of three US soldiers killed in Jordan and Iraq.

The US military said it launched another wave of strikes across Iran for the ninth night in a row.

It said military sites and communication networks were targeted to reduce Iran's attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran said it responded with an attack in Syria and targeted US aircraft at an airport in Jordan. Kuwait also said it stopped Iranian drones.

Iranian media reported strikes in several cities. It also said two oil tankers exploded while trying to cross the strait, but the US disputed that claim.

Iran warned that the strait would remain unsafe for oil and gas ships while US attacks continued.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said America was still open to talks. But efforts to end the fighting have made little progress since Trump said a temporary agreement was over on 8 July.

Image source: File

Trump claims China targeted US election systems

US President Donald Trump has claimed that China tried to interfere in the 2020 election.

Trump made the claim during a speech from the White House, three months before the US midterm elections.

He said China had obtained 220 million voter files containing personal information. He claimed data from 18 states had been bought, stolen or hacked.

Trump did not provide evidence that China changed votes, hacked voting machines or affected the election result.

US intelligence previously found that China did not interfere in the 2020 election, which Trump lost to Joe Biden.

China also denied Trump's claims. Its embassy in Washington said Beijing had never interfered in US presidential elections.

Trump also said US voting machines were open to attacks from countries including China, Russia and Iran. He called for new voting rules requiring proof of citizenship and photo identification.

Democrats accused Trump of trying to make voters doubt the November elections. They said Americans should still trust the voting system and take part.

Image source: File

Trump gets his face on new US one dollar coin

The US Mint will soon begin making a new one dollar coin featuring President Donald Trump's face.

The coin will mark America's 250th birthday in 2026. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said it would be available later this year.

Trump's face appears beside the words "In God We Trust". The coin also includes the words "Liberty" and "1776 2026".

The other side shows an eagle holding arrows and olive branches. The coin is gold in colour but does not contain real gold.

The coin will be made in Philadelphia. It will be slightly bigger than a quarter and made from a metal called manganese brass.

Questions have been raised about whether putting a living president on US money is legal. US law says only dead people may appear on US currency and financial documents.

Bessent said the design was legal. He pointed to a coin made for President Calvin Coolidge while he was still alive.

Officials at the US Mint also said legal checks had been completed. They said the Trump coin did not break any laws.

Image source: File

Trump threatens to bomb Iran if talks do not restart

US President Donald Trump has threatened to bomb Iran's bridges and power plants unless it returns to talks.

Trump said the attacks could begin next week. His warning came as the US and Iran exchanged fire for a fourth straight day.

"We're going to knock out all their power plants. We're going to knock out all their bridges unless they get to the table and negotiate," Trump told Fox News.

Trump also restarted a US blockade of Iranian ports. A blockade uses military forces to stop ships from entering or leaving.

The US military said it struck dozens of Iranian military targets near the Strait of Hormuz. Iran said at least seven of its soldiers were killed.

Iran then fired missiles and drones at US targets in Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain. Kuwait and Bahrain said they stopped some of the attacks.

Trump dropped an earlier plan to charge a 20% fee on cargo moving through the Strait of Hormuz. He said Gulf countries would instead make large trade and investment deals with the US.

Iran said it would not return to talks because of US military attacks and the blockade. The renewed fighting has slowed shipping through the strait and pushed oil prices higher.

Image source: File

Trump tariff plan costs US billions in refunds

Donald Trump's tariff plan has forced the US government to pay back $81-billion to companies.

Tariffs are taxes placed on goods brought into a country. Trump has used them as a major part of his economic plan since returning to office last year.

But in February, the US Supreme Court ruled that many of Trump's extra tariffs were illegal. The government then had to return money to companies that had paid them.

Budget figures released on Monday show that $81-billion has been refunded since October 2025. Only $5-billion was refunded during the same period a year earlier.

A Treasury official said most of the increase came from the court ruling. Most refunds were paid in May and June.

Trump said tariffs would bring factories back to America, improve trade deals and help reduce government debt. But the US budget deficit has grown by 2% to $1.367-trillion.

The US also spent more than $1-trillion paying interest on its debt. Military spending rose by 5% because of the war in the Middle East.

Trump is still planning more tariffs. New taxes of between 10% and 12.5% could affect countries including the UK, Japan, India, Taiwan and China.

He has also threatened a 100% tariff on European countries that tax large US technology companies such as Apple, Google and Amazon.

Image source: File

Trump says US will destroy Iran if it tries to kill him

US President Donald Trump has warned Iran not to try to kill him. He said the United States would destroy large parts of Iran if there was an assassination attempt against him.

Trump said 1,000 US missiles were ready to hit Iran, with thousands more prepared to follow.

His warning came after mourners in Iran carried signs calling for the deaths of Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Trump also said talks with Iran would continue. But he said the ceasefire agreed in June was over.

The deal had called on both countries to stop fighting. Iran was also meant to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, an important route used to move oil and gas.

The US said it hit about 170 Iranian military targets this week. Iran then attacked US military bases in Bahrain and Kuwait.

Iran said it had followed the ceasefire deal. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accused the US of breaking it by bringing in new sanctions.

Image source: File

Trump gets Florida airport named after him

A Florida airport has officially been renamed President Donald J Trump International Airport.

The airport was previously called Palm Beach International Airport. New signs went up on Thursday, but officials said the full change would take several weeks.

Its three letter airport code will also change from PBI to DJT on 18 August.

Trump said on Truth Social that the new name was a great honour. He also promised that planned renovations would make the airport one of the best in the world.

A Boeing 757 owned by the Trump Organization was the first plane to arrive after the name change. The aircraft is known as Trump Force One.

Trump's son Eric was on board. He said nobody had done more for Florida and the United States than his father.

Eric said he would be proud to see the letters DJT on his boarding pass when using the airport.

The Trump family often uses the airport when visiting Trump's Mar a Lago home in West Palm Beach. A road between the airport and the estate was renamed Donald J Trump Boulevard in January.

Image source: File

Trump declares Iran ceasefire over

The United States has struck Iran for a second day in a row after Donald Trump declared that the interim peace deal ending the war was "over," less than a month after it was signed.

Iranian state media reported explosions on Wednesday night in the port city of Bandar Abbas, in Sirik, and in Bushehr province, home to Iran's nuclear power plant. "This is in retribution for yesterday's bombing of ships by Iran. If it happens again, it will get much worse!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The strikes came after three cargo ships were attacked while passing through the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, the most serious clash between the two sides since the ceasefire deal was signed on 17 June. The US also cancelled a waiver that had allowed Iran to keep exporting oil.

Iran hit back at US military bases in Bahrain and Kuwait for a second day running. Sirens sounded in Bahrain, home to the US Navy's 5th Fleet. Kuwait said it was shooting down incoming drones and missiles.

Speaking at the Nato summit in Turkey, Trump said the US would "probably hit Iran hard again tonight" and suggested America might "just finish the job." He accused Iran of "behaving very badly."

Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf was defiant. "The era of bullying and extortion is over. It leads nowhere. We don't fold," he wrote on X.

US senator Bernie Sanders criticised Trump's decision to restart the war. "Restarting his reckless war with Iran won't make America stronger. It will cost more lives and waste more taxpayer dollars," he said.

Oil prices jumped more than 5% to close to $80 a barrel after the news broke, and US stock markets fell.

The fresh strikes came as Iranians prepared to bury their former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed on the first day of the war, following a funeral procession that drew millions of mourners.

Image source: File

Trump says Ukraine war is close to ending

Donald Trump has said the war in Ukraine is "getting closer than people realise" to being resolved, after speaking to both Russian president Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky over the weekend.

"I think we're getting much closer than people realise. President Putin wants it to end. I will tell you that very strongly," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Monday.

Trump gave no specific reason for his optimism. Overnight, Russia fired missiles and drones at Kyiv and the surrounding region, killing at least 28 people. He said he had a "good call" with Putin on 4 July that lasted 85 minutes, according to a Kremlin aide.

Zelensky described his own call with Trump as "very good." He told the Financial Times that Trump seemed to be viewing the war differently after recent Ukrainian successes, including a drone campaign that has caused fuel shortages inside Russia. "President Trump wants to be where there's success," Zelensky said.

Trump is due to meet Zelensky on Wednesday at the Nato summit in Turkey, where the war will be a major topic. A US official said Trump is likely to speak to Putin again after that meeting.

In Moscow, a Kremlin spokesman said Russia's position on the war had not changed, despite Trump's comments. "President Trump has a fairly consistent stance," he said, denying any suggestion Trump had shifted his views.

The war has now lasted more than four years. Trump's latest optimism comes after past comments in which he pressured Zelensky to strike a deal with Russia quickly.

Image source: File

Trump made calls to Fifa to get a US player's World Cup ban lifted

Donald Trump personally called Fifa three times to help get a red card ban lifted for US striker Folarin Balogun, clearing him to play in Tuesday's last 16 match against Belgium.

Balogun was sent off during the US win over Bosnia and Herzegovina on Wednesday after stepping on an opponent's ankle. On Sunday, Fifa suddenly announced it was suspending the ban. Sources told the Guardian that Trump had been calling Fifa since Wednesday to push for the change.

Trump thanked the organisation on Truth Social. "Thank you to Fifa for doing what was right, and reversing a great injustice!" he wrote.

Belgium's football federation was furious. It called the decision "astonishing" and said it went against Fifa's own rules, which normally make a one-game ban automatic after a red card. The federation said it was "investigating all potential options."

Belgium's manager Rudi Garcia was blunt. "I didn't know that 5 July was equal to 1 April at Fifa," he said, comparing the decision to an April Fools' joke.

US players said they found out about the decision from social media while sitting on the team bus on their way to training. "My family probably sent me eight tweets," said defender Chris Richards. "Nobody told us ahead of time that this was happening."

Balogun has scored three goals in three matches so far at the tournament and is seen as key to the US reaching the World Cup quarter-finals for the first time since 2002.

Image source: File

Trump plays doctor in fake AI video curing celebrities who criticise him

Donald Trump has posted an AI-generated video showing himself as a doctor who claims to have cured celebrities of what he calls "Trump derangement syndrome," a made up illness used to describe people who criticise him.

The video, shared on Trump's social media account on Thursday, uses fake footage of stars including Whoopi Goldberg, Edward Norton, Julia Roberts and Robert De Niro pretending to thank him for treating them. A fake version of De Niro says: "I couldn't eat, I couldn't sleep, constantly angry. I made everyone miserable around me."

In the video Trump wears a white coat and stethoscope. "They were so far gone, I wasn't really sure," fake Trump says, before giving his cure. He tells people to "turn off fake news, say your prayers, and if you ever feel anxious, just have a Diet Coke like me."

One of the celebrities featured, Rosie O'Donnell, made clear the video was not real. "He's quite ill and getting worse daily," she said in a statement. "The 25th amendment exists for exactly this reason. Remove. Impeach. Convict."

This is not the first time Trump has used AI to target critics or boost his own image. He previously posted an image of himself as Jesus healing the sick, which he deleted after Christian commentators called it blasphemous. He has also portrayed himself as the pope and as a king on a fake magazine cover. In February he shared a racist video showing Barack and Michelle Obama as apes, which he deleted but did not apologise for.

A White House spokesperson defended the latest video, saying posting it was Trump's "right" and calling the fictional illness "a crippling disease that has unfortunately rotted the brains of many people." Officials did not say whether the celebrities featured had given permission for their likeness to be used.

Image source: File

Trump made billions from a Bible, a perfume and crypto coins

Donald Trump's official financial report for 2025 has just been released and it shows just how much money he made from putting his name on products while serving as president.

His merchandise business is booming. Trump earned $1.8-million from his coffee-table book, $208,000 from a Trump-branded Bible and $67,000 from branded trainers and fragrances, including a $249 perfume called Victory 47. Fans even spent $36,000 on a limited edition guitar with his signature on it.

Melania has her own product line too. The first lady earned $10.7-million from a documentary about her life made by Amazon, plus $6-million from selling digital tokens and $520,000 from her own book.

His crypto coin dwarfs everything else. Trump made $635-million in royalties from a meme coin he launched days before taking office, even though the coin has since dropped sharply in value. He made another $500-million from a crypto company started by his own sons.

Trump bought and sold shares 21,285 times in 2025, including buying up to $25-million worth of Nvidia stock just weeks after his administration struck a deal with the tech giant over its computer chips.

He still gets paid for old acting work. Trump receives more than $86,000 a year from two actors' union pensions, thanks to appearances in Home Alone 2 and The Apprentice.

His lawsuits against media companies paid off big. He made $86.5-million suing Meta, CBS, ABC, YouTube and Twitter owner Jack Dorsey, all linked to his accounts being suspended after the 6 January 2021 Capitol riot.

Image source: File

Trump made over $1 billion from crypto in 2025

Donald Trump made more than $1-billion last year from cryptocurrency deals, according to his official financial report, while the White House insists he is not profiting from being president.

The report shows he earned $635-million in royalties from a Trump meme coin he launched days before taking office, even though the coin has since dropped sharply in value. He also made more than $500-million from World Liberty Financial, a crypto company started by his own sons and the children of his special envoy Steve Witkoff.

This is far more than the roughly $600-million he made in 2024, before he was back in the White House.

The White House says there is nothing wrong with any of it. "Neither the president nor his family has ever engaged, or will ever engage, in conflicts of interest," said deputy press secretary Anna Kelly. She said Trump has proudly made America "the crypto capital of the world."

Not everyone agrees. Richard Painter, who served as the chief White House ethics lawyer under George W Bush, called the $1-billion figure "extraordinary." "Of course it's a conflict of interest," he said.

Trump once called Bitcoin a "scam" back in 2021. He changed his mind while running for president in 2024 and has spent his time back in office pushing to grow the crypto industry.

He also made money from real estate, including $122-million from his golf club in Doral, Florida, and $77-million from Mar-a-Lago. He earned millions more from Trump-branded watches, Bibles, trainers, fragrances and guitars.

Trump's estimated fortune has grown from $2.3-billion in 2024 to around $6-billion today, according to Forbes.

Image source: File

Trump orders petrol stations to cut prices

Donald Trump has told fuel retailers across the United States to drop their prices immediately, warning of "big problems" if they refuse.

"Gasoline retailers must get their prices down, immediately," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday. He told them to aim for around $2.50 a gallon and accused some retailers of illegal price gouging. "Drop your price for our great American people!" he wrote.

Trump took particular aim at California, calling on the state to lower its fuel taxes too. "Soon the tax will be higher than the product itself," he said. California governor Gavin Newsom, a frequent critic of Trump, has been pushing the state toward renewable energy and a carbon-neutral power grid within 20 years.

This is not the first time Trump has gone after fuel prices in recent weeks. Last week he said he had ordered an investigation into major oil companies, accusing them of not lowering prices at the pump even though the cost of oil itself had dropped sharply. "Customers are being gouged," he wrote, saying he had told the Department of Justice to look into it.

Petrol prices have surged since the war between the US, Israel and Iran began in late February, and Trump is facing growing criticism over the impact on ordinary Americans as midterm elections approach in November. He has repeatedly promised prices would "come down like a rock" once the war ends, though economists say the damage may last much longer than that.

Image source: File

Joe Biden calls Donald Trump 'a loser'

Joe Biden has called Donald Trump "a loser" in a speech at a Democratic party event in Maryland on Saturday.

Biden, 83, used his first major public address since leaving office to paint Trump as corrupt, vain and incompetent, pointing to a string of expensive projects in Washington that he said showed what kind of president Trump really was.

He listed Trump's demolition of the White House East Wing to build a ballroom, his attempt to put his name on the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, his plans for a giant triumphal arch, and the algae bloom that ruined his $14.7-million makeover of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool.

"Whoa!" Biden said after running through the list. "What a loser."

But Biden saved his sharpest words for what he called corruption on a scale never seen before in American history, pointing to a government contract for the reflecting pool that went to a Trump donor who lives near the president's private club in Florida.

Biden also attacked Trump over his relationship with Russia, his handling of the Nato alliance and the Iran war. "He has diminished our standing in the world more than any president in history," he said.

The speech came exactly two years after Biden's disastrous debate performance against Trump that led him to drop out of the 2024 race, paving the way for Trump to win a second term by beating Kamala Harris.

Image source: File

People started walking out on Trump in the middle of his own speech

Donald Trump was left red-faced on Wednesday when supporters began leaving while he was still talking at the Great American State Fair on the National Mall in Washington DC.

A large number of people in the crowd headed for the exits just as Trump started complaining about news organisations reporting on his falling approval ratings and shrinking follower numbers.

Trump used the event to repeat his well-known talking points about making America great ahead of the July 4 Independence Day celebrations. But the crowd was not exactly electric and the moment people started leaving while he was mid-speech became an instant talking point.

The event had been troubled from the start. Several musicians who were originally booked to perform pulled out because they did not want to be associated with what they saw as a political event. Trump ended up with military bands and his favourite singers Lee Greenwood and Christopher Macchio on stage instead.

Trump is going through one of the toughest stretches of his presidency. The Iran war has dragged on for nearly four months. Prices are at their highest in three years. And his approval rating has dropped to just 37% according to the latest polling.

Image source: File

Trump asks for $87 billion to pay for the Iran war

Donald Trump has asked Congress to approve $87-billion, mostly to cover the costs of the war against Iran, on the same day that some of his own Republican senators voted to restrict his war powers.

The bulk of the money, $67-billion, is for the military, including $21-billion to restock weapons used during the war and $17-billion for running costs. There is also $11-billion for US farmers and $1.4-billion to tackle an Ebola outbreak in Central Africa.

But the request is likely to face a tough fight in Congress. The Iran war is deeply unpopular with voters and midterm elections are just months away. On Tuesday, four Republican senators joined Democrats to pass a largely symbolic vote telling Trump to end the military action. It was the first time Congress had ever passed such a resolution against a sitting president.

Trump was furious. He called the four Republican senators "losers" on social media. At a closed-door lunch with Senate Republicans on Wednesday he reportedly had a shouting match with one of them, Bill Cassidy of Louisiana.

"I stood and said: you have not told the American people what is going on," Cassidy told journalists afterwards. "This was supposed to last four weeks. It has lasted four months. Our original objectives have not been achieved."

The war has now cost at least $29-billion according to Pentagon figures, though analysts say the true cost is likely much higher.

Image source: File

Trump will present the World Cup trophy at the final next month

Donald Trump will attend the World Cup final and help hand over the trophy to the winning team, Fifa president Gianni Infantino has confirmed.

"We will be together with the president enjoying the final and handing the trophy to the winner," Infantino told Fox News. The two men have become close friends since Trump took office.

The final takes place on 19 July at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. Trump has not yet attended a single game at the tournament, which started on 11 June across the United States, Canada and Mexico.

A White House official said Trump likes to "leave people watching" and has been too busy to attend a match so far.

Trump has previous form when it comes to trophy ceremonies. Last summer he handed the Club World Cup trophy to Chelsea captain Reece James at the same stadium but refused to leave the stage.

"They told me he was going to present the trophy and then exit, but he wanted to stay," James said.

Trump was also booed in New York recently when he became the first sitting US president to attend the NBA Finals.

Image source: File

Trump warns Iran 'he will do what he has to do' if they break peace deal

Donald Trump has warned Iran that he will act if the country does not stick to the peace agreement signed last week, telling reporters "I will do what I have to do."

Trump and Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian signed the deal more than three months after the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran. The agreement is meant to be a starting point for bigger talks on Iran's nuclear programme.

But the two sides are already telling different stories about what the deal actually means.

Trump said on Monday that billions of dollars in frozen Iranian money being released must be used to buy food from the United States. "All that money is going to go to our farmers," he said. But Iran's central bank governor said Tehran was under no obligation to buy food from America and could use the money to buy other goods too.

Trump also posted on social media saying Iran would agree to nuclear weapons inspections to ensure what he called "nuclear honesty."

The war between the US, Israel and Iran has killed thousands of people, displaced millions more and pushed up the cost of food, fuel and everyday goods around the world.

Image source: File

Trump says America should charge ships to use the world's key oil route

Donald Trump has said Iran will not be allowed to charge ships to pass through the Strait of Hormuz but suggested the United States might do so instead.

"There will be no tolls in the Hormuz Strait," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Saturday, before adding: "unless they are imposed by and for the United States of America." He said the US deserved the money as the "guardian angel" of the Middle East.

The peace deal signed just three days ago was already wobbling. Iran closed the strait again on Saturday, saying Israel had broken the terms of the agreement by continuing to bomb Lebanon. The US military said the strait was still open and denied Iran's claim.

Israel has killed dozens of people in Lebanon since the ceasefire was announced, which Iran says is a clear breach of the deal. Iran has said it will not start the 60-day countdown on the agreement until the US shows it is keeping its side of the bargain.

Despite all of this, new talks are now set to begin in Switzerland. An Iranian delegation led by its foreign minister and chief negotiator arrived on Saturday. JD Vance, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are heading there for the US side.

Before the war the strait was free to use for all ships. Nearly one fifth of the world's oil and gas passes through it.

Image source: File

The Iran peace deal is already falling apart

Peace talks between the US and Iran in Switzerland were called off on Friday, just two days after Donald Trump signed a deal to end the war, as fresh fighting broke out in Lebanon and threatened to blow up the agreement before the ink had dried.

JD Vance was supposed to fly to Switzerland to begin follow-up talks with Iran. His staff were already at the airbase and dozens of officials and journalists were waiting in Switzerland when the trip was suddenly cancelled.

The problem is Israel. Despite the peace deal requiring a stop to all fighting, Israel launched fresh airstrikes on south Lebanon that killed at least 16 people and wounded 33 more. Hezbollah fired back at Israeli forces with rockets.

Iran said it needed to see the US actually keeping its side of the deal before it would send anyone to talks. The US has lifted its blockade of Iranian ports, but the Strait of Hormuz is still quiet with very little oil traffic moving through it.

Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who approved the deal on Thursday, warned it would not be easy. "If the American side wants to be too demanding, we will not accept it," he said. He also said Trump had signed the deal "out of desperation."

Israel has refused to pull its forces out of south Lebanon, despite the deal requiring it to do so. Trump and Vance have both criticised Israel publicly over its continued attacks in Lebanon.

The deal gives both sides 60 days to work out a permanent agreement. Right now, that looks very difficult.

Image source: @JDVance

Trump ends the Iran war by signing a peace deal he says saved the world

Donald Trump has signed a deal to end the war with Iran after nearly four months of fighting that pushed up the price of food, fuel and everyday goods for people around the world.

Trump signed the agreement in France on Wednesday. Iran's president signed from Tehran. Both sides say they won.

The deal means ships can now pass through the Strait of Hormuz again. That is the stretch of water that carries one fifth of the world's oil. Iran had kept it mostly closed since the war started. Oil prices dropped sharply when the deal was announced, which should bring down fuel costs over time.

Iran will also get back billions of dollars that the US had frozen, and will be allowed to sell its oil again. A fund of $300-billion will be set up to help rebuild Iran, paid for by Gulf countries. Trump said the US would not be putting in a single cent.

In return, Iran agreed it would not build a nuclear weapon. It also agreed to stop supporting armed groups like Hezbollah in Lebanon. The deal covers Lebanon too, meaning Israel must stop its military operations there.

But Iran's top negotiator said the deal showed America had failed. Hezbollah called it a great victory for Iran. That is likely to anger some of Trump's own supporters who wanted a tougher deal.

Trump said he had no choice but to make a deal. "The alternative would be a worldwide depression," he said.

Image source: File

Five men planned to bomb Trump's White House UFC event

Five men have been charged with planning to blow up and open fire on government officials at Trump's UFC "Freedom 250" fight night at the White House last Sunday in what prosecutors are calling one of the most serious assassination plots in recent memory.

The men allegedly planned to fly drones packed with explosives over the packed White House event to force a panicked evacuation. Then, as officials and guests ran for their lives, snipers would open fire on what the plotters called "high value targets" in the fleeing crowd.

The FBI tracked them down and moved fast, arresting the five men across four states including Ohio, Missouri, Nebraska and California before a single shot was fired or a single drone launched.
