World.title: Baseless conspiracy theories about Argentina's defeat go viral and are debunked
World.content:
Baseless conspiracy theories about Argentina's defeat go viral and are debunked

21st Tuesday, July 2026 - 21:34 UTC Full article

The coach attributed the defeat to the opponent's performance: “We lost because they played better, it's good to acknowledge that.”

In the hours after Argentina's 1-0 defeat to Spain in the 2026 World Cup final, social media filled with posts claiming, without offering evidence, that the result was “fixed.” Fact-checkers and Argentina's own coach, Lionel Scaloni, moved to dismiss those versions.

The narratives, spread on X, TikTok, Facebook, and YouTube, attribute the loss to alleged pressures or hidden interests. Among the most repeated are a supposed FIFA-UEFA deal to crown Spain, an alleged “punishment” over the banner reading “Las Malvinas son argentinas” that players displayed after knocking out England, and purported threats to the footballers. None of those claims rested on documents, identifiable testimony, or formal complaints, as verification organizations such as Argentina's Chequeado and Spain's Maldita.es confirmed.

One of the most widely shared items was a video of Lionel Messi's team talk before the match, in which he is heard saying “let's forget everything,” a phrase some users read as a supposed sign of outside pressure. In its full context, the captain was urging his teammates to focus on the game.

Scaloni rejected the speculation when asked by reporters. “I don't look at social media, I don't know anything,” he said, dismissing both an internal squad conflict and a supposed surprise anti-doping test before the match. On the banner, he said FIFA had told them nothing. The coach attributed the defeat to the opponent's performance: “We lost because they played better, it's good to acknowledge that.” The course of the match supported that reading: Argentina did not have a shot on target across the 120 minutes. Spain's ambassador to Argentina, Joaquín María de Arístegui, also rejected the notion of a fix, attributing it to the champions' game plan.

The phenomenon was not new at this World Cup. During the tournament, opposing narratives circulated accusing FIFA of favoring Argentina through refereeing or VAR, which fact-checkers also found baseless. After the final, the story reversed.

Disinformation specialists explain that conspiracy theories tend to grow after emotionally charged events, because they offer simple explanations for complex facts. According to a report by Chequeado, Africa Check, and Full Fact, such narratives attribute events to the secret action of powerful groups and reinforce group identity by avoiding the need to review one's own performance. Major sporting events, which draw millions and stir intense emotions, provide fertile ground for their spread. Fact-checkers recommend being wary of extraordinary explanations without evidence and checking the source of information before sharing it.

World.title: US reacts to Ortega's announcement that Nicaragua will hold no more elections
World.content:
US reacts to Ortega's announcement that Nicaragua will hold no more elections

21st Tuesday, July 2026 - 21:23 UTC Full article

“Daniel Ortega's declaration that under his family's dictatorship Nicaragua will never again hold elections lays bare their true authoritarian nature,” Rubio said

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned on Tuesday that his country “will not stand idly by” after Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega announced that the country will no longer hold elections. In a State Department statement, Rubio called on the international community to “join forces” to respond to what he described as the Nicaraguan government's attacks on the democratic principles of the hemisphere.

Ortega made the announcement on Sunday, during the commemoration of the 47th anniversary of the 1979 Sandinista Revolution, in which he took part in the overthrow of the Anastasio Somoza dictatorship. “There won't be any more elections here for them to try to seize the government and power,” he said, in his first public appearance in two months. The 80-year-old president added that he would work with the National Assembly, which he controls, to pass laws barring opposition parties from reaching power through the ballot box. He did not specify how the measure would be formally implemented.

The announcement effectively cancels the elections scheduled for November 2027, after a constitutional reform approved in January 2025 extended the presidential term from five to six years and designated Ortega's wife, Rosario Murillo, as “co-president.” The two exercise control over nearly all branches of the state, including the armed forces, the police, and the judiciary.

“Daniel Ortega's declaration that under his family's dictatorship Nicaragua will never again hold elections lays bare their true authoritarian nature,” Rubio said in the statement, titled “A Call to Action.” The text added that the Ortega and Murillo government “cannot expect to maintain business as usual with other nations” while undermining the region's democratic foundations. Rubio, who has placed Latin America among his priorities, had already described the Nicaraguan government as a “dictatorship” in June.

The United States, which does not recognize Ortega's presidency, has imposed sanctions and visa restrictions on more than 2,350 Nicaraguan officials and their relatives in recent years. It is unclear whether Rubio's warning will be followed by new pressure measures.

The last election, in 2021, was deemed illegitimate by international observers and by Washington, after Ortega jailed the main opposition candidates; he then claimed about 76% of the vote. Since the 2018 crisis, in which a crackdown on protests left hundreds dead, much of Nicaragua's opposition is in exile or barred from office. In early July, UN experts denounced the mass revocation of lawyers' licenses in the country.

World.title: Conmebol presses FIFA for a 64-team 2030 World Cup and more matches in South America
World.content:
Conmebol presses FIFA for a 64-team 2030 World Cup and more matches in South America

21st Tuesday, July 2026 - 21:08 UTC Full article

The proposal, originally presented by Uruguay's Ignacio Alonso to the FIFA Council in March 2025 and taken up by Domínguez, faces strong opposition

The South American Football Confederation (Conmebol) has stepped up its pressure on FIFA for the 2030 World Cup to be played with 64 teams, which would allow Uruguay, Argentina, and Paraguay to host more matches than currently planned. A day after the 2026 World Cup final, won by Spain, the body's president, Alejandro Domínguez, treated the format as all but settled in a message on the social network X: “In 2030 the World Cup is coming to Uruguay, Argentina, and Paraguay,” he wrote, proposing to mark the centenary “with a 64-team competition.”

FIFA has not confirmed the expansion. Its president, Gianni Infantino, said the matter “will be examined and discussed in the relevant committees” once the 2026 tournament — the first with 48 teams, up from 32 in previous editions — concludes. A 64-team World Cup would mean 128 matches, double the format in place between 1998 and 2022. The final decision rests with the FIFA Council, made up of representatives of the six confederations.

The proposal, originally presented by Uruguay's Ignacio Alonso to the FIFA Council in March 2025 and taken up by Domínguez, faces strong opposition. The presidents of UEFA, Aleksander Čeferin, of Concacaf, Victor Montagliani, and of the Asian confederation, Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, came out against it. Čeferin called it “a bad idea,” and critics warn that a tournament of that size would weaken the quality of play, devalue the qualifiers, and overload the calendar. The 2030 World Cup will already be the most sprawling in history, split among six countries across three continents: the opening matches will be played in South America, marking the centenary of the tournament born in Montevideo in 1930, and the rest in Spain, Portugal, and Morocco.

For South America, the expansion carries a strong sporting incentive: it would guarantee direct qualification for all ten Conmebol nations, including Venezuela, the only one never to have played a World Cup. In Uruguay, the economic dimension is central. According to the weekly Búsqueda, Yamandú Orsi's government told the Uruguayan Football Association that the viability of public investment and possible international financing lines depends on the Centenario Stadium hosting more than one match.

Domínguez has made the demand a fixture of his public appearances. At Conmebol's congress in Quito in April, he placed a captain's armband on Infantino and invoked the centenary to request an exceptional 64-team format, in a staged gesture he closed by announcing South American backing for Infantino's reelection in 2027. The FIFA president, who has promoted larger tournaments during his tenure, initially supported the idea but later declined to comment.

World.title: Falklands Assembly congratulates Burnham and looks to continuity with London
World.content:
Falklands Assembly congratulates Burnham and looks to continuity with London

21st Tuesday, July 2026 - 21:01 UTC Full article

The Assembly reaffirmed the principle that, it said, has been and will remain the foundation of its bond with the United Kingdom

The Falklands Legislative Assembly congratulated the United Kingdom's new prime minister, Labour's Andy Burnham, and expressed confidence in the continuity of the relationship between the islands and London, in an official statement issued on Tuesday. The territory's legislative body said it looks forward to working with the new prime minister and his government, and to “continuing the close and productive relationship” between the two sides.

In the text, the Assembly's members also thanked Keir Starmer for his support of the islands during his tenure as prime minister. Starmer left office on Monday, replaced by Burnham after resigning the Labour Party leadership, without a general election.

The Assembly reaffirmed the principle that, it said, has been and will remain the foundation of its bond with the United Kingdom: the democratic wishes of the Falklands people. “We are confident that that principle will continue to guide the new government,” the statement said, also expressing the wish that Burnham have the opportunity to visit the archipelago during his term.

The statement comes at a moment of transition in London. Burnham's new government placed British foreign policy — including the position on the Falklands — in the hands of Chancellor Ed Miliband, appointed foreign secretary. Under the current arrangement, the United Kingdom retains responsibility for the territory's defense and foreign affairs, while the Assembly administers internal matters.

Successive British governments have maintained that the sovereignty of the islands is not open to discussion as long as their inhabitants wish to remain a British overseas territory, a position London reiterates at the United Nations. That principle rests on the 2013 referendum, in which, on a turnout above 90%, 1,513 of 1,517 voters chose to keep the current status.

Argentina, for its part, maintains its sovereignty claim over the archipelago, located about 300 kilometers off its coast, and has on various occasions called for reopening negotiations. President Javier Milei has reiterated that his country will seek to recover the islands through diplomacy.

The Assembly's statement follows a week of tension over the issue, after Argentine players displayed a banner about the Falklands following the World Cup semifinal against England, an episode that prompted a protest from the outgoing British government and FIFA's assessment of possible sanctions. The relationship between the islands and the United Kingdom now awaits the first signals from Burnham's government on South Atlantic policy.

World.title: Argentina joins FAO treaty against illegal fishing, tightening control in the South Atlantic
World.content:
Argentina joins FAO treaty against illegal fishing, tightening control in the South Atlantic

21st Tuesday, July 2026 - 20:18 UTC Full article

The area is cut across by the sovereignty dispute between Argentina and the United Kingdom over the Falklands

Argentina on July 17 enacted the law approving its accession to the Port State Measures Agreement (PSMA) of the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), a significant step for fisheries governance in the southwest Atlantic. The treaty, in force since 2016, is the only binding international instrument specifically designed to combat illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing.

The agreement seeks to prevent, deter, and eliminate such fishing by keeping the vessels involved from accessing ports and landing their catches, thereby blocking products of illicit origin from reaching national and international markets. Its more than one hundred parties — among them large-scale fleets such as those of the European Union and China — must apply strengthened controls, inspections, and data sharing, both to foreign-flagged vessels and to their own fleets.

The accession came days after Buenos Aires hosted a regional workshop marking the treaty's tenth anniversary, and follows Argentina's adoption in February of the International Maritime Organization's Cape Town Agreement on fishing-vessel safety. With this step, Argentina aligns with Chile and Uruguay, also parties to the PSMA, so that much of the Southern Cone coastline is now covered by the mechanism. According to The Pew Charitable Trusts, which promotes cooperation against illegal fishing in the region, coordination among these countries will enable joint implementation and make it harder for irregular operators to market illicit catches.

The southwest Atlantic is one of the world's most active fishing areas, with large distant-water fleets operating on the high seas at the edge of Argentina's exclusive economic zone. High-value species such as squid, hake, and shrimp are intensively targeted in the region.

The area is cut across by the sovereignty dispute between Argentina and the United Kingdom over the Falklands. Argentina does not recognize the fisheries conservation zone administered by the islands' government, and the two sides manage shared stocks separately, which has for years complicated coordinated regulation of activity in the South Atlantic. Accession to the PSMA concerns port control of foreign-flagged vessels and does not alter the parties' positions on sovereignty.

Argentina's accession was presented by its proponents as a signal of greater transparency and cooperation in the fishing sector, at a time when port states are seen as key actors in shutting illegal catches out of international trade.

World.title: Chile declares state of catastrophe in the north after storm leaves at least ten dead
World.content:
Chile declares state of catastrophe in the north after storm leaves at least ten dead

21st Tuesday, July 2026 - 17:59 UTC Full article

The weather front began on July 15 in the south of the country and moved north, where it hit the desert regions — areas where rainfall of this magnitude is uncommon

Chile's president, José Antonio Kast, declared on Monday a 30-day constitutional state of catastrophe in the Coquimbo region and the Huasco province, in the Atacama region, in response to the intense storm battering the country's north. According to the government's latest tally, the phenomenon has left at least ten people dead nationwide, four missing, and nearly 100,000 residents cut off by road closures. Authorities warned the toll could rise, as numerous areas remain unreachable.

“As the situation in the Coquimbo region and the Huasco province has grown more serious,” Kast said in announcing the measure, which allows the deployment of military personnel, restrictions on movement when necessary, and faster delivery of resources and assistance. The government mobilized the army for rescue operations.

The weather front began on July 15 in the south of the country and moved north, where it hit the desert regions of Coquimbo and Atacama with particular intensity — areas where rainfall of this magnitude is uncommon. Swollen rivers blocked the main access routes and left many towns isolated from one another. In Coquimbo, about 460 kilometers north of Santiago, flooding, mudslides, and power cuts also affected the drinking-water supply. In the town of Andacollo, more than 300 millimeters of rain fell in a single night.

The National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) recorded more than 1,100 homes destroyed or seriously damaged and about 2,200 people affected, along with more than 33,000 isolated in Atacama and Coquimbo. The Energy Ministry said around 150,000 people were without electricity. Classes were suspended in several regions.

“What normally falls in a month fell in an hour, which leads us to classify this event as abnormal and extreme rainfall,” said Deputy Interior Minister Máximo Pavez. Arnaldo Zúñiga, of Chile's Meteorological Directorate, said the country had not seen an episode of this kind in about two decades.

The storm comes during a season of extreme events in the region. In recent weeks, a double earthquake in Venezuela left thousands of casualties, and various parts of the Southern Cone have faced severe storms. Chilean authorities expect the rains to continue through the week, and are maintaining alerts and precautionary restrictions at dozens of ports, also affected by high seas and wind gusts of more than 100 kilometers per hour.

World.title: PM Andy Burnham’s first conversation was with President Trump, whom he invited to visit Manchester
World.content:
PM Andy Burnham’s first conversation was with President Trump, whom he invited to visit Manchester

21st Tuesday, July 2026 - 07:16 UTC Full article

The Prime Minister also hoped that he would be able to show the President what Manchester had to offer during a visit in the future.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke to the President of the United States, Donald Trump, shortly after taking office Monday afternoon, 20th July 2026. According to 10 Downing Street, the Prime Minister began by congratulating the President on a successful World Cup and agreed that England had an excellent tournament.

The Prime Minister also hoped that he would be able to show the President what Manchester had to offer during a visit in the future.

Setting out his vision as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, the Prime Minister said he would be focused on ensuring reindustrialization up and down the country to ensure good growth in every postcode.

The Prime Minister also underlined his commitment to defense and security and said ensuring the security of the UK and its Allies was at the top of his agenda.

The President then updated on the situation in the Middle East, and the Prime Minister outlined the UK’s commitment to securing the movement of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz to support global supply chains and drive down costs for businesses and families across the country. They concluded looking forward to speaking again soon.

The report from Washington said the newly appointed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and US President Donald Trump held a phone call immediately following Burnham's inauguration.

The conversation was described by Trump as “interesting” and going “very well,” and covered the long-standing UK-US alliance, trade, North Sea oil and gas, and stability in the Middle East.

Details of the call indicate that Burnham assured the US President of London's continued commitment to defense, explicitly confirming UK support for securing shipping lanes in the Strait of Hormuz.

Likewise on the North Sea Oil, and energy policy, Trump expressed strong interest in expanding oil drilling in the North Sea.

Finally Burnham used the introductory call to officially invite President Trump to visit Manchester, England, an offer Trump reportedly accepted. The visit may coincide with the 2027 G20 summit, which is rumored to be hosted in Manchester.

Other phone calls by PM Burnham on Monday afternoon included, Chancellor Merz. Germany; President Antonio Costa of the European Council; NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte; President of France, Emmanuel Macron; President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen, and Ukraine’ president Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

World.title: The Falklands, FIFA and the Future of the British Overseas Territories
World.content:
The Falklands, FIFA and the Future of the British Overseas Territories 21st Tuesday, July 2026 - 07:10 UTC Full article Members of the Argentine team held up a banner exclaiming ‘Las Malvinas son Argentinas’ (‘The Falklands are Argentine’). By Peter Clegg (*)

I have been researching the British Overseas Territories (BOTs) and their geopolitical relationships for over twenty years, and I cannot remember so much focus on them as there has been in recent days. The FIFA World Cup match between England and Argentina provoked heated discussions over the future of the Falkland Islands (or Malvinas if you are Argentine). Gibraltar has received significant media coverage with the removal of the border infrastructure with Spain. The Caricom Reparations Committee has called for the British Virgin Islands (BVI) to be decolonized by the UK, and new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will likely retain the government’s commitment to return the Chagos Islands to Mauritius. So, are we witnessing centrifugal forces that could fracture the BOTs’ relationship with the ‘UK family’? Let us start with the Falkland Islands. It is not unusual for the Falklands to be the source of heated debate when England play Argentina, but there has certainly been a lot of rhetorical exchanges. Before the game, Argentina’s vice-president, Victoria Villarruel, called England ‘usurping pirates’, which The Sun newspaper called ‘a hate-filled tirade’. Then, after Argentina’s win, members of the team held up a banner exclaiming ‘Las Malvinas son Argentinas’ (‘The Falklands are Argentine’). The response from the UK was swift, the government said: ‘The World Cup might not be ours, but the Falkland Islands definitely are’, while Conservative Party leader, Kemi Badenoch declared: ‘The Conservatives fought for them before; we will do so again if necessary’. And Nigel Farage, leader of Reform UK, called for the capacity of the Royal Navy to be boosted. So, what can be discerned from all of this? First, nothing will change in the foreseeable future, but arguably the extent of diplomatic support for UK sovereignty is fraying. The Trump administration has hinted a more sympathetic position towards Argentina’s claim, and it defended the Argentina team’s right to unfurl the banner, while since Brexit the European Union has used ‘Malvinas’ in official communiqués. However, there is not a clear view at the United Nations or in international courts in relation to who has the strongest territorial claim, and the view of Falkland Islanders themselves is important when it comes to self-determination. It is also worth remembering that the Falklands has over 60 nationalities living there and should no longer be considered as a ‘white British’ population. Second, although it is highly unlikely that there will a repeat of the 1982 military conflict, concerns have been raised over the UK’s capability to defend the Falklands, however, the UK government is confident defenses are adequate. Gibraltar was the focus of media attention on 15th July when the border infrastructure with Spain was removed—the last frontier fence in Western Europe. This was the culmination of protracted negotiations to avoid a hard border, which was a possibility after Brexit. The deal eliminates controls and customs checks at the border and gives Spain responsibility for Schengen controls at Gibraltar’s airport and port. In a related development, Spain removed Gibraltar from its blacklist of tax havens; Gibraltar had been on the list since 1991. Gibraltar Chief Minister Fabian Picardo said: ‘The frontier that has so often divided and constrained our region will now become a place of cooperation and shared opportunity’, while Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, stated that an ‘open wound’ was finally being closed. Commentary in sections of the UK’s right-wing media was highly critical. For example, Stephen Glover in the Daily Mail, claimed that Gibraltar ‘has virtually been handed to Spain’. Glover admitted that Brexit had posed a problem but then criticized the EU for behaving in a ‘bloody-minded way’. He also slated Picardo for going along with ‘this charade’. This illustrates two points: First, the widespread cognitive dissonance on the part of those who strongly argued for Brexit but can never bring themselves to admit the real challenges the decision caused and that pragmatic compromises are needed to resolve them. Second, the paternalist view towards Gibraltar—the local government was centrally involved in the negotiations and felt that on balance the deal was the right one. If UK politicians and commentators say they support the BOTs, they also need to accept the autonomy of the territories to make their own decisions. The removal of the border infrastructure will undoubtedly bring new challenges, but many opportunities—and it is this effective functional cooperation that is most important and may well lessen the centrality of formal sovereignty. Caribbean BOTs. Then there is the Caricom (Caribbean Community) Reparations Commission, which has recently called on the UK to ‘decolonize’ its remaining territories in the region—the Caribbean BOTs. The Commission focused particularly on the BVI. Sir Hilary Beckles, chair of the commission, argued: ‘We object to the fact that in the Virgin Islands, our people cannot make fundamental decisions because they have to consult with the British governor and consult with Downing Street to make decisions’. This is to an extent true, but the BVI has significant autonomy, though it has not always used that power in the best way (see for example, Commission of Inquiry Report). The focus on the BVI by the Commission coincides with the beginning of constitutional review talks between the territory and the UK. The House of Assembly of the Virgin Islands is asking for a significant reduction in the power of the Governor and greater devolved responsibilities to the local government. It will be interesting to see what is negotiated, but it is unlikely the BVI will get everything it wants and there is little appetite for independence. Thus, the Caricom Reparations Commission intervention is timely, but does not fully acknowledge the nuances of relations between the BVI (and other Caribbean BOTs) and the UK—that independence is not an option and while that remains the case the UK believes it should have certain powers to intervene, if necessary, to ensure its international obligations are upheld. Finally, there is the situation in the Chagos Islands, also known as the British Indian Ocean Territory. I have written previously on the issue, and the handover has been paused because of opposition from the Trump administration despite earlier support. This is because US agreement is needed due to the UK/US military base on Diego Garcia. There is recognition from the UK that there will be a delay, and this was recently illustrated by the renewal of an agreement with another BOT, St Helena—that any migrants arriving in the Chagos Islands will be sent to St Helena (St Helena will receive £9 million from the UK as part of the deal). Notwithstanding, it seems that Burnham will stick to the original agreement and push it through once the US is again supportive. The decision was criticized by many on the right but as has been the case throughout this saga there remains a failure to recognize the real international legal pressures that will lead to the return of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius. In conclusion, while recent events have generated an unusual degree of attention for the BOTs, it would be mistaken to view them as evidence of an imminent unravelling of the UK’s relationships with its remaining territories. One of the most important points is that the BOTs are too often discussed as though they constitute a single category with common interests and identical political aspirations. In reality, big differences exist between territories such as the Falkland Islands, Gibraltar, the BVI, and the Chagos Islands. These distinctions are not always recognized in public debate, yet such nuance is essential if recent developments are to be properly understood. There are undoubtedly pressures on UK relations with the BOTs, but few of these are entirely new. Questions of sovereignty, self-determination, constitutional reform, international law, and decolonization have shaped these ties for decades. Such pressures may have become more acute in the current geopolitical environment, but they are not fundamentally different in character. Indeed, the Chagos agreement is an attempt to address colonial legacies, any new constitutional settlement with the BVI is likely to mitigate similar concerns, and Gibraltar has largely resolved one of the most difficult practical consequences of Brexit. Arguably, the Labour government is achieving a considerable amount in this policy space. Nevertheless, because the BOTs are deeply connected to questions of history, empire, war, and national identity, they will continue to provoke strong opinions and intense political debate. (*) Peter Clegg is Professor of Politics and Head of Social Sciences at University Western England, UWE Bristol. He has written extensively on the political economy of the Caribbean and non-independent territories. Recent publications have focused on the Falkland Islands, the impact of Brexit, and COVID-19.

World.title: Semarnat halts Nayarit luxury beach development over environmental violations
World.content:
Mexico’s Environment Ministry has halted a luxury beach development in the Pacific coast state of Nayarit, marking the nation’s second major tourism project scrapped in recent months.

The Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat) said Monday it revoked a federal concession for the Las Cocinas beach project in Punta Mita after finding unauthorized construction and environmental violations by developer Cantiles de Mita, part of Grupo Dine.

The agency said a review confirmed “non-compliance” with concession terms, including works carried out within the federal maritime-terrestrial zone (Zofemat) without approval.

Zofemat is the strip of federal land, usually 20 meters wide, that runs along the nation’s seashore — walkable areas that must remain publicly accessible under Mexican law.

Developers can build there only if they obtain a concession from the federal government.

In a press release issued this week, Semarnat said it had “decided to rethink the project” with a focus on “environmental impacts” and “the protection of coastal ecosystems and free passage along the beach.”

Three months ago, the Interior Ministry (Segob) vowed to guarantee free public access to Las Cocinas, but Semarnat’s new move goes further by revoking the Zofemat concession.

The project was to include a 145-room hotel, more than 60 luxury residences and amenities on roughly 20 hectares, with a planned 2027 opening. It was to be part of Montage Hotels & Resorts, which operates Montage Los Cabos and other luxury properties.

Environmental concerns centered on Las Cocinas as a nesting site for leatherback, olive ridley and hawksbill turtles.

Protests by residents of Punta de Mita and nearby communities intensified in recent months, including clashes with police and allegations of arbitrary arrests. Punta de Mita is a coastal town in the municipality of Bahía de Banderas, Nayarit.

The luxury resort area of Punta Mita is part of the region, but the gated compound is legally and commercially run separately. Montage Punta Mita was to be within its boundaries.

Semarnat’s decision follows its May rejection of the “Perfect Day Mexico” megaproject on the southern Caribbean coast of Quintana Roo, which it said posed risks to reefs, mangroves and coastal ecosystems.

The private cruise-ship playground had been planned by Royal Caribbean near Mahahual, a town of fewer than 3,000 people known for its clear, warm waters and proximity to the Mesoamerican Reef.

The cruise-ship giant had touted the project as including more than 30 waterslides, the world’s longest “lazy river,” and roughly 12 eateries and 24 bars — including the Tipsy Sombrero Bar, a standalone cantina topped by the “world’s largest sombrero.”

With reports from La Jornada and Infobae

World.title: Imports hit by new tariffs are down 23%, with China posting the steepest losses
World.content:
Tariffs imposed on imports from countries with which Mexico does not have free trade agreements are having a significant effect, with China being the most impacted.

Even so, overall imports during the first five months of the year from Asian markets — those most directly affected by the new duties — rose notably.

The government reported on Monday that the new tariffs approved by Congress in December 2025 had reduced imports from the 1,463 tariff classifications included in the decree by 23.2% between January and May. These imports fell from US $15.383 billion in the same period of 2025 to US $11.808 billion this year.

China, the main supplier of the goods on which duties were imposed, suffered the most as its tariffed goods fell by 28.4%, down from US $10.099 billion to US $7.228 billion.

The impact also landed on other important Asian markets including Taiwan (down 32%), South Korea (down 22%), India (down 12.3%) and Thailand (down 6.3%).

The effect of the new tariffs is reflected in specific industrial sectors, most particularly the light vehicle industry.

In monetary terms, this sector saw a decrease of US $1.18 billion in import revenue, equivalent to 29.7% compared to the same period last year.

Auto parts also experienced a significant decline, with imports falling by 39.5%, while steel products saw a 30% drop and the footwear sector declined by 37.9%.

Meanwhile, the data released by the Undersecretariat of Foreign Trade of the Economy Ministry indicated that overall imports from Asia rose by 42.5%, up from US $108.97 billion during the first five months of 2025 to US $155.23 billion this year.

Taiwan stood out, its imports to Mexico increasing by 233.76% annually during the January-May period, up from US $10.77 billion in 2025 to US $35.94 billion this year.

This surge is attributable to the increased demand for Artificial Intelligence services, prompting Mexico to import more products such as data processing units (chips and semiconductors) from Taiwan.

Overall, purchases from Asian countries represented 49.85% of total imports. In contrast, imports from the Americas stood at 39.61%, nearly all of this total — representing US $112.6 billion — coming from the U.S. and Canada (92.2%).

As such, the growth rate of imports from Asia grew 8.5 times more during the January-May period than those from the American continent.

Still, the United States remains Mexico’s top trade partner, boasting a 34.32% share of total imports in the period from January to May, followed by China with 17.42% and Taiwan with 11.54%.

With reports from El Financiero, Vanguardia and El CEO

World.title: Mexican high schoolers win 5 medals at the prestigious International Mathematical Olympiad in China
World.content:
Mexican high school students won five medals at the 2026 edition of the extremely challenging International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO), with a special honor going to Andrea Sarahi Cascante Duarte of the state of Morelos, who won the Maryam Mirzakhani Award for having achieved the highest overall score among all the female participants in the Americas.

The five medals — all bronze — placed Mexico third in Ibero-America after Brazil and Peru, and down one position from last year’s competition. The country ranked 40th this year in the overall medal count among nearly 100 nations competing.

The students who won bronze medals were Takumi Higashida Martínez (from Mexico City), Juan Luis Manríquez Sequera (Baja California Sur), Sebastián Sotomayor Trujillo (Nuevo León), Javier Caram Quirós (Mexico City), and Iker Torres Terrazas (Chihuahua).

China, which hosted this year’s competition in Shanghai, leads the global ranking, followed by the United States, Russia, Singapore, and Vietnam.

The Mexican teenagers’ accomplishments were made possible by the Mexican Mathematics Olympiad (OMM), which congratulated the national delegation.

Guadalupe Russell Noriega, head of the OMM, told the newspaper La Jornada that the support of the private sector and the general public has allowed the national team’s continuous participation in the IMO since Mexico’s debut in the tournament in 1981. That Olympic community is made up of nearly 300 volunteers, including teachers and students, who contribute their talent and time to support the OMM’s activities.

Begun in Romania in 1959, the IMO has become a global benchmark for high school students, who face six highly challenging problems in individual written exams over two days.

About half of the competitors win a medal, with an approximate distribution of one gold medal for every two silver and three bronze.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Mexico announces 3 forums to debate social media, AI regulation for minors
World.content:
The federal government is set to hold three regional forums to canvass views on children’s use of social media and artificial intelligence tools and platforms ahead of drafting a legislative proposal to regulate these technologies.

The three forums, announced by President Claudia Sheinbaum at her Monday morning press conference, will be held in Nuevo León on Aug. 19, in Chiapas on Sept. 3 and in Guerrero on Sept. 17.

“We don’t want this to be a government idea imposed on society,” Sheinbaum said, referring to planned legislation to regulate the use of social media and AI by Mexico’s children and adolescents.

Rather, the aim is to build a “consensus” regarding the regulation of minors’ use of AI and “especially” social media sites, such as TikTok and Instagram, she said.

Earlier in the press conference, Education Minister Mario Delgado said that Sheinbaum had proposed an “urgent” debate on the “impact of technologies, social media and artificial intelligence on our lives” and especially on children’s lives.

“This has changed the way in which we relate to each other, communicate, learn and research,” he said.

“It’s an issue that, without doubt, concerns all mothers and fathers,” Delgado said before noting that more than 70% of Mexicans over six, and over 90% of adolescents, use the internet.

He said that the government has a responsibility to not just “guarantee access” to the internet, but also ensure the “safety” and “mental health” of users.

The government needs to establish “regulatory frameworks capable of protecting fundamental rights,” Delgado said.

The education minister said there is evidence that the “massive proliferation” of smartphones and “the expansion of certain dynamics on social media have aggravated the emotional fragility” of young people, creating “insecurity, anxiety and symptoms of depression.”

“The idea that is being proposed in this national debate is not that we need to turn back the clock to a time before [electronic] devices, social media and artificial intelligence, but rather how do we create healthier, less competitive and more supportive environments in our schools and outside them in order to strengthen a protective community for our sons and daughters?”

Delagado said earlier this year that the Mexican government was exploring the possibility of imposing age restrictions on the use of social media.

“The State has the responsibility for the guardianship and education of minors. And that’s why we should think about setting certain limits, because I don’t see any responsibility from [technology] companies to take charge of this,” he told the AFP news agency in March.

It is not yet known whether the government will seek to ban young people under a certain age from using social media as part of a legislative proposal that could be submitted to Congress later this year.

Deputy education minister: ‘We have to go to the communities, we have to speak to parents’

Delgado said there will be a “broad and deep” debate on the use of social media and AI by minors in Mexico.

Deputy Education Minister Ricardo Villanueva subsequently said that the Ministry of Public Education (SEP), on Sheinbaum’s instructions, initiated a study on young people’s use of new technologies a year ago.

Villanueva noted that countries around the world have regulated the use of cell phones in schools in different ways, while countries such as Australia and France have banned social media for children under the age of 16 in the former case and 15 in the latter.

“It has been identified and there have been court cases that have documented that infinite scrolling, autoplay and [social media] algorithms are designed to create addiction,” said the official, who noted that the use of cell phones at schools is already subject to regulations in 16 of Mexico’s 32 states.

Villanueva highlighted that the SEP has already held discussions on young people’s use of the internet in Mexico City and in Mexico’s northwest and central-west regions. He said that 20,000 people have participated in those discussions, before noting that three regional forums will be held on the topic during the next two months.

“We want everyone to participate, to give us their opinion,” Villanueva said.

“We have invited … all the higher education institutions, all the research centers, asking them to send their experts … in order to approach this from the perspectives of economics, law, psychology, all the academic disciplines in order to enrich the national debate,” he said.

Villanueva added that “the conversation about digital devices can’t remain only among specialists.”

“… We have to go to the communities, we have to speak with parents,” he said before announcing that the SEP is organizing a “National Week of Traditional Games” in September to promote offline activities.

Sheinbaum: ‘It’s not about regulating just for the sake of regulating’

Speaking after presentations from educational psychologist Cimenna Chao Rebolledo and UNESCO’s representative in Mexico, Andrés Morales Arciniegas, Sheinbaum said that the “excessive use” of social media has an impact on children’s development.

Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo informó que iniciaron formalmente las discusiones y debates sobre el uso de las redes sociales en las infancias, adolescencia y juventudes de México.

Aclaró que “no se trata de regular por regular” pic.twitter.com/JwYdOdbZbQ — Monica Garza (@monicagarzag) July 20, 2026

“If a girl or a boy takes a telephone at the age of three or two, her or his development will be very different from a girl or boy who only uses a phone at certain times or doesn’t use one at all,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the consultation process with experts, parents, teachers, young people and others should lead to “some scheme of regulation” on the use of social media by minors.

However, she stressed that the government’s aim was not to regulate “just for the sake of regulating,” but rather to protect young people from potential harm.

“It’s not about banning [social media use] just for the sake of banning. It’s not about what the president thinks and putting it in a law,” Sheinbaum said.

The aim of “these debates” and “this discussion” is to understand the impact of social media, and technology more broadly, on children and young people, she said.

Sheinbaum also said that in upcoming Monday morning press conferences, the government will present “scientific evidence” on young people’s use of social media.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: From the archive: The joys of furniture shopping at La Lagunilla market in Mexico City
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Andrea Fischer article — originally published in Sep. 2025 — is a perfect example, as it beautifully balances personal reminiscences with the historical legacy of some of Mexico City’s most important markets, while also pointing out the charms (and challenges) associated with visiting the iconic La Lagunilla market in Tepito.

I’ve had a very close relationship with Mexico City’s Historic Center ever since I was a child. From my first time at Mercado de Sonora, at the early age of 7, to learning how to ride a bike in Avenida Paseo de la Reforma, some of my dearest childhood memories were collected in the Cuauhtémoc borough.

When I was in middle school, my mother started teaching at Universidad del Claustro de Sor Juana, so I often accompanied her to work and took two-hour-long strolls to the Zócalo and back. On Sundays, after attending mass at some 17th-century Baroque church, my family never missed the chance to visit La Lagunilla market.

My father was rather reluctant to go, but he almost always gave in. Everyone falls for the mysterious charm of a market selling Bauhaus furniture and pieces by Rafael Coronel (potentially real, potentially fake) side-by-side, scattered on the street, eventually. But what exactly is La Lagunilla, and what can you find there?

What exactly is La Lagunilla market?

Present-day Mexico City was built on a lake — actually, on a set of five lakes. In pre-Columbian times, what is now known as the Valley of Mexico was divided into several ancient bodies of water: Texcoco, Chalco, Xochimilco, Xaltocan and Zumpango. Although “their boundaries were fluctuating and unstable,” notes the UNAM Institute of Historical Research, “they did not constitute a single body of water but rather distinct basins.” This is also why Mexico City is so prone to flooding during the rainy season.

La Lagunilla — or “little lake,” in Spanish — was a distinct, separate lake from the greater ones in the Valley of Mexico. That’s where she got her name, originally. Today, however, it could easily be described as the Mexican version of a flea market, or tianguis.

Tianguis and traditional Mexican markets have, indeed, been around for a long time, especially in the area. Archaeological remains show that the present-day Plaza de las Tres Culturas held one of the largest markets in Mesoamerica, dating back to 1337. La Lagunilla market, however, is not as ancient as the “little lake” after which it was named.

Underground ruins suggest La Lagunilla was established as a residential and working-class neighborhood around the 16th century. At that time, the area was “used to receive and unload canoes arriving at the giant and famous Tlatelolco market, just to the west (of the area).”

Once the Tlatelolco marketplace dissolved, merchants migrated to this place, right in the vicinity of their previous workplace. Impressively enough, La Lagunilla continued to receive merchant canoes and trajineras until the early 20th century. In the 1950s, however, the last lake was artificially dried up, and the ancient merchant families moved in to found their own residential neighborhood.

What can one find at La Lagunilla market?

There is no official area or square footage that defines La Lagunilla. In fact, there are parts where the barrio bravo of Tepito and the antiques market not only adjoin, but also merge and blend into one another.

However, what locals often refer to as Mercado de la Lagunilla is bordered by Avenida Paseo de la Reforma, República del Perú and Tenochtitlán (of course, Tenochtitlán) streets, in the Colonia Centro neighborhood of Mexico City. On a Sunday morning, one can easily take the Reforma route on a bike and get there in 30 to 40 minutes. One block east of the monument to José de San Martín, on Paseo de la Reforma, you’ll find the heart of this Sunday flea market.

La Lagunilla encompasses over 5,000 stands, per La Jornada, with roughly 17,000 people earning a living from the Sunday market. On a regular weekend, merchants in the area receive 100,000 clients from Mexico City and abroad. What exactly can one find at the Sunday market? Honestly, the sky’s the limit.

First edition books, lithographs allegedly signed by Leonora Carrington, LP records, Van Beuren desks and mid-century bedroom sets: all of this (and really, so much more) is available at La Lagunilla market. Everything and anything that screams antiquities is on sale. I even remember finding a Space Age dining room set, which my grandmother must have seen at a department store when that style was fashionable. You can also find Fender bass guitars and jukeboxes from the 1960s, if you’re lucky.

Is it safe to visit La Lagunilla market?

My mother used to say that even Mexico City natives are foreigners when it comes to Tepito and its neighboring areas. And it’s true. It is called barrio bravo for a reason, after all. It is also “common knowledge” that local merchants take care of their customers, especially on Sundays, when they can sell entire living room sets — or “authentic” Diego Rivera paintings — for 12,000 pesos on average.

There is no sugarcoating it: Tepito and the surrounding areas can be very dangerous. Although there has been a heavy tourism wave to the area in recent years, visitors should not arrive after dark. La Lagunilla market is really a sight to be seen, but try arriving before noon — to avoid the crowds — and leaving before dusk.

Also, try not to wear anything fancy. Sweatpants and a simple T-shirt will do. No jewelry, of course, and no iPhone 18 (or whatever this year’s model is). All of these warnings could suggest that the La Lagunilla market is not safe to visit.

This is not the case: again, merchants take care of their customers. However, to visit consciously and responsibly, avoid diving too deep into the Tepito area. This way, you’ll be able to focus on refurbishing your new CDMX apartment, or buying a magnificent Kodak Brownie camera that still works.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: MND Local: July community activities in San Miguel de Allende
World.content:
A housing nonprofit is building hope in rural areas, an arroyo mural project is coming together, the municipal government is offering free summer camps for kids and the 2027 writers’ conference program will soon be announced. Read on for a sample of the many community activities happening in and around San Miguel de Allende this month.

Casita Linda is building its 173rd rural home

A San Miguel nonprofit that builds homes in poor areas outside the city is now working on its 173rd project, said Louise Gilliam, president of Casita Linda. It’s in Alonso Yáñez, a small town about 30 miles southwest of San Miguel.

The homes all have three bedrooms so parents, boys and girls have their own rooms, she said, adding that they’re built by construction teams using sustainable materials, including specially designed concrete blocks that fit together like Legos.

“People call us a small Habitat for Humanity, but we don’t use wood,” Gilliam said.

Casita Linda was founded in 2001 to respond to the “really terrible conditions” people were living in outside of the city following a bad winter with lots of rain, she recalled.

“The houses that they live in are made from stuff they found, like sheet metal. They sleep on dirt floors,” Gilliam said.

How families qualify for homes

Rural families must meet several criteria to have a house built for them, she noted. These include having a maximum income of about US $600 per month, a deed to the property and children in school.

“The family has to contribute 100 hours, whether it’s the family themselves, their neighbors, whatever,” Gilliam added. “They have to be in the game.”

She said it’s amazing to see what happens to these families when they have a home with a door that locks and screens on the windows so bugs don’t come in and make the kids sick.

“When they have a house, there’s hope,” Gilliam said. “We’re trying to put an end to generational poverty. And the houses we build are so sustainable we’re hoping the children inherit the house.”

Casita Linda houses take about six weeks to build and cost about US $25,000 each. Gilliam said the organization doesn’t build without the funds in hand. The organization holds one annual fundraiser, which this year will have a Studio 54 theme and is scheduled for Oct. 6 at Agua Bendita in Atotonilco. More information can be found here.

Mural project next to the arroyo has begun

Painting began July 11 on a dozen large-scale murals along 90 meters of the Las Cachinches Arroyo just west of Calzada de la Aurora and across from Fábrica La Aurora.

The project, coordinated by Audubon de México, is transforming the previously neglected area into an open-air gallery celebrating the arroyo’s history, ecology and enduring presence.

The project was delayed for about a month due to a municipal permitting issue, but that has now been resolved, according to April Gaydos, president of Audubon de México. She said 18 talented local artists are contributing their work to the mural project and that the inauguration date will be coming soon.

More details on the Las Cachinches Arroyo mural project are available on the website.

Free local summer camps being offered this summer

San Miguel’s municipal government is sponsoring free summer camps starting this month and running through mid-August for children ages 5 to 12. These camps offer physical fitness and competitive sports, art, music and cooking workshops.

Depending on the activity, the venue will either be the CEDECOM facility near the Luciernaga mall or the Bosque Deportivo sports park fields and courts east of the city. The latter will offer soccer, basketball, taekwondo, handball and tennis, while the former will present the creative and recreational workshops.

Writers’ conference to announce its 2027 program

The San Miguel Writers’ Conference and Literary Festival plans to announce the program and keynote speakers for the 2027 event on Aug. 1. Scheduled for Feb. 10-14, 2027, at the Hotel Real de Minas, the next writers’ conference will be the 22nd annual and could beat the record 1,750 participants from 15 countries who attended the conference this year.

Along with the Aug. 1 announcement will be an opportunity to 

Cathy Siegner is an independent journalist based in San Miguel de Allende and Montana. She has journalism degrees from the University of Oregon and Northwestern University.

World.title: Azteca, unearthed: Google tool digs into the legendary stadium’s 65-year history
World.content:
Google and the historical archive ICA Foundation have launched an interactive project through the Google Earth platform that invites users to digitally explore Mexico’s legendary Estadio Azteca (now Banorte) from the 1960s to today.

The virtual tour allows you to explore the stands and other parts of the iconic stadium, also known as Mexico City Stadium for the duration of the 2026 FIFA Men’s World Cup.

It also includes information about the stadium’s construction, initial engineering challenges and its appearance throughout renovation works in the lead-up to the 2026 FIFA World Cup, where it became the first stadium in the world to host matches in three World Cup tournaments: 1970, 1986 and 2026.

“Mexico didn’t want to just put on a World Cup — we wanted to put on the best World Cup the world had ever seen,” Guillermo Canedo said upon his 1960 appointment as Mexican Football Federation president. “And for that we needed the best stadium the world had ever seen.”

Canedo broke ground in 1961 on the iconic 100,000-plus-seat stadium, budgeted at 95 million pesos (approximately US $7.6 million in 1961, or roughly $86 million in today’s economy). That figure eventually snowballed to over 200 million pesos due to a range of unforeseen challenges.

Due to the presence of extremely hard volcanic rock at the work site, the architect, Pedro Ramírez Vázquez, had to gather a group of 10 architects, 17 technicians, 35 engineers and 800 laborers to establish a surface on which the stadium could be built.

The team had to remove 180 million kg of rock from 64,000 square meters of land, which took almost one year and required a lot of dynamite.

Much of this is documented on the new Google platform alongside several defining moments in world sport’s history, including:

The “Game of the Century:” the legendary 1970 World Cup semifinal between Italy and West Germany.

The famous match between Mexico and Denmark at the unofficial 1971 Women’s World Cup, which attracted a record 110,000 spectators.

Argentine player Diego Maradona’s iconic “Hand of God” goal in the 1986 World Cup final against England.

“There’s just something very special about the Azteca,” Brazilian soccer legend Edson Arantes do Nascimento, better known as Pele, once said. “You need to be inside it, to feel it to understand. It’s unique.”

And now you can do just that, albeit on a virtual level.

With reports from López Dóriga Digital and EL PAÍS English

World.title: Mexico’s World Cup hero Julián Quiñones earns a top 10 spot in FIFA’s latest player ranking
World.content:
Julián Quiñones, the naturalized Mexican who scored the first goal of the 2026 World Cup and helped Mexico win its first four matches to reach the round of 16, has been ranked as the eighth-best player of the global tournament.

Quiñones started all five games for El Tri as a winger and found the net four times, tying a national team record for goals scored in a single World Cup tournament.

The honor he received came to light Monday when FIFA released its final Power Rankings of outfield players (non-goalies), with Golden Boot winner Kylian Mbappe of France finishing at No. 1, followed by England’s Jude Bellingham and Argentina’s Lionel Messi.

FIFA’s evaluation system rates each player with a score from 0 to 10 in three areas: attack, creativity and defense.

The other players in the Top 10 were:

4. Erling Haaland (Norway)

5. Ousmane Dembele (France)

6. Charles DeKetelaere (Belgium)

7. Vinicius Junior (Brazil)

9. Johan Manzambi (Switzerland)

10. Harry Kane (England)

The 29-year-old Quiñones was graded with 6.86 points in attack (8th overall), 6.66 in creativity and 5.22 in defense, figures that allowed him to finish above global stars such as Kane, Lamine Yamal of Spain and Michael Olise of France.

His defensive rating (Quiñones constantly tracked back to help El Tri recover possession) was key to his Top 10 place in the Power Rankings as it surpassed that of other star forwards including Mbappe (4.02), Messi (4.55), Dembele (4.68) and Vinicius Junior (4.66).

Quiñones was also ranked 29th in Fox Sports’ Top 50 Players from the 2026 World Cup, in which his performance was described as “one of the finest individual campaigns by a Mexican player on the sport’s biggest stage.”

Also joining Quiñones on the Fox Sports list were: 17-year-old midfielder Gilberto Mora, the youngest Mexican to play at a World Cup and the second-youngest player ever to start a World Cup knockout match; and winger Roberto Alvarado who led El Tri with three assists and ranked 10th overall in the creativity category of FIFA’s Power Ranking.

The four goals Quiñones scored place him in a tie atop Mexico’s all-time World Cup scoring list, even with Luis “El Matador” Hernández and Javier “Chicharito” Hernández.

With reports from FIFA, Nación 321 and Record

World.title: WEG Q2 Preview: Analysts See an 8% Profit Dip
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Net revenue estimate. Analysts project net revenue around R$ 9.97 billion (US$ 1.96 billion), a roughly 3% decline from a year earlier. —Net income forecast. Bradesco BBI sees net income falling 8% year-on-year to approximately R$ 1.47 billion (US$ 289 million). —Margin pressure. The EBITDA margin is expected to hover near 21%, squeezed by currency effects and factory expansion spending. —Release timing. WEG typically publishes second-quarter results in late July or early August, putting the report days away. —Share price context. Bank of America and Citi hold neutral ratings with target prices near R$ 50 (US$ 9.84), implying modest upside.

WEG, the Brazilian multinational that manufactures electric motors, generators, and transformers, is expected to report weaker second-quarter results within the next two weeks, according to estimates compiled from major financial institutions.

WEG manufactures electric motors and industrial equipment for global markets.

What WEG Makes and Why It Matters

WEG is one of Latin America’s largest industrial groups, producing everything from industrial electric motors and power transformers to automotive alternators and home-appliance components. Its equipment drives factory floors, wind turbines, transmission grids, and household appliances across more than 135 countries.

For Brazil’s export story, an electric motor maker carries outsized weight. WEG converts domestic engineering into high-value manufactured goods sold abroad, making it a bellwether for the country’s industrial competitiveness and a direct beneficiary—or victim—of currency swings.

To understand why a motor manufacturer matters so much, it helps to think of WEG as the hidden backbone inside other industries. When a mining company in Chile installs a conveyor belt, a water utility in the Middle East upgrades its pumps, or a wind farm in the United States raises new turbines, there is a good chance a WEG motor or transformer sits at the heart of that operation. That reach means the company’s quarterly numbers are not just a report card on one firm—they are a temperature check on global industrial investment.

The Numbers: What Analysts Are Previewing

Bradesco BBI forecasts net revenue of R$ 9.97 billion (US$ 1.96 billion), down roughly 3% from the same quarter in 2025. Safra and Citi publish similar top-line estimates, while BTG Pactual’s consensus sits slightly lower at R$ 9.8 billion (US$ 1.93 billion).

Net income is expected to land near R$ 1.47 billion (US$ 289 million), an 8% year-on-year decline. EBITDA should reach about R$ 2.1 billion (US$ 413 million), implying a margin around 21%, a touch below last year’s level.

For readers less familiar with Brazilian financial shorthand, EBITDA stands for earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization. It is a widely used gauge of a company’s operating profitability because it strips out costs that can vary heavily depending on accounting choices and debt structure. A 21% EBITDA margin means that for every R$ 100 of revenue, WEG keeps roughly R$ 21 as operating profit—a healthy level for a manufacturer, though the expected dip signals that costs are rising faster than sales right now.

Why WEG’s Results Are Under Pressure

A stronger Brazilian real is the main headwind. The exchange rate has hovered near R$ 5.05 per US dollar, reducing the local-currency value of revenue earned abroad by an estimated 3% to 5%.

WEG generates a large share of its sales outside Brazil, so a firmer real directly compresses reported top-line figures.

Costs tied to transformer factory expansion in Brazil are also eating into margins. While the new capacity should support future revenue growth, the near-term drag is showing up in analyst spreadsheets.

Slower domestic demand for industrial equipment adds a third layer of caution.

The currency effect deserves a closer look because it works in a way that can feel counterintuitive. WEG sells products in dollars, euros, and other foreign currencies, but it reports its financials in Brazilian reais. When the real gains strength against those currencies—as it has done recently—each dollar of foreign sales translates into fewer reais on the income statement. The underlying business may be perfectly healthy in local terms abroad, yet the reported revenue and profit shrink simply because of the exchange-rate math. That is why analysts and investors watch the real so closely when assessing Brazilian exporters.

The Bigger Picture: WEG’s Role in a Shifting Economy

WEG’s performance often mirrors broader trends in Latin America’s largest economy. When the real strengthens, Brazilian exporters across the board see their overseas earnings shrink when converted back to local currency, and WEG is no exception.

The company’s transformer expansion is a strategic bet on long-term electrification demand, both in Brazil and abroad. For foreign investors, this kind of capital expenditure signals confidence in future orders, even if it temporarily weighs on profitability and keeps the stock in a holding pattern.

That electrification trend is worth understanding on its own terms. Around the world, grids are being upgraded to handle renewable energy, data centers are multiplying, and industrial processes are switching from fossil fuels to electricity. Transformers are the critical link that steps voltage up for long-distance transmission and back down for safe use in factories and homes. By expanding its transformer capacity now, WEG is positioning itself to capture orders that may take years to materialize fully—a classic case of short-term pain for long-term gain.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For expats and foreign investors holding Brazilian assets, a weaker quarterly report from a blue-chip industrial name like WEG can reinforce caution about the country’s near-term growth story. Currency volatility remains a double-edged sword: a stronger real helps your purchasing power locally but can hurt the companies in your portfolio that depend on exports.

Analysts at Safra and Itaú BBA note that as transformer capacity comes online and if currency pressures ease, revenue growth could reaccelerate in the second half of 2026. That potential recovery makes the current dip worth watching for those considering entry points into Brazilian industrials.

What Comes Next for Investors

WEG has not yet confirmed the exact publication date, but the company historically releases second-quarter figures between July 30 and early August. That puts the report roughly ten days away from the current date of July 21, 2026.

Despite the cautious preview, some analysts see a progressive recovery later in the year. Bank of America and Citi maintain neutral ratings with target prices near R$ 50 (US$ 9.84), implying modest upside from current levels.

The market will be listening closely for any update on transformer orders and export demand during the earnings call.

Beyond the headline numbers, several open questions will shape how investors react. Will management signal that the currency headwind is easing, or could the real strengthen further? Are the new transformer lines already booking orders that will show up in the second half, or is the demand picture still uncertain? And how is WEG navigating the softer domestic market—through price adjustments, cost cuts, or a shift in sales mix toward export markets? The answers to those questions, rather than the raw profit figure alone, are likely to drive the stock’s next move.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does WEG manufacture?

WEG produces electric motors, generators, power transformers, automotive components such as alternators and starters, and motors for home appliances and HVAC systems. The company sells to more than 135 countries and is a key player in industrial electrification.

Why are WEG’s Q2 2026 earnings expected to decline?

Analysts point to a stronger Brazilian real reducing export revenue, costs tied to transformer factory expansion, and softer domestic demand for industrial equipment. The exchange rate near R$ 5.05 per US dollar has trimmed the local-currency value of overseas sales by an estimated 3% to 5%.

When will WEG publish its second-quarter 2026 results?

WEG has not confirmed the exact date, but based on historical patterns the report is expected between late July and early August 2026. Investors typically receive the full earnings release and a conference call with management shortly after publication.

World.title: Argentina’s Javier Milei Heads to Brazil for Trade, Not Lula
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts —Primary event Milei will headline a campaign rally for presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro in São Paulo on July 25. —Blocked visit A Supreme Court justice barred Milei from visiting former President Jair Bolsonaro, who remains under house arrest in Brasília. —No Lula meeting The agenda includes no bilateral talks with President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva or his ministers. —Trade mission Milei frames the trip as part of an outward-looking strategy to attract commerce and investment to Argentina. —Regional tour The Brazil stop precedes visits to Peru, Colombia, and Ecuador to meet conservative allies.

Javier Milei touches down in São Paulo on July 25 for what his team calls an investment and trade outreach mission, though the official agenda revolves around a single campaign rally for a key political ally.

Argentine President Javier Milei is a libertarian economist leading South America's second-largest economy.

A Campaign Stop With a Commercial Pitch

The Argentine president will headline an event backing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL), who is mounting a bid to unseat President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in next year’s general election.

Milei’s advisers insist the trip is not purely political. They describe it as one leg of an outward-looking tour designed to unlock more commerce and investment for Argentina’s struggling economy.

The rally is contingent on Flávio Bolsonaro’s formal anointment as the PL candidate at the party convention, a step that is scheduled for July 25 and would clear the way for the high-profile endorsement.

For foreign observers, the fusion of a campaign event with a trade mission reflects Milei’s unconventional diplomatic style, one that often blurs the line between statecraft and ideological alliance-building.

Why Javier Milei Is Betting on Brazil

Brazil remains Argentina’s largest trading partner, absorbing roughly 15 percent of its exports, from wheat and automobiles to natural gas.

Milei wants to deepen those commercial channels and has signaled he will use every foreign stop to pitch Argentina as a deregulated, investor-friendly destination.

Argentina’s economy has long relied on Brazilian demand for its manufactured goods and agricultural products, a relationship that becomes even more critical during periods of domestic recession.

By framing the São Paulo stop as a trade mission, Milei aims to reassure Brazilian business leaders that political drama will not derail the deep commercial interdependence between the two neighbors.

Mercosur Tensions Simmer in the Background

The trip highlights the awkward state of the Mercosur trade bloc, which also includes Uruguay and Paraguay. Milei has criticized the group’s protectionist rules and, as our reporting has shown, has repeatedly threatened to exit the bloc if necessary to pursue a free trade agreement with the United States.

Brazilian officials note that no Mercosur summit or formal negotiation session is scheduled during the visit, leaving the bloc’s reform debate for another day.

Mercosur has struggled for years to finalize a long-awaited trade agreement with the European Union, and Milei’s skepticism toward the bloc adds a new layer of uncertainty for investors watching the region.

For expats and companies operating across South America, any move to weaken Mercosur could reshape supply chains, customs procedures, and the ease of moving goods and personnel between member countries.

The Blocked Bolsonaro Visit and What Comes Next

As The Rio Times previously reported, Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes rejected Milei’s request to visit former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is confined to his Brasília home and barred from receiving political visitors.

The court ruling, issued on July 18, specifically prohibits visits of a “political-electoral nature” to the former president, who is already restricted to receiving only family, doctors, lawyers, and healthcare staff.

Milei had publicly stated his intention to greet Jair Bolsonaro personally, making the judicial block a symbolic setback that underscores the legal constraints surrounding Brazil’s former leader.

After São Paulo, Milei travels to Lima for Keiko Fujimori’s inauguration on July 28, then to Colombia in early August for Abelardo de la Espriella’s event, and finally to Ecuador to meet President Daniel Noboa, reinforcing his strategy of aligning with conservative leaders across the region.

What This Means for Expats and Investors

For foreign residents and investors in Argentina and Brazil, Milei’s trip signals both opportunity and political risk. His pro-market rhetoric may open doors for deregulation and foreign capital, but the absence of formal government-to-government talks leaves bilateral policy uncertain.

Brazilian companies with Argentine subsidiaries, and vice versa, should watch for any post-visit shifts in trade facilitation or regulatory tone, even if no agreements are signed this week.

The political polarization on display—Milei campaigning for Lula’s rival while ignoring Brasília—could also affect the mood in cross-border business forums and investor conferences in the months ahead.

The Broader Regional Picture

Milei’s multi-country tour reflects a deliberate effort to build a network of like-minded conservative leaders at a time when left-leaning governments still hold sway in several major Latin American economies.

By visiting Peru, Colombia, and Ecuador immediately after Brazil, Milei is stitching together a coalition that could influence regional policy debates on trade, security, and the future of multilateral blocs like Mercosur and the Pacific Alliance.

For tourists and short-term visitors, the political maneuvering is unlikely to disrupt travel plans, but those doing business across borders should monitor whether the ideological alignment translates into concrete bilateral deals down the line.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Javier Milei meeting President Lula during this trip?

No. The agenda contains no bilateral meeting with President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva or any Brazilian government minister. The visit is focused entirely on the campaign rally for Flávio Bolsonaro and Milei’s broader investment outreach.

Why was Milei barred from visiting Jair Bolsonaro?

A Brazilian Supreme Court ruling, issued by Justice Alexandre de Moraes on July 18, prohibits visits of a political-electoral nature to the former president. Jair Bolsonaro remains under house arrest in Brasília and is only allowed to receive family members, doctors, lawyers, and healthcare staff.

What is the main trade goal of Milei’s Brazil stop?

Milei aims to attract Brazilian investment and strengthen commercial ties by promoting Argentina as a deregulated, investor-friendly market. However, no formal trade talks or Mercosur negotiation sessions are scheduled during this visit, making the commercial pitch largely rhetorical for now.

World.title: French Firm Ships 1M Barrels of Venezuelan Crude Under US Waiver
World.content:
Venezuela · Business

Key Facts —Second cargo volume. Approximately 1 million barrels of Merey 16 heavy crude. —First cargo. 500,000 barrels shipped in June 2026. —US authorization. Operates under OFAC General License 50A, issued February 18, 2026. —Venezuelan partner. Joint operator with state-owned PDVSA in the Urdaneta Oeste field. —Production share. Maurel & Prom holds a 40% working interest, yielding roughly 9,000 barrels per day.

Maurel & Prom, the Paris-based oil explorer, is loading a second cargo of roughly 1 million barrels of Venezuelan crude at the end of July 2026, a small logistical event that signals a tectonic shift in Washington’s sanctions architecture.

Tankers transport unrefined petroleum from production sites to refineries around the world.
