World.title: Jamaica received more than 1,300 deportees in 2025, says PIOJ
World.content:
The majority of the deportees, also referred to as involuntary returned migrants (IRMs), came from the United States.

The survey also found that the total number of voluntary returned migrants (VRMs) stood at 852 in 2025, an increase of 52.1 per cent when compared with the 560 who returned home in 2024.

VRMs are individuals who choose to return to their home country or place of origin due to personal decisions, economic opportunities or family reasons.

Conversely, IRMs are those who are forcibly returned or repatriated to their country of origin due to legal reasons such as immigration violations or criminal activities.

In the meantime, the number of Commonwealth Citizens who migrated to Jamaica in 2025 decreased by 3.8 per cent to 3,491 from 3,630 in 2024.

The PIOJ said there was also an increase in the number of aliens registered in 2025, with the figure jumping to 11,029 when compared to the 2024 figure, which stood at 10,146, an 8.7 per cent increase.

The planning institute said that at 49.0 per cent, Asians accounted for the largest share of individuals who requested extension of stay beyond six months, followed by Caribbean nationals at 19.4 per cent, and Africans at 11.4 per cent.

World.title: Zelenskyy fires top army commander amid nationwide protests
World.content:
"We will jointly determine an updated strategy of our defense [and] steps to continue the reform of the corps system, to fulfill the supply requests of combat commanders," Zelenskyy said in an address to the nation on Tuesday evening.

He also expressed gratitude to Syrskyi for previous successful operations in 2022 in Kyiv and Kharkiv and the 2024 incursion into Russia's Kursk region.

Joint Forces Commander Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi will become the Ukrainian Army's new commander-in-chief, Zelenskyy said in his speech.

Drapatyi is an experienced field commander who successfully organized the protection of Kharkiv in 2024 from a Russian counteroffensive. He was among the first of Ukraine's top commanders to openly support Fedorov last week.

Ukraine has seen nationwide protests since Zelenskyy ousted Fedorov, and it's far from certain that Syrskyi's ouster will suffice to quell them.

Fedorov has refused to take any post besides his old job as defense minister, two officials familiar with the talks told POLITICO. It's not clear whether he has accepted Zelenskyy's latest offer to return to government.

He congratulated Drapatyi, however, describing him as a "breath of fresh air." He also called Syrskyi to thank him for his successes in Kyiv and Kharkiv, calling them now "part of history."

"But we need to move even faster and write new chapters, correcting all previous mistakes," Fedorov said.

World.title: Canada joins British-Italian-Japanese fighter jet project
World.content:
“My focus is on maximizing our deterrence and ensuring that should deterrence fail, we're ready to fight and win alongside allies,” Defence Secretary Streeting said alongside his counterparts from Italy, Japan and Canada near Buckingham Palace as they announced Ottawa’s observer role.

The Global Combat Air Programme means “reindustrialization and building back up our production capacity, so we can give our armed forces the kit they need, as well as building and buying British, so that we deliver good jobs in communities in every part of our country,” Streeting said.

On the steps of Downing Street on Monday, Burnham — who took over from Keir Starmer this week — promised that “reindustrializing Britain” will be a key focus as PM. “We are going to honor our commitments on defense — and use that investment to transform people's lives,” Burnham said in a statement on the fighter jet project.

The British government earmarked £8.6 billion for the jet over the next four years in its Defence Investment Plan.

The sixth-gen fighter jet already supports 4,500 jobs in the U.K. at about 600 different firms in the supply chain throughout the country.

As the first observer nation to join the project, “Canada will gain direct insight and privileged access into GCAP, including capability development, industrial collaboration, and long-term delivery plans,” Streeting said. While there is “no commitment” for Canada to buy the jet, he added later, it will set a pathway for discussions with Canada about its aerospace and manufacturing base contributing to the project.

World.title: Jordan Bardella to address Nigel Farage’s Reform UK conference
World.content:
Bardella is a political star in France, whose electoral appeal is expected to form a key part of party leader Marine Le Pen’s strategy as she vies for the French presidency in 2027.

He met Farage in December last year and told the BBC he thought the “extremely resilient” Reform UK chief would be Britain’s next prime minister.

“I look forward to discussing how France and Britain can co-operate to finally stop the boats once and for all,” Farage added on Tuesday.

The volume of small boats crossing the English Channel from France has long been a contentious debate in British politics, with parties largely agreeing the number must be reduced.

The National Rally president has backed greater police cooperation between London and Paris, but wishes to return migrants to “countries of origin” rather than the French coast.

The Spectator first reported Bardella’s upcoming appearance, which follows other right-wing political figures addressing the conference in previous years. Former Finnish Deputy Prime Minister Timo Soini spoke to delegates in 2024 while the Reform Party of Canada’s founder Preston Manning gave a speech in 2025.

Farage is currently fighting a by-election in Clacton, a seaside town on the Essex coast which he represented for two years in parliament, after facing scrutiny over his financial arrangements. The contest will be held on Aug. 13, though no mainstream parties are standing against him.

National Rally did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.

World.title: Natural gas prices surge as violence in Middle East flares again
World.content:
A digital display shows the price of petrol at an Aral petrol station in Berlin on July 19, 2026. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images

Traders fear that they’re going to need to permanently price in instability in the Strait of Hormuz as shortages loom and Asian demand heats up.

BRUSSELS — European natural gas prices shot to a four-month high as renewed violence around the Strait of Hormuz triggered concerns about the feasibility of transporting energy through the world’s most vital energy chokepoint.

The benchmark European natural gas price — known as the Dutch TTF — briefly crossed €60 per megawatt-hour on Monday, the highest level since mid-March, and settled at €59 per megawatt-hour on Tuesday after the United States launched a tenth consecutive night of strikes against Iran. Tehran responded by targeting U.S. allies in the region and tankers in the Persian Gulf.

Before a ceasefire was struck in June, gas prices had consistently stayed below €50 per megawatt-hour, with traders wary of placing big bets during a war that had become impossible to predict.

World.title: French environment minister to resign after passage of controversial farm bill
World.content:
Barbut was against the pesticide and water storage proposals, both of which were added late in the legislative process to ensure the bill’s passage in the conservative-majority Senate. She made her opposition clear over the weekend in an interview published by Sunday newspaper La Tribune Dimanche.

“This government bill, which was intended to address an emergency situation facing our farmers, has — since the Senate’s amendments — significantly altered the policy governing the allocation of water resources in our country,” she said.

Annie Genevard, France’s conservative agriculture minister, directly opposed her colleague at the Ministry of Ecological Transition, warning that “allowing this bill to fail — whether out of ideology, self-interest or fear — would push farmers to the brink of despair,” in an interview with another Sunday publication, Le Journal du Dimanche.

Balancing farming and the environment

The debate over the legislation has highlighted the tensions between calls to protect the environment and efforts to keep French agriculture economically viable.

It has also exposed serious rifts among Macron’s centrists, most notably between Lecornu and Gabriel Attal, the head of Macron’s centrist Renaissance party and a candidate in next year’s presidential election in France.

Attal and Lecornu both supported reintroducing the pesticide in question, acetamiprid, under exceptional circumstances, but in a parliamentary debate Monday night the centrist lawmaker nonetheless expressed frustration that the government allowed the provision to be introduced at such a late stage.

World.title: EU farming support contributing to pricier healthy food, says UN
World.content:
This amounts to “indirect taxation,” said David Laborde, one of the authors behind the report and the FAO’s lead director of agrifood economics.

The EU’s direct farm subsidies from the Common Agricultural Policy, which Europe has paid since the 1960s, is partly to blame. Europe's agricultural subsidies (CAP) form one of the largest EU funding programs.

But, the lack of investment into research to bring down the costs of producing fruit and vegetables, which tend to be labor-intensive, has had an even bigger effect on the affordability of healthy foods in Europe, Laborde said.

“This has increased productivity in some sectors. But we have done nothing for pulses and beans,” Laborde told POLITICO.

For the average European citizen, that means that the cost of buying a meal every day that meets the minimum requirements for a healthy diet — the right balance of nutrients, calories and variation — rose by $1 between 2021 and 2025, to $3.97. The European price surge is higher than the world average of a 25 percent increase, the FAO report found.

For every healthy meal, vegetables, fruit and legumes eat up nearly 60 percent of the total price, while starchy crops like wheat or rice take up just 13 percent. Still, most farm subsidies worldwide end up in grain, sugar, dairy, beef and oil crops for animal feed.

World.title: Zelenskyy replaces Oleksandr Syrskyi with Mykhailo Drapatyi as Ukraine's commander-in-chief
World.content:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has dismissed four-star General Oleksandr Syrskyi as commander-in-chief and appointed Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi to replace him, well into the fifth year of Russia's all-out war against Ukraine.

 

Zelenskyy announced the decision after days of mass protests across the country, triggered by the dismissal of Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov over what he said was an increasingly fiery clash with General Syrskyi.

Zelenskyy said that after numerous consultations with the military command over the past few days, it has been “determined how the structure of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine is to be reorganised.”

Zelenskyy also praised General Syrskyi for his contribution to Ukraine’s defence.

“It is a fact that Oleksandr Syrskyi ensured Ukraine’s success in the defence of Kyiv, in the Kharkiv offensive and in the Kursk operation,” Zelenskyy said.

“The defence of Ukraine continues, and every soldier deserves to be treated with respect,” he added, referring to widespread criticism of Syrskyi's military management style and lack of support in the military.

“We all share the same desire, to defeat the enemy and to create conditions on the front line and exert sufficient pressure on Russia to force it to make peace.”

FILE: Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left, listens to Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi's report during his visit in Izium, Kharkiv region, Ukraine, Wednesday, Sept. 14, 2022. AP Photo

General Drapatyi previously praised Fedorov’s six-month tenure at the defence ministry, saying he saw a genuine effort to change long-standing military rules and tackle problems the system had grown used to ignoring.

Supporting Fedorov’s push for faster decision-making and a change in approach, Drapatyi, like Fedorov, has called for a systematic overhaul of the army.

“The military needs change, but without justice, no change will make sense to the people who carry this war on their shoulders every day,” the general said in a Facebook post last Thursday, backing Fedorov the day after his dismissal.

“A commander has no right to remain silent about problems, especially when their cost is measured in lost opportunities, time and human lives," Drapatyi said.

"Silence does not protect the army, it only allows mistakes to accumulate until they become much more difficult to correct.”

Who is Ukraine’s new commander in chief?

Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi has built a reputation as a favourite among civil society activists and many in the military.

He had been leading the Joint Forces, the newly-created command covering the front line in and around the northeastern Kharkiv region.

Since taking charge of the area in autumn of last year, Ukrainian units, including the Khartiia Brigade, have recaptured swathes of territory around Kupiansk, which had been under threat from Russian troops.

Before that, Drapatyi led the Dnipro operational-strategic group (OSUV), a wider eastern command that Syrskyi dissolved in October 2025.

As Russia’s initial invasion of eastern Ukraine escalated in 2014, Drapatyi, then a major and battalion commander in the 72nd Mechanised Brigade, was sent into the battle for Mariupol, which was briefly occupied by Moscow's army.

An armoured vehicle from his unit later gained lasting fame after breaking through a barricade erected by Russian forces on one of Mariupol's main streets.

What about Fedorov?

Last week's decision to dismiss Defence Minister Fedorov has turned Zelenskyy’s latest wartime reshuffle into a political crisis of his own making.

The removal of the reform‑minded, tech‑savvy minister — widely supported by civil society and within the armed forces — immediately sparked a wave of anger, with critics accusing Zelenskyy of siding with Syrskyi and entrenched military hierarchies over a figure associated with transparency, cleaner procurement and better conditions for soldiers.

Dmytro Koziatynskyi, a military veteran and protest organiser on Monday has set out a list of demands to the president.

These include dismissing Syrskyi as commander‑in‑chief and reinstating Fedorov as defence minister.

“If by Friday, 24 July, Syrskyi is not dismissed and Fedorov’s candidacy for the position of minister of defence is not submitted, we will begin a general indefinite protest,” he warned.

Zelenskyy made no further comment on the possible return of Fedorov to the defence ministry after announcing his decision to let go of Syrskyi.

World.title: Trump promises US support for Lebanon in White House meeting with president
World.content:
US President Donald Trump pledged to help Lebanon “a lot” during a White House meeting on Tuesday with his Lebanese counterpart, Joseph Aoun, who travelled to Washington seeking US support for long-term stability following months of war between Israel and the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group.

 

“It’s been a very badly treated place and country and we’re going to have it properly treated and treated with the respect it deserves,” Trump told Aoun.

“We’re gonna help it a lot," he said, without giving concrete details.

Aoun thanked the US President for his support, writing in the White House guest book that he felt "deep appreciation for President Trump's friendship and for the support the United States of America provides to Lebanon, its sovereignty, its legitimate institutions, and the Lebanese Armed Forces".

Asked about a full Israeli military withdrawal from Lebanon, Trump said: “They’re in the process of doing that. They’re in the process of redeploying,” but did not elaborate.

Aoun praised Trump’s approach, telling him: “Your vision is peace,” and describing it as his “legacy.”

“I do agree with that,” Trump joked. He then called Aoun handsome and said he “knows how to get to me,” adding: “Now he can have anything.”

President Donald Trump meets with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun in the Oval Office at the White House, Tuesday, 21 July, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein) Pro AP Photo

The US has pushed for peace in Lebanon but has become increasingly focused on a new escalation in the war with Iran, which has further destabilised the Middle East. On Wednesday, Trump said he had little interest, at least for now, in holding talks with Iran’s leader to end the conflict.

Lebanon hopes the talks result in Israeli troops withdrawing from large swaths of southern Lebanon that they currently occupy, and the Lebanese military receiving support to assert full control in areas where Hezbollah militants had held sway.

Meanwhile, the US said operations had begun in three villages under a pilot plan aimed at facilitating the deployment of the Lebanese army as Israeli forces prepare to redeploy from parts of southern Lebanon.

World.title: US appeals court rejects Biden bid to block release of memoir ghostwriter recordings
World.content:
A federal appeals court has rejected former US President Joe Biden's bid to block the release of audio recordings and transcripts of interviews he gave to a memoir ghostwriter before he was elected president.

 

In a 2-1 ruling issued late Monday, the panel found there is a "substantial" public interest in disclosing the material Biden wants to keep under wraps, adding that redactions to the recordings would help protect his privacy.

“We conclude that any remaining incursion on personal privacy from disclosure of the now-redacted materials likely does not outweigh the public interest in disclosure,” the ruling said.

The recordings stem from interviews conducted by Mark Zwonitzer at Biden's home in 2016 and 2017 while they were working on his books. Biden's lawyers argue the conversations were candid, personal and intended to remain private.

The recordings were obtained by special counsel Robert Hur, who investigated Biden's handling of classified documents from his time as a senator from Delaware and as Obama's vice president.

Related Former President Joe Biden to publish memoir after November US midterm elections

Republicans in Congress demanded the material after Hur declined to file charges against the then-president.

Judge Florence Pan, who was nominated by Biden, wrote a dissenting opinion arguing that the former president has a "substantial privacy interest" in keeping the material hidden.

“The conversations at issue took place in Biden’s home, and the recordings of them were obtained by the government in the course of a criminal investigation that did not lead to an indictment,” she wrote.

Biden sued to stop the Trump administration's Justice Department from releasing the recordings to Congress and the conservative Heritage Foundation, but appealed after US District Judge Dabney Friedrich ruled in June that the public interest in the material outweighed his privacy rights.

In her dissent, Pan said the majority's decision effectively clears the way for the recordings' immediate release, making the case "moot."

World.title: Aliyev visits Berlin to deepen energy and trade ties with Germany
World.content:
Azerbaijan's President Ilham Aliyev arrived in Berlin on Tuesday for his first state visit to Germany, with energy security and the Middle Corridor trade route at the top of the agenda as Europe continues to reduce its dependence on Russian fossil fuels.

 

Aliyev met Chancellor Friedrich Merz for bilateral talks before a wider meeting with cabinet ministers.

The two sides signed a joint declaration on a strategic partnership and a series of agreements covering energy, transport, infrastructure, trade and investment, and science and technology — with Germany becoming the second European country after Italy to sign the same agreement with Azerbaijan. A joint business forum ran alongside the talks.

“I would like to express my gratitude to President Ilham Aliyev,” Merz said. “You are creating an opportunity for us to receive larger volumes of gas from Azerbaijan. This issue is also reflected in the Joint Declaration that we signed today.”

“Azerbaijan can supply the required volume of oil,” Aliyev said. “This can be done both through domestic sources and through the trading division of SOCAR.”

Germany has become one of Baku's newest gas customers, after Azerbaijan's gas began flowing to Germany in 2024 via the Southern Gas Corridor and onward connections. Aliyev said he expected annual deliveries to reach 2 billion cubic metres by next year.

Merz described the Southern Gas Corridor as a reliable supply route and said Germany intended to build a long-term relationship with Azerbaijan.

Azerbaijan currently supplies around 12 billion cubic metres of gas per year to Europe, with Italy, Greece, Bulgaria and Hungary among the largest recipients.

"Azerbaijan is ready to increase energy supplies to Germany and other European Union countries as Russia’s energy infrastructure continues to suffer damage from the war in Ukraine," Aliyev said.

Berlin's decision to diversify away from Russian energy after Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022 has increased the strategic value of the Southern Gas Corridor for EU member states.

The Middle Corridor, linking China to Europe through Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey, also featured prominently. Aliyev said Azerbaijan had invested heavily in expanding its port capacity at Alat on the Caspian Sea and that freight volumes through the corridor had grown significantly.

Germany, as one of Europe's main industrial economies and a major importer of Asian goods, has a direct interest in reducing dependence on trans-Russian routes.

Aliyev separately addressed the ongoing war between Iran and the US, which has disrupted regional energy and trade flows and increased the importance of overland and Caspian routes as alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz.

He said Azerbaijan had maintained a balanced position throughout the war and was ready to support any diplomatic efforts to restore stability.

In turn, Merz lauded the Armenia-Azerbaijan peace process, expressing support for a lasting settlement and calling on both sides to finalise the peace agreement.

Europe's reliable partner

According to Orkhan Yolchuyev, director and co-founder of the CASPIA analytical think tank in Baku, the significance of the visit lies in the wider range of sectors included in the new strategic agenda.

“For the first time at such a high level, bilateral cooperation includes green energy, low-carbon hydrogen, digital transformation, industrial modernisation, transport connectivity and innovation,” Yolchuyev said.

“Germany increasingly sees Azerbaijan not only as an energy supplier but also as a partner for new industrial and logistics projects linking Europe, the South Caucasus and Central Asia.”

Yolchuyev said the newly established Business Council could help turn political agreements into practical cooperation, while the inclusion of education, science and cultural exchanges gives the partnership a broader foundation.

Shahin Ismayilov, a member of Azerbaijan’s parliament and chairman of the Youth and Sport Committee, said the agreements reached in Berlin could strengthen cooperation in energy, trade, transport and investment.

“President Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Germany marks an important step in further strengthening the strategic partnership between Azerbaijan and Germany,” he told Euronews.

“Azerbaijan remains a reliable partner for Europe, particularly in ensuring stable energy supplies and advancing the Middle Corridor initiative.”

Aliyev further discussed bilateral cooperation between the two countries in a one-on-one meeting with German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier later on Tuesday.

Steinmeier, who previously served as Germany's foreign minister, described Azerbaijan and Germany as “islands of stability” amid ongoing global conflicts and broader challenges.

World.title: Spanish singer Julio Iglesias sues Spain's deputy PM Yolanda Díaz, demands €50,000
World.content:
Spain’s Deputy Prime Minister, Yolanda Díaz, has been sued before the Supreme Court by singer Julio Iglesias, who accuses her of "unlawful interference with his right to honour and privacy" after two former employees came forward in January with allegations of sexual abuse.

 

Iglesias has asked the judge to order the Sumar leader to pay him €50,000 in compensation over remarks she made on her Bluesky account and on RTVE’s programme ‘La Hora de la 1’ at the start of the year, which he argues amounted to “unlawful interference with his right to honour”. The lawsuit also calls on the deputy prime minister to issue a public retraction.

According to Iglesias’s complaint, Díaz voiced “clear prejudices”, alleging that “sexual abuse was taking place in his home, that staff were kept in conditions akin to slavery and that their fundamental rights were systematically violated”.

The deputy prime minister had previously rejected a conciliation bid, arguing that her remarks had not harmed the artist’s reputation, prompting Iglesias to take the case to the Supreme Court through civil proceedings.

Iglesias has also filed a criminal complaint in a Madrid court against several journalists from Diario.es, the outlet that first reported the former employees’ allegations, accusing them of insult, slander and violating his moral integrity.

The singer’s defence argues that the publication’s editor, Ignacio Escolar, along with several of its reporters, published “false and defamatory” statements intended to “undermine” his public image.

In January, two women who had worked for the Spanish artist at his mansions in Punta Cana, Dominican Republic, and Lyford Cay, Bahamas, came forward alleging that Iglesias had sexually assaulted them.

The investigation, carried out by Diario.es in collaboration with Univisión over three years and based on additional testimonies and documents, alleges that one of the former employees was forced to have sexual encounters with the artist. She claims that during those encounters Iglesias slapped her and penetrated her without her consent.

Shortly after the allegations came to light, journalist Paloma García-Pelayo, who is known for her closeness to Iglesias, said the artist was “worried”, believing his image had “absolutely” collapsed. She added that he was living through the situation “as if he had been killed internationally because of his image.”

Ultimately, the National Court prosecutor’s office decided to shelve the proceedings against Iglesias over the alleged sexual assaults. The prosecutor’s office based its decision on the court’s “lack of jurisdiction” to hear the case, as the alleged incidents took place at the artist’s residences in the Caribbean.

World.title: France becomes the first country in Europe to officially ban social media for under-15s
World.content:
French lawmakers have adopted a bill banning children under 15 from using social media, making France the first country in the European Union to approve a blanket ban on platforms as concerns grow worldwide over the harmful effects of digital content on kids.

 

Both chambers of the Parliament voted Tuesday in favor of the measure, a flagship initiative of French President Emmanuel Macron’s second term. The bill also bans the use of mobile phones in high schools.

The legislation is one of the final major measures adopted under his presidency before he leaves office next year. Macron wants the law to take effect at the start of the new school year in September. However, a review to determine whether the bill complies with the French Constitution is likely to take place and could delay its implementation.

The compromise text was approved behind closed doors by MPs and senators in a joint committee on Monday. Only the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) opposed the text, while socialists abstained.

"Do we decide to impose a blunt, blanket ban on all social media for minors, or do we instead decide – as the European Commission is actually advocating – to ban only the harmful features of social media? We’re more aligned with the latter position", socialist MP Arthur Delaporte said.

Other EU countries such as Greece, Slovenia and Sweden are planning to restrict minors' access to social media: Spain considers banning social media for children under 16 and Austria for children under 14.

In parallel, the President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen called earlier this month for "phased and gradual access for different age ranges" to digital platforms.

Children under the age of 13 would have time-limited access to social media under the supervision of parents, caregivers or teachers. From the age of 13 on, there would be gradual access provided platforms can prove they are age-appropriate and safe for teenagers.

In addition, the European Commission advocates a ban on screens for toddlers.

Von der Leyen said the European Commission would present a proposal on the matter "after summer".

World.title: Russia at Venice Biennale, Brussels cuts €2 million in EU funds: appeal planned
World.content:
The European Commission has confirmed the withdrawal of the €2 million grant earmarked for the La Biennale di Venezia Foundation, opening up a new front of tension between Brussels and one of Italy's most important cultural institutions.

 

The decision, formalised on Tuesday by the European Education and Culture Executive Agency (Eacea) after a legal assessment and on the Commission's recommendation, is linked to Russia's controversial participation in the 2026 Art Biennale.

According to the EU executive, cultural events supported with Union funds must promote and uphold democratic values, dialogue, diversity and freedom of expression, principles that 'are not respected in today's Russia'. This is the reasoning with which Brussels has justified cutting off the European contribution.

Why Brussels decided to cut the funding

The affair stems from Russia's return to the Venice Biennale for the first time since the start of the invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The Russian pavilion, owned by the Russian state, hosts the performance and music project 'The Tree Is Rooted in the Sky', created by around fifty artists selected by the Moscow authorities. Although the pavilion has remained closed to the public, the installation has been made visible from outside via a large screen.

The choice prompted strong protests from Ukraine and from numerous artists, curators and cultural professionals from around the world, who accused Moscow of using its presence at the Biennale as an instrument of cultural propaganda and 'hybrid war'. Kyiv also challenged the alleged ties of the pavilion's curator with the Russian arms industry.

In recent months the European Commission had already warned the Foundation that the choice could lead to the suspension of EU funding. After deeming the explanations provided by the Biennale insufficient, Brussels has decided to proceed with the definitive withdrawal of the contribution.

The Biennale: 'We will defend our position'

The La Biennale di Venezia Foundation has announced that it will lodge an appeal against the decision.

In a statement, the institution stresses that the move had 'long been signalled' and reiterates that it is ready to defend its position before the competent authorities.

The Biennale also points out that the European grant did not concern the artistic event at the centre of the controversy, but activities in the Cinema Sector, in particular Biennale College and the Venice Production Bridge.

'The grant co-funded activities that have nothing to do with Russia's participation in the Art Biennale,' the Foundation says, specifying that the decision 'has no significant impact on the budget, the accounts or the planned activities, which remain fully confirmed'.

Government reaction: Borgonzoni hits out at Brussels

The Italian government responded immediately. Undersecretary for Culture Lucia Borgonzoni expressed full support for the Biennale's decision to challenge the European measure.

'In Eacea's reasoning, no grounds are set out that would justify a decision of this magnitude. This is yet another shameful political and ideological attack on an institution that creates culture and refuses to bend to become a tool for those who like to throw their weight around in the European Union,' she said.

In recent days other centre-right figures have also criticised Brussels' choice. The president of the Veneto region, Luca Zaia, described the withdrawal of the funding as 'unacceptable', arguing that artists cannot be treated as 'soldiers' of their respective governments and that culture must continue to provide a space for discussion and dialogue even in times of international crisis.

A dispute set to continue

The Biennale case is one of the most delicate entanglements between foreign policy, culture and EU funding since the start of the war in Ukraine.

Brussels reiterates that Union funds must be consistent with the EU's founding values, while the Foundation insists on its cultural autonomy and contests the link between the European contribution earmarked for film activities and the participation of the Russian pavilion in the Art Biennale.

The clash is now set to shift onto the legal terrain, with the appeal announced by the Biennale which could open a new chapter in the dispute between the Venetian institution and the European Commission.

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.title: Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended
World.content:
On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

Advertising

On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

A decade ago, factions within the Turkish military, composed of rebellious officers and followers of the Islamic cleric Fethullah Gulen, launched a dramatic attempt to topple President Erdogan.

"I remember, as a soldier, those who started the coup," recalls Murat Aslan, an army officer at the time. "I had no idea that there were members of this organisation (Gulen followers); they were very secretive."

Erdogan tightens his grip

Now a security analyst at SETA, a pro-government think tank, Aslan describes the failed coup as a turning point that reshaped the course of Turkish democracy.

"The message was very clear. Turkish society collectively rejected it," said Aslan. "Thousands took to the streets; that's more than challenging, because you see tanks rolling and people trying to stop them, trying to capture the soldiers with their rifles. It takes more than courage." More than 250 people died resisting the coup.

In the aftermath, Erdogan imposed emergency rule and expanded his presidential authority through a sharply contested national referendum. "This military intervention actually consolidated the Erdogan-led government," Aslan added.

Turkey's military, relations with US to survive failed coup, ruling party vice-president

Hundreds of soldiers and officers faced prosecution as the government declared an end to the army's long history of political interference. Since 1960, the military had orchestrated three coups, the most recent in 1980.

A decade of purges and closures

In the wake of the failed takeover, tens of thousands were purged from state institutions, many never returning even after being cleared.

More than a thousand NGOs were shut down during two years of emergency rule. Milena Buyum, senior Turkey campaigner for Amnesty International, acknowledges the grave threat to democracy posed by the attempted coup: "The state has a responsibility to ensure the safety and security of its citizens and to investigate criminal acts like the ones carried out that night," said Buyum.

Turkey's Erdogan warms to Russia after West coup response

However, Buyum warns that many of the measures introduced under the state of emergency have since been written into ordinary law, permanently curtailing fundamental freedoms: "The right to freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association: the impact on civil society was felt very sharply and starkly in the immediate aftermath of the coup, but that impact continues," said Buyum.

Ankara's alliances

The failed coup also drove a wedge into Turkey's long-standing alliance with the United States. "Ankara saw the hand of the United States behind the failed coup attempt," claims Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, who leads the Ankara office of the German Marshall Fund.

Even before the attempted coup, Erdogan's relations with President Barack Obama had been tense. Obama's belated support, offered only after the coup had failed, fuelled Ankara's suspicions of US complicity, particularly as Washington refused to extradite Fethullah Gulen, whom Erdogan blamed for orchestrating the plot. Gulen denied the accusation until his death in 2024.

Turks in France divided on failed coup

Unluhisarcikli observes that US-Turkish relations remained strained for years, while Erdogan gravitated towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose rapid show of support stood in sharp contrast to Washington's hesitation.

"Putin was among the first leaders, I believe even the first, to extend political support to the elected government in Ankara, and in those days I believe that support mattered greatly to President Erdogan," Unluhisarcikli said.

Rumours still persist in Turkey today that Moscow warned Erdogan on the day of the failed coup. Unluhisarcikli says it was only with the election of President Donald Trump, who shared Erdogan's animosity towards Obama and Joe Biden, that US-Turkish relations began to thaw, a shift highlighted at this month's NATO summit in Ankara. Yet the wave of mass arrests during the summit, enabled by post-coup emergency powers, served as a stark reminder that the shadow of the failed takeover still looms over Turkey.

World.title: Hegseth says Iran war has cost $37.5 billion so far
World.content:
07/22/2026 July 22, 2026 Pentagon seeks billions more for Iran war

US Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth faced tough questioning from lawmakers on Tuesday as he defended the growing cost of the US military campaign against Iran.

Speaking before the Senate Appropriations Committee, Hegseth said the conflict has so far cost $37.5 billion (€32.89 billion), a figure significantly higher than earlier estimates. He argued that additional funding is urgently needed, warning that the military faces critical shortfalls without it.

The hearing was repeatedly interrupted by protesters and came days after the Pentagon confirmed that three more US service members had died in the conflict, bringing the American death toll to 17.

Hegseth's remarks to US senators were met with protesters expressing opposition to the war with Iran Image: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo/picture alliance

Democratic senators challenged both the cost and direction of the war. Senator Patty Murray warned of "another forever war," while other lawmakers questioned why the Pentagon was seeking more funding when some previously approved military spending has yet to be used.

The debate comes as Republicans push a $95 billion budget package that includes tens of billions for the military and national security, as well as funding for agriculture and election-related measures.

Meanwhile, opinion polls suggest many Americans remain critical of US President Donald Trump's handling of the conflict as fighting with Iran continues.

World.title: Trump allows direct US flights to Lebanon in historic move
World.content:
It comes over 40 years after the US suspended the direct route with Lebanon. The announcement was made after US President Donald Trump met with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun.

The US will allow direct flights to Lebanon, President Donald Trump announced on Tuesday.

It comes over 40 years after the US suspended direct flights between the two countries in 1985, during US President Ronald Reagan's administration, in the wake of the hijacking of TWA Flight 847.

"I am hereby directing my Administration to allow all US airline carriers to fly directly to Lebanon so that Americans can easily visit this beautiful land," Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform.

Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam hailed Trump's announcement. Salam said it "represents a significant opportunity to enhance travel and connectivity between Lebanon and the United States, and to support the Lebanese economy."

What did Trump say about the resumption of direct flights between the US and Lebanon?

The announcement comes after Trump hosted Lebanese President Michel Aoun at the White House on Tuesday.

During that meeting, Trump told Aoun that Lebanon had "been a very badly treated place and country and we’re going to have it properly treated and treated with the respect it deserves."

"We’re gonna help it a lot," he said, without providing specific details.

Lebanon appeals to US, Trump to help secure lasting peace

Washington has been mediating rare talks between Israel and Lebanon, but has become distracted in recent weeks by the resumption of full-scale hostilities between the US and Iran.

Could US-backed Israel-Lebanon deal lead to civil war? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Aoun, who was making the first visit to the US capital by a Lebanese president since 2009, had traveled to Washington, D.C. to appeal for a longer-term, more stable peace in his country, which has been plagued by months of war between Israel and the Iran-backed, Lebanon-based militant group Hezbollah.

Aside from the resumption of direct flights between the US and Lebanon, authorities in Beirut will be hoping that this week's talks in Washington yield an Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon, where Israel's ground forces have occupied swathes of territory as part of its campaign against Hezbollah.

Trump claimed Israel's military was "in the process of doing that. They’re in the process of redeploying," he said, without elaborating.

Israel is occupying southern Lebanon in what it says is an effort to protect northern Israeli communities from Hezbollah attacks. Israel, along with the US, Germany and some other countries, recognize Hezbollah as a terror group.

Aoun hails Trump as 'great president'

Aoun, for his part, heaped praise on Trump, whom he called a "great president" whose "vision is peace."

Aoun met with Trump at the end of a 4-day visit to Washington Image: Evelyn Hockstein/REUTERS

"I do agree with that," Trump jokingly replied, calling Aoun handsome and someone who "knows how to get to me."

"Now he can have anything," Trump added.

World.title: Spain: Firefighters battle major wildfire north of Madrid
World.content:
Officials say the blaze, which has forced about 1,200 people to evacuate and has burned at least 30,000 hectares of land, is one of the most complex to affect the country in years.

Hundreds of firefighters and soldiers were battling a massive wildfire northeast of Madrid on Tuesday that has been raging since last week.

Authorities say the blaze, which broke out on Thursday in Guadalajara province about 100 kilometers (60 miles) north of Spain's capital, is one of the most difficult they have faced and is considered the most significant wildfire to affect the country this year.

What do we know about the fire north of Madrid?

"It is the most complex of those that have been tackled in recent years in Spain," Castilla-La Mancha regional president Emiliano Garcia-Page told reporters.

The fire has been raging in an area just 100 kilometers from Madrid Image: Ana Beltran/REUTERS

Garcia-Page added that more than 600 firefighters and nearly 50 aircraft and helicopters had "practically stopped" the blaze from spreading toward the provincial capital of Soria, but that it was not yet under control.

"We can now see light at the end of the tunnel," he said.

The blaze has forced some 1,200 people to evacuate from their homes across the region of Castilla-La Mancha, while at least 30,000 hectares (74,000 acres) of land have been burnt, officials said.

The fire has been so difficult to bring under control because the area is made up of scrubland and has been under prolonged, severe drought conditions. High winds have also complicated the situation.

At least 30,000 hectares have been destroyed Image: Nacho Valverde/Europa Press/IMAGO

Spain's risk of more fires 'remains high'

Spain on Tuesday entered the third heatwave of the summer so far, with temperatures expected to soar above 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) in much of the country, hindering firefighting efforts.

According to Spain's national weather agency AEMET, the heatwave is expected to only last about three days.

Spain is still reeling from one of the deadliest wildfires in modern times that killed 13 people and destroyed 7,000 hectares in southern Almeria province earlier this month.

According to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), wildfires have destroyed over 115,000 hectares of land in Spain this year.

"We are going through particularly complex weeks, and the risk of fires remains extremely high," government spokeswoman Elma Saiz told a press conference.

Last year, the EFFIS said more than 393,000 hectares were destroyed by wildfires, the most in Spain's history.

Spain has been fighting multiple fires in recent weeks and is already in its third heatwave this year Image: Ricardo Rubio/Europa Press/IMAGO

France also battling major fires

In southwestern France, two firefighters were killed near an airport in Gironde, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said Tuesday.

On Monday, firefighters tackled a fire at a Roma camp on the outskirts of Nantes in western France.

Around 200 people were evacuated after the blaze, which began after a car caught fire, spread to nearby woodland and to caravans belonging to people living in the settlement.

Human-driven global heating is making heatwaves longer, more intense and more frequent, most scientists say, which creates dry conditions that increase the likelihood of destructive wildfires.

World.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy fires military chief after days of protests
World.content:
Mass protests in recent days in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities had called for the removal of commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi. Volodymyr Zelenskyy has named Mykhailo Drapatyi as the army's new chief.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Tuesday that he was removing Oleksandr Syrskyi, the army's commander-in-chief, from his post.

"I have decided that the new Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine will be Mykhailo Drapatyi... I am grateful to Oleksandr Syrskyi and to each of our warriors for Ukraine's strong front-line positions," Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram.

"Our shared wish is one — victory over the enemy and conditions at the front and in pressure on Russia that would force Russia toward peace," Zelenskyy said. "A significant path has been traveled, the defense of Ukraine continues, and every warrior deserves dignified treatment."

Why did Zelenskyy sack his commander-in-chief?

The move comes as Zelenskyy has been facing mounting criticism over the dismissal of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov last week.

Following his sacking, Fedorov, 35, went public with his conflict with Syrskyi. Their dispute was mainly over a disagreement about the direction of Ukraine's war effort against Russia's ongoing invasion.

Fedorov had accused Syrskyi of blocking his attempts at reforming and modernizing the army.

Fedorov's removal triggered massive, nationwide protests that saw several thousand, mostly young people demonstrate in Ukraine's capital, Kyiv and other cities. They demanded that Syrskyi be removed and that Fedorov be reinstated.

Zelenskyy, who had initially sided with Syrskyi, eventually bowed to public pressure on Tuesday, after days of meetings with dozens of Ukraine's top military figures.

Zelenksyy's sacking of Fedorov triggered massive protests across Ukraine Image: Oleksandr Savytskyj/DW

Who is sacked Ukrainian general Oleksandr Syrskyi?

Syrskyi, 60, was born in Russia and was trained in Moscow during the Soviet era.

He had led some of Ukraine's most decisive campaigns, including halting Russia's initial advance towards Kyiv in 2022 and leading Ukraine's incursion into Kursk, Russia in 2024.

"It is a fact that Oleksandr Syrskyi ensured Ukraine's successes in the defense of Kyiv, in the Kharkiv offensive operation, and in the Kursk operation," Ukraine's president said on Tuesday when announcing the change.

But the military veteran had clashed with reformers over a range of issues, including the use of drones and technology.

His dismissal caps a dramatic week in Ukrainian politics, which has seen Zelenskyy botch a leadership reshuffle that has triggered some of the largest protests the country has seen since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022.

Critics had called Syrskyi the 'butcher' for not caring about the number of his troops who were killed Image: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

How has ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov reacted?

Fedorov, a reformist, was associated with Ukraine's drone strikes against targets in Russia, which have helped turn the tide of the war and garnered wide praise in the West.

Fedorov said Syrskyi's replacement as Ukraine's commander-in-chief by Drapatyi brings "fresh hope" to the country.

"This is a breath of fresh air and a new hope in the struggle of free people for freedom and justice," Fedorov said on social media.

World.title: Jordan faces growing risk of becoming latest frontline state in US-Iran conflict
World.content:
As Iranian attacks intensify, Jordan is emerging as the latest frontline state in the widening Middle East conflict. Why is the Hashemite Kingdom a target for Tehran?

Air raid sirens again sounded in parts of Jordan early Tuesday as Iranian missiles targeted the kingdom.

"The air defense system intercepted and downed tonight three missiles coming from Iranian territory that entered Jordanian airspace and targeted the kingdom's territory," the army said in a statement.

No injuries were reported, but the latest strikes follow a series of attacks that have raised the stakes for one of the United States' closest Arab allies in the past days: Two US service members were killed and around 30 others injured by an Iranian missile strike on a US base in Jordan last week.

Jordan is one of the eight Arab countries that host permanent US military facilities. Some of the other host countries — particularly the Gulf states — have been the targets of Iranian attacks since the United States and Israel launched joint attacks on Iran in late February.

Though Iran launched missiles toward Jordan shortly thereafter, there has since been a lull in direct attacks on the kingdom, which has helped to intercept Iranian missiles launched toward Israel, arguing that it is acting in defense of its own airspace.

"Iran has reserved itself the right to return fire on any state in the region that hosts US military assets or bases, and Jordan is one of them," Erwin van Veen, a senior research fellow at the Clingendael Institute in The Hague, told DW. "Only the options of Jordan's King Abdullah II are quite limited as Jordan is in a very precarious balance with respect to military and economic dependence on the Americans."

On Sunday, in a first diplomatic escalation, Jordan summoned Iran's top diplomat in Amman to demand an immediate end to what the foreign ministry called "unjustified and blatant Iranian attacks."

Jordan's political and economic tightrope walk

The US is Jordan's largest single foreign supporter. Under a seven-year Memorandum of Understanding signed in 2022, Washington agreed to provide $1.45 billion (€1.27bn) annually in economic and military assistance. In 2025, Congress increased this to $1.65 billion, which was triple the amount from 2010.

Furthermore, a Defense Cooperation Agreement signed in January 2021 grants US forces formalized access to Jordanian military facilities. According to a recent report , there are currently 4,000 US troops, more than in previous years, stationed in Jordan.

In March, however, Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi insisted that there were no foreign military bases in the country. Kelly Petillo, program manager for Middle East and North Africa at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said one reason for downplaying foreign military presence in Jordan could be anti-US sentiment.

"Despite Jordan's efforts to remain neutral in this war, existing alliances such as the one with the US not only affect Jordan's fragile security but also cause public discontent," she told DW.

She speculated that Jordan, like its Gulf allies in the region, might be beginning to question whether its alliance with the US was beneficial to the country's stability or actually a cause of instability.

A 2026 poll by Arab Barometer, a nonpartisan public opinion research network, concluded that only 12% of Jordanians view US President Donald Trump's foreign policy favorably.

For Jordan's King Abdullah II and Queen Rania the Palestinian issue is of particular importance Image: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty Images

Jordan-Israel ties

"The other risk for Amman is that Iran's attacks could also place it in the same camp as Israel," Petillo warned. "This impression could cause further discontent among the wider public, creating space for protests as they were already seen during the war in Gaza, when people called for an end to the Israel-Jordan 1994 peace treaty."

In the past three years, relations between Israel and Jordan have become increasingly strained. In November 2023, the two countries recalled their ambassadors after Jordan's condemnation of Israel's conduct during the early days of its war in Gaza, which was unleashed after the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023. Hamas is considered a terrorist organization by the US, the EU and others.

Jordan has been at the forefront of efforts to push for a two-state solution, which would grant Palestinians their own state alongside Israel.

The Palestinian issue is of particular importance for Jordanian citizens as more than half of the population, including Queen Rania, has Palestinian roots. Around 2.4 million Palestinian refugees live in Jordan, according to the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA).

But Jordan has repeatedly rejected any more displacement of Palestinians into the kingdom, particularly considering the high cost of hosting refugees whose return is anything but guaranteed.

"Jordan has been faced with a massive decline in USAID funding and the US pullback from UNRWA," Petillo said.

This comes as Jordan continues to struggle with high public debt and unemployment.

Aid organizations warn that increasing settler violence has forced more than 1,000 children from their homes in 2026 Image: Leo Correa/AP Photo/picture alliance

Popular anger related to Israel has recently been exacerbated by the expansion of settlements in the occupied West Bank, which the United Nations and rights groups say has accelerated since 2023. Increased settler violence has made life even worse for Palestinians in the West Bank.

According to the aid organization Save the Children, more than 1,000 Palestinian children were displaced by a surge in settler violence in the West Bank in the first six months of 2026. This was half the total number of children forced from their homes by settler violence over the entire previous three-year period.

"As the current Israeli coalition wrote in its own coalition agreement at the start of its tenure in 2022, it ultimately intends to annex the West Bank," Erwin van Veen said.

"Jordan is, in many ways, between a rock and a hard place, as it has little room for manoeuvre — neither toward Israel, Iran nor Washington," he added.

The West Bank, a landlocked territory of about 5,655 square kilometers (2,183 square miles), lies between Israel and Jordan. Israel took control of it from Jordan in the 1967 Six-Day War. According to the United Nations Security Council, "Israel's establishment of settlements in Palestinian territory occupied since 1967, including East Jerusalem, had no legal validity."

World.title: Germany records rise in sexual violence against children
World.content:
Germany's Criminal Police Office has reported over 17,000 cases of sexual violence against children in the past year. Organizations such as Zartbitter provide support to victims.

Leonie Kirschstein knew that the number of sexual violence cases involving children and adolescents would not decline. The psychologist works for the registered nonprofit Zartbitter e.V. , which has served as a support center for young victims in city of Cologne in western Germany for nearly four decades. This pioneering organization counsels victims, conducts educational outreach in schools and even stages plays on the topic of sexual violence.

Kirschstein, who has worked for Zartbitter for three years, told DW that the number of unreported cases was much higher: "Crime statistics only include cases that have been reported to the police. But not the ones we deal with every day, such as cases involving peer violence. In many cases, these aren't reported at all, especially when the children are still very young. This group makes up the largest portion of the cases we handle in our counseling process."

Germany: Child sex abuse probe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Victims of sexual violence in every classroom

The issue of sexual violence is more topical than ever: The World Health Organization estimates that up to 1 million children and adolescents in Germany have experienced or are currently undergoing sexual violence at the hands of adults.

This means that, on average, in every German school classroom, there are one to two children who are victims of sexual violence. Kirschstein, who specializes in psychotherapy with children and adolescents, says: "We receive new cases every day; parents, in particular, call for an initial consultation. Unfortunately, I still very often find the victims wonder whether they themselves did something wrong — that is, whether they said 'no' explicitly and whether their refusal was understood as such by the perpetrator."

Cyber grooming - criminals home in on children To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt wants to retain IP addresses

Leonie Kirschstein's observations align with the "Federal Assessment of Sexual Offenses Against Children and Adolescents 2025 ," which was released on July 21 in Berlin.

It states that the number of cases of sexual abuse of children and adolescents remains alarmingly high and has even risen in many areas. The number of sexual abuse offenses against minors under the age of 14 alone rose to 17,126 cases from 16,354 in 2024.

New record highs have also been reached for crimes involving "child pornography" and for the sexual abuse of children without physical contact.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt is sounding the alarm: "The high number of cases of sexual abuse of children and adolescents shows that we must protect our children even better — especially in the digital world," he said. "Perpetrators must not be allowed to feel safe and hide in the anonymity of the internet. In the fight against these repugnant crimes, our law enforcement agencies need effective tools such as IP address logging — to identify perpetrators, prosecute them consistently, and put an end to active abuse," Dobrindt told the media.

BKA President warns of 'cybergrooming'

To better prosecute cybercrime, the federal government is currently pushing for a law allowing the retention of IP addresses for three months. Dobrindt is confident that such a law could be passed as early as this fall. He has also called for the establishment of the post of European Commissioner for the Prevention of Sexual Abuse of Children and Adolescents.

Holger Münch, the president of the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), meanwhile, has warned against "cybergrooming." This refers to adults deliberately contacting children and adolescents online to initiate sexual contact.

"More than 98% of all perpetrators are male, with an average age of about 24; the victims are predominantly female and, on average, just under 12 years old. The primary risk factor is a lack of awareness of the risks associated with one's own online behavior. While teenage perpetrators tend to act out of boredom or just to pass the time, adult perpetrators often have sexual motives and specifically target minors," Münch said, adding that this often leads to a subsequent meeting and abuse.

Young people lack adequate legal protection

Independent Federal Commissioner Against Sexual Abuse of Children and Adolescents Kerstin Claus is calling for better protection, especially for teenagers in Germany

"Instances of 'sextortion' are increasing dramatically, and cybergrooming affects nearly one in three people between the ages of 14 and 17," she said. "And yet it is not currently categorized as a criminal offense."

What is not a criminal offense does not appear in statistics, and what is not counted there is not combated, Claus said. "That is why adolescents must be protected from cybergrooming, and sextortion must be classified as a distinct sexual offense. The federal situation report cannot even begin to reflect the true extent of the sexual violence to which young people are exposed online every day," she warned.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Ousted Turkey opposition leader  plans to create a new party
World.content:
Turkey's main opposition CHP faces a potentially historic rupture after months of infighting over its leadership.

Turkey's ousted opposition leader, Ozgur Ozel, on Tuesday announced he would resign from the Republican People's Party, or CHP, and launch a new political party.

"Today, we are on the brink of a sad farewell that has become inevitable and whose time has come. However, we would like to share with the people that we carry the hope of a new beginning," Ozel said to more than 80 CHP lawmakers.

Ozel was removed as head of the CHP by court orderin May, in a ruling that also reinstated former leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu as interim leader.

Ozel and Kilicdaroglu disagreed on how to resolve the leadership issue permanently, leading to a dispute within the CHP.

New party did deepens split in Turkish opposition

Ozel's supporters say the case is part of a broader campaign by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to weaken the opposition, while the government insists Turkey's courts operate independently.

Ozel is reportedly due to submit an application to the Interior Ministry to establish the new party, which, according to reports, will be called the "Yeni Party" ("New Party").

He enjoys strong support from CHP parliamentarians, and many of them are expected to defect from the CHP to join the new party once it is formed.

"Once the necessary procedures are completed, the new party we are about to establish will become the main opposition force in the Grand National Assembly by a wide margin," Ozel said. "We carry within us an unwavering hope for a new beginning," Ozel told lawmakers, who gave him a standing ovation.

Crackdown on the CHP

The dispute comes as investigations targeting CHP-run municipalities continue, including cases against Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, a prominent rival to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Imamoglu has been imprisoned since March last year and faces multiple criminal cases that could result in decades-long sentences.

Why Europe stays silent in Turkey's opposition crisis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

After Imamoglu's arrest, Ozel played a key role in mobilizing Turkey's largest street protests in more than a decade, which saw the party's popularity rise in the polls.

Under Ozel's leadership, the CHP also made major gains in the 2024 municipal elections, strengthening its control of key cities including Istanbul and Ankara.
