Jaksha Shah, who has lived in Mt Atkinson for about three years, said she does not blame either side of politics for what she describes as a lack of infrastructure.

"I feel like the vision itself is missing, the holistic vision," she said.

Ms Shah said the council needs to do its bit too, arguing there was a need for an expanded and linked-up bus network to help residents get around locally.

A Victorian government spokesperson said electrification of the Melton line was on the way to deliver more trains, more often, with site investigations to finalise the project design now underway.

"Whether it's making the Werribee Line and Melton level crossing free, getting on with Airport Rail, putting more services on the Werribee Line or opening the West Gate and Metro Tunnel — we are reducing congestion, helping busy families in the west get home sooner," they said.

While the opposition did not commit to funding the projects if elected, the Coalition's transport infrastructure spokesman, Evan Mulholland, said Labor had lied to Melton residents for two straight elections.

"Labor don't care about Melton; they never have. It's why they're spending one-fifth of the entire infrastructure budget in Victoria over the next four years on the Cheltenham to Box Hill line in the eastern suburbs," he said.

World.title: 'Massive' drop in tourists this winter hits WA's south
World.content:
The winter tourism industry is taking a hit in Western Australia's south, with businesses reporting a noticeable downturn.

In Denmark, 420 kilometres south of Perth, business owner Christine Weston said the region had recorded a significant decline in visitor numbers.

"I can confirm visitor numbers are certainly down," Ms Weston said.

Christine Weston says her business, Southern Coast Escapes, is one of several affected by the quieter season. (Supplied: Christine Weston)

Ms Weston said there had been a few last-minute bookings, but she and several other accommodation providers told the ABC the decline in tourist numbers was impacting revenue.

"If there's a lot of availability, the prices automatically get adjusted down," she said.

" So it is affecting our revenue. "

Ms Weston said she believed many people were not booking holidays too far in advance due to the global economic uncertainty.

"With the diesel fuel supply being a little bit insecure as well … I think there's just a bit of uncertainty in the world and people don't want to commit too far out," she said.

"A couple of years ago, people would walk out from a Christmas holiday and book their next Christmas holiday. They're certainly not doing that anymore."

Drop in visitors

Winter can be the best time of year to see whales migrate off the coast of Albany, 400km south of Perth.

Tour operator Aaron Franaigh said this year, fewer people were coming to see the spectacle.

Tourists usually flock to the Great Southern region in winter to see migrating whales. (Supplied: Naturaliste Charters Whale Watching)

"Everyone's holding on to their money. No-one's forward-looking at the moment," he said.

Mr Franaigh said the "massive" drop was a worry for his business.

"Normally for school holidays, we're a full boat every single day, and we're sort of at half capacity now. We've had a couple of full days, but we are mainly at half capacity," he said.

"Because it is our major source of income for the boat to stay here, it is a bit of a worry. What can you do?"

Albany is usually popular with tourists in winter. (ABC News)

In the neighbouring town of Bremer Bay, Community Resource and Visitor Centre manager Fiona Murray was also worried about the impact on local businesses.

"This year seems to be very similar to years where we've had COVID," she said.

"With everything that's going on around the world, the fuel prices are definitely a big issue."

Bremer Bay is a popular holiday destination on WA's coast. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

Paul Zip, who runs a whale-watching charter further north in Augusta, has noticed the drop in tourists in the coastal town.

"I've been doing this business for 18 years and sitting at the harbour here in Augusta you'd look out, and there'd be caravans and trailers and campervans and people just wandering around, but they're not here at the moment," he said.

Cost of living pressures

Sophie Zalokar, manager at Australia's South West National Tourism Organisation, acknowledged it was a "challenging time for all" in the region.

"Visitor numbers across the Great Southern have softened over winter, reflecting cost-of-living pressures, fuel prices and broader economic uncertainty," she said.

"We are continuing to work with industry, government and local partners to encourage year-round visitation … and remain confident in the region's resilience and long-term visitor appeal."

Whale watching is traditionally a popular activity in Albany during the winter months. (ABC Great Southern: Will Corbett)

Tour boat operator Mr Franaigh also hoped the downturn would be short-lived.

"All I can do is offer the best tour that we can and just hope that word of mouth keeps us going."

World.title: Husband says he should have died with his wife in house fire
World.content:
A man who escaped a fatal house fire south of Brisbane says he should have died with his wife of 42 years.

Leanne Gay Laver, 62, and family friend Phillip Gordon, 73, died when the house caught alight in the Logan suburb of Kingston on Tuesday afternoon.

Ari and Leanne Laver had rented the two-storey Adelaide Street home for 35 years.

The couple had three children, including a daughter they informally adopted as an adult.

Leanne Laver, 62, died in the house fire on Tuesday afternoon. (Supplied)

Mr Laver said his wife had stage four lymphoma, but they thought she was on the "right route" after good reports on her health.

"She was right at the front door, I ran down for the hose thinking that she would be following," he said.

"When we realised the fire was right under the house, I tried to go back but I couldn't get back in.

"I called to her, I told her to try for the door. I don't know what to say, we got out in our underwear and with a phone, that's it."

Mr Laver said it was about three minutes from when they first heard "a thump" until they were driven out of the house.

Family friend Phillip Gordon, 73, also died in the blaze. (Supplied)

Mr Laver and four others got out of the house unharmed.

"What am I going to do for my kids? That's all that's going through my head," he said.

Mr Laver said he is partially paralysed and his wife had been his carer.

" For 42 years, [she was] the most faithful, loving, selfless, sacrificing woman … She was faithful beyond the extreme in every way that mattered. "

He also said he had known the other victim, Phillip Gordon, since he was 17-years-old.

"I called him my brother in every way. I was an only child and he's all I knew of a brother. My parents loved him."

A crime scene has been declared after a house fire south of Brisbane. (ABC News)

'I smelt it before I heard it'

Neighbour Tiffany Tinker said the blaze spread fast.

"The kids just came in and started yelling the next door neighbour's house was on fire, and I smelt it before I heard it and then by the time I looked outside I saw the flames just engulfing the house next door," she said.

Investigators are at the scene today to work out what caused the fire.

World.title: Spanish chief accuses FIFA boss of 'destroying the football industry'
World.content:
Gianni Infantino should resign as head of FIFA for "destroying the football industry" by expanding international competitions, according to Javier Tebas, the president of Spain's football league La Liga

It is not the first time he has lashed out at Infantino over fixture congestion and for considering a proposal to expand the 2030 men's World Cup from 48 teams to 64.

"Increasing the number of national teams makes no sense. The football industry isn't just the World Cup, which is the most important event. But not everything can revolve around the World Cup," Tebas told La Gazzetta dello Sport.

Players and fans made the World Cup a success, but the politics shouldn't be forgotten The biggest ever World Cup brought diverse communities together and galvanised its non-traditional footballing co-hosts, but the concerns raised from the start have not disappeared in the positive afterglow.

"In my opinion, yes, I think his time is up," he said of Infantino. "However, he has the support of the system and the federations, so there's not much more to add, is there? There's no opposition candidate, nobody wants to stand just to lose. This is the system and it's rotten at its core.

"He shouldn't stay, but he won't leave. I've heard many people who are against Infantino. They say it, but then they do nothing. I don't know what's worse, the silence or the complicity, because those who stay silent are perfectly aware of the damage football is suffering."

South American soccer's ruling body CONMEBOL has made an official proposal to expand the 2030 World Cup to 64 teams. The competition is already set to be the most sprawling edition, with six host nations spread across three continents.

"It's national competition that sustains this sport," Tebas added. "They are destroying the football industry, which generates tens of thousands of jobs, for an event that lasts 40 days and involves a minority of players."

The World Cup final had a 27-minute half-time interval thanks to a half-time show featuring artists such as Justin Bieber (pictured). (Reuters: Amanda Perobelli)

He also criticised world football's governing body FIFA over the new hydration breaks implemented at the World Cup, which ended on Sunday, as well as the extended 27-minute half-time interval — rather than the standard 15 — during the final which saw Spain defeat Argentina 1-0.

The hydration breaks midway through each half were introduced to help players deal with the summer heat in the United States, Canada and Mexico. But critics say they had unintended consequences, ruining the flow of the game and giving coaches a chance to tactically shift momentum in their team's favour.

"FIFA arranges things as it pleases, for what it wants, for its own interests, certainly not for football," Tebas said. "Hydration breaks are a lie. We have them in La Liga, but only when it's genuinely hot. Here, the pitches in Dallas, Los Angeles, and Atlanta had air conditioning. It was a lie and just a break for advertising."

Infantino announced in April that he would run for re-election for a fourth term as president. The vote for the 2027–2031 period is scheduled for March 18 in Morocco.

La Liga boss Javier Tebas has not been shy about attacking Infantino in the past. (Getty Images: Oscar J. Barroso/Europa Press)

The Football Supporters Europe (FSE) group also called on the wider soccer community to hold FIFA to account.

In a statement on its website headlined "A World Cup that failed supporters", the FSE demanded "structural governance reforms to hand decision-making power back to the FIFA Council and Congress and ensure full consultation with clubs, leagues, players and supporters".

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

It added: "The 2026 World Cup should have been a celebration of the game and the supporters who give it life. Instead, it has too often become a case study in what is so deeply wrong with football today.

"From the outset, supporters were asked to place their trust in FIFA and "chill", but it prioritised spectacle and commercialisation over the match-going experience with key elements of football's identity being messed with. Over the last month, we've seen football contorted to the whim of Gianni Infantino and the Trump administration."

The FSE, accepted by European soccer's governing body UEFA as the recognised group representing fans in the region, then went on to attack "historically high ticket prices" and "skyrocketing transportation costs, bending of rules and procedures, exclusion of swathes of the global population and a lack of transparent communication".

"All this created an environment of confusion and distrust that has severely damaged the reputation of FIFA, the World Cup, and the integrity of football itself," its statement said.

"The lessons from this World Cup are clear: FIFA is unfit to govern global football. The future of the game cannot rest in the hands of a man who has proven yet again that he puts financial and political interests ahead of the future of our game."

AP

World.title: $30m biochar facility could help replace coal at Rio Tinto refineries
World.content:
A $30 million biochar facility proposed for central Queensland has signed a sales agreement with Rio Tinto as the miner investigates ways to replace coal.

Rio Tinto said it would use bana grass bio pellets produced by Australian company SuperChar Limited to further assess how it could substitute coal in boilers at its emissions-intensive Queensland refineries.

The initial five-year agreement would see 35,000 tonnes of the bio pellets supplied in 2028, subject to approvals.

"That 35,000 tonnes, as we burn it, will reduce our carbon emissions by 90,000 tonnes per annum," Rio Tinto's general manager of bauxite and alumina, Tim McDougall said.

Mr McDougall said a feasibility study had already proved the coal used in boilers at its Gladstone refineries could be replaced by a blend of up to 30 per cent bio pellets.

Bio pellets produced by SuperChar were trialled at Rio Tinto's Gladstone refineries in 2024 and 2025. (Supplied: Rio Tinto)

The company plans to assess bio pellet blends of up to 50 per cent under the agreement, and it is one of several solutions Rio Tinto is exploring to reduce fossil fuel use in alumina refining.

SuperChar is proposing to produce the bana grass charcoal pellets in Boynedale, about 50 kilometres from Gladstone.

Bana grass is a perennial, fast-growing semi-tropical grass.

A young bana grass planted in a trial crop in central Queensland. (ABC Capricornia: Jasmine Hines)

SuperChar still needs Gladstone Regional Council approval, with the company lodging its development application earlier this year.

"Boynedale has got a suitable climate … it was a dairy area until about 10 years ago … There's abundant water and potential there," executive chairman Mike Palmer said.

The company plans to make the biochar by heating the bana grass at high temperatures with limited oxygen — a process known as pyrolysis.

"There are no chemicals involved, there are no waste products involved, so, environmentally, it's a very friendly process," Mr Palmer said.

He said, in addition to the 35,000 tonnes of bio pellets, the facility would produce a further 25,000 tonnes of charcoal briquettes a year, which could be used for cooking.

Mr Palmer said the grass could also be used to make an animal feed product, and was used internationally in Central Africa and Central America as cattle feed.

"Because of the high protein content of the bana grass, we can produce a 15–18 per cent protein animal pellet," he said.

Briquettes produced using bana grass. (ABC Capricornia: Jasmine Hines)

Mr Palmer said this would be the company's first production facility.

It also has bana grass plantations in Ingham and Mossman in Far North Queensland.

Potential employment boost

The initial processing plant and farming activities are expected to provide employment for about 25 people.

Paul Whiteman with the bana grass on his property in central Queensland. (ABC Capricornia: Jasmine Hines)

Farmer Paul Whiteman is working with SuperChar and, in May, planted 12 hectares of the crop to trial on his property in the Boynedale area.

"We're the guinea pig … I really hope it's successful, and it looks like it has great potential to be quite profitable," he said.

Mr Whiteman said he hoped the project would go ahead to improve local employment opportunities and attract young families to the area, as local schools faced dwindling enrolments.

"A lot of people have to seek employment off-farm, and this might be able to bring some of those people back onto farm and save them having to do the 45-minute drive in and out of town each day," he said.

Paul Whiteman is interested in bana grass as the product can also be used to feed cattle. (ABC Capricornia: Jasmine Hines)

Mr Whiteman said while the trial crop was planted late in the season, it was starting to shoot as soil temperatures were warming.

"In the last couple of weeks, it's really started to shoot," he said.

Mr Palmer said the project was "well advanced in terms of funding", but the company was seeking government support.

World.title: Zelenskyy names new Ukrainian commander-in-chief
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has named a young general, Mykhailo Drapatyi, as the commander-in-chief of Ukraine's military in the biggest shake-up of country's military leadership since Russia invaded.

Protesters criticise Zelenskyy after Ukrainian defence minister's sacking A dispute between the now former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov and Kyiv's top general is spilling into public, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy orders a second reshuffle of this year.

Mr Zelenskyy replaced former commander-in-chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi, 60, with General Drapatyi, 43, a respected and experienced commander who led the country's land forces from 2024 to 2025.

The change followed days of street protests sparked by a surprise governmental reshuffle that ousted popular defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov.

It also reflects tensions between Ukrainians who see the use of technology as key to winning the war and an old guard with a traditional approach.

Clash of ideas

Mr Zelenskyy last week dismissed tech-savvy reformist Mr Fedorov, 35, who had led an effort to advance drone innovation and clashed with General Syrskyi, accusing him of sabotaging his work.

General Drapatyi was supported by some of the protesters who rallied outside Mr Zelenskyy's office for several days, demanding Fedorov be brought back and General Syrskyi removed.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has replaced Oleksandr Syrskyi as chief of the Ukrainian armed forces. (Reuters: Valentyn Ogirenko)

Mr Zelenskyy said the Ukrainian defence forces' operations must continue steadily.

"Ukraine's plan for long-range sanctions and our program of middle-range strikes will be carried out with absolute precision," he said.

The reshuffle has come as Kyiv seeks to gain the upper hand in the war against Moscow by heavily striking Russia's energy sector — its main source of budget revenue — and logistics.

Mr Fedorov's dismissal stirred concerns among military analysts that Ukraine's recent battlefield momentum could be lost.

In a Facebook post, General Drapatyi thanked General Syrskyi for his work strengthening the military.

"I grew up in it," he said, referring to the army.

"I will work responsibly, with focus and with respect for the people defending our state today."

Moscow targeted by drones while Russia bombards Kyiv Ukraine launches its latest attack on the Russian capital, firing more than 400 drones, while the Kremlin deploys more ballistic missiles against targets across Ukraine.

General Syrskyi played a key role in Kyiv's defence in the early days of the war and had been in his top post since early 2024.

But he has faced harsh criticism for a rigid command style that some service members have said results in high troop losses.

Mr Zelenskyy did not mention any new post for General Syrskyi, saying he discussed the four-star-general's future service with him.

He also said he had offered Mr Fedorov, who previously said he only wants his former job back, a "decent post" to oversee the technological component of the state.

Daring and determined fighter

Mykhailo Drapatyi has spent nearly his entire career in combat postings, including leading Ukraine's joint forces. (Ukrainian Presidential Press Office)

The new commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian military forged his reputation as a daring and determined fighter in the early days of the country's battle against Russia, then spent a decade in combat assignments while steadily rising through the ranks.

General Drapatyi spent nearly his entire career in combat postings, including leading Ukraine's joint forces, which direct day-to-day combat operations across branches of the army.

His reputation was forged in 2014, early in Russia's war in eastern Ukraine, when he led an armoured column into central Mariupol to rescue police officers and territorial officials besieged by pro-Russian militants who had threatened to burn them alive.

When the column's path was blocked by a barricade more than a metre high, General Drapatyi, riding in the lead vehicle, ordered the driver to accelerate, and the vehicle bounced over the barrier as if off a ramp.

The moment, which was captured on video that circulated widely, is considered one of the most remarkable episodes in the early resistance.

It was a bold move for the Ukrainian army at the time, when decisive and independent moves by field officers were rare. The army was still poorly equipped, largely untested and wary of any action that might escalate tensions with Russia.

Months later, General Drapatyi's battalion spent weeks encircled by Russian-backed forces near the Russian border.

Rather than disarm and walk out, General Drapatyi chose to fight his way free, leading 260 soldiers and more than 30 vehicles out of the pocket at night.

Reuters/AP

World.title: Boy charged with murdering mother, attempting to kill sister in Perth
World.content:
A 16-year-old boy has been charged with murdering his mother and attempting to kill his sister in an alleged domestic violence homicide at the family home in Perth's south-east.

Two crime scenes were established after the 35-year-old woman's body was found in a house on Mills Street in Bentley about 6:15am yesterday.

A 12-year-old girl was also found injured on Albany Highway in Cannington, about 600 metres away from the home.

After taking the boy into custody at the home, they have now charged him with the alleged stabbing murder of his mother as well as attempted unlawful killing.

Police arrested the boy at the scene. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

He is due to face Perth Children's Court today.

The ABC is unable to identify the accused or his alleged victims for legal reasons.

In a media conference on Tuesday, WA Police Detective Acting Inspector Jessica Securo said the girl managed to escape the residence and call police after she was also allegedly stabbed by her brother.

"While the investigation remains in its early stages, police are investigating this as a suspected family violence homicide and homicide squad have carriage,” she said.

The girl is understood to be in a serious but stable condition in Perth Children's Hospital.

Police said in a statement this morning she was receiving medical treatment and support.

They also said their investigation was ongoing and detectives urged anyone with any information relating to the alleged murder to contact Crime Stoppers.

Inspector Securo said police would also examine any past interactions the family had with police.

World.title: Queensland parliament updates: Bates and Bleijie front budget estimates
World.content:
Finance Minister Ros Bates and treasury’s top official have refused to say if former federal opposition leader Peter Dutton met a checklist of skills sought by the Queensland Investment Corporation for new board members.

The former defence minister, who lost his Brisbane seat of Dickson, was appointed to the board as part of an overhaul in April – a move that was called a “jobs for mates appointment” by the state Labor opposition.

Former federal opposition leader Peter Dutton. Alex Coppel

World.title: ‘My wife didn’t deserve that’: Family devastated after two lives lost in blaze
World.content:
NationalQueenslandFire ‘My wife didn’t deserve that’: Family devastated after two lives lost in blaze Julius Dennis July 22, 2026 — 10:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Just four of the six people who tried to escape a devastating fire south of Brisbane managed to get out, leaving a family to mourn the loss of a mother and a friend who perished inside. Leanne Laver, 63, and 73-year-old Phillip Gordon were trapped inside the timber house in Kingston when it burst into flames at about 3pm Tuesday. Police declared an exclusion zone in the Logan suburb while seven crews of firefighters doused the flames, which had quickly taken over the entire building. Leanne Laver had lived in the house for 35 years. Facebook Leanne’s husband Sean Laver, who goes by Ari, escaped unharmed, along with the couples’ daughter, Chloe, their son Jay, and housemate Lucas Kirby.



Neighbours described hearing screams and yells of panic as flames took hold, destroying the house and burning five vehicles parked outside. Laver had lived in the house for 35 years, and the family told reporters at the scene they had done everything they could to save the now deceased pair. Phillip Gordon was a longstanding friend of the Lavers. Sean Laver told Today on Wednesday morning that he and his wife had been together for 40 years, describing her as “the most faithful, loving and selfless person”. He said he believed an electrical fault on the ground floor sparked the blaze, and the house went up in about three minutes.



“I’m not feeling anything except, I should have died with my wife, and what am I going to do for my kids? That’s all that’s going through my head,” he said. “My wife didn’t deserve that, she’d been battling stage four lymphoma, we’d just had good reports, we thought we were on the right route.” He said he thought Gordon may have gone back to try and save the family’s pet cats. Police were still investigating the cause of the blaze on Wednesday morning, and a report will be compiled for the coroner. A 16-year-old Perth boy has been charged with murder over an alleged stabbing attack that killed his mother and left his 12-year-old sister with serious injuries in hospital. Police were called to the scene of the attack in Bentley, in Perth’s south-east, early on Tuesday morning after the young girl fled to a nearby highway to raise the alarm. Police at the scene of a fatal stabbing in Bentley on Tuesday. 9News Perth Bystanders provided the girl with life-saving first aid. She remained in hospital recovering from her injuries on Wednesday. At the home, officers found the body of a 35-year-old woman, and the teenage boy was arrested at the scene.



Speaking to media on Tuesday, WA Police Major Crime Acting Inspector Jessica Securo said the incident was being treated as a suspected family violence homicide. “This incident will have a significant impact on the family, friends and loved ones of all those involved ... our thoughts are with them all, particularly the 12-year-old girl,” she said. The boy’s sister ran to the nearby Albany Highway, where bystanders provided live-saving first aid. 9News Perth Securo said the boy was known to police, and detectives were examining previous interactions the family and boy had with authorities. A source close to the family told this masthead the boy had been before the justice system on a number of occasions.



And the source said the family, who were allegedly known to the state’s child protection system, had reached out for support that never came. “He was failed by the courts,” the source said, after explaining that the boy had lived “a transient lifestyle” since he was 10 or 11 years old. “They reached out for support and got nothing,” the source said. “His family loved him. It’s a sad tragedy.” On Wednesday morning, police revealed the boy had been charged with murder over his mother’s death, and had also been charged with attempted unlawfully to kill over the injuries inflicted on his sister.

World.title: How a Sydney developer bypassed council to gain approval for 250 homes
World.content:
Eastern suburbs developer Arash Tavakoli has for the past four years been hatching plans for one of his Landmark Group’s most prominent projects yet: demolition of 106 low-rent apartments in Edgecliff to make way for a 25-storey tower overlooking Trumper Park. There have been more than a few hurdles along the way, not least of which were the half a dozen owners who didn’t want to sell, Woollahra Council’s rejection of the proposal, strong community opposition, and its location in Paddington’s Heritage Conservation Area. The 1970s complex Cameron Court in Edgecliff has 106 low-rent apartments. Sitthixay Ditthavong Despite that, the state planning minister Paul Scully has delivered good news for Tavakoli, giving the go-ahead for about 250 new homes on the site. It’s a win not only for Tavakoli, but also for former premier-turned-lobbyist Morris Iemma, given his work in recent years shepherding the development through the state’s planning approval processes.



Tavakoli is one of a growing number of developers to turn up on the books of Iemma’s registered lobby firm Iemma Patterson Premier Advisory since Labor won the state election in 2023. For Tavakoli, his association with Iemma not only brought the planning minister’s full attention to his Edgecliff development, but coincided with Tavakoli’s negotiations with the planning department over an enforced undertaking over unauthorised works he carried out on the waterfront site adjoining his Rose Bay home. Premier Chris Minns, Arash Tavakoli and Morris Iemma at the opening of Landmark Group’s Victoria and George development at Kogarah. Instagram Neither Tavakoli nor Iemma responded to requests for comment, but a tranche of documents obtained by the Herald via freedom of information requests and through parliament offer an inside look at the wizardry and influence of one of Sydney’s best-placed lobbyist in navigating the state’s planning approval process. The Cameron Court complex behind Edgecliff train station has long been a tempting acquisition for developers given it sits on a sprawling 7200 square metres in one of the most expensive locales in the country.



The 106 apartments, all separately owned, made the 1970-built complex an expensive acquisition process. Tavakoli, brother of high-profile plastic surgeon Dr Kourosh Tavakoli, who calls himself the “king of boobs”, had started doing just that by early 2022, buying up the majority of studio and one-bedroom apartments. Rents average between $500 and $700 a week. Arash Tavakoli heads up property developer Landmark Group. Landmark Group Despite snapping up the requisite 75 per cent of apartments to force a collective sale of the block, half a dozen owners held out, forcing Landmark to resort to legal proceedings to secure a new strata renewal plan. The last hold-out owners agreed to sell to Landmark’s acquisition company in 2024, by which time the developer was already in discussions with Woollahra Council to have it rezoned and included in its draft Edgecliff Commercial Centre Planning and Urban Design Strategy aimed at boosting building heights and floor space, among other things.



Landmark was not successful, and council raised further objections over the project’s excessive bulk and scale, traffic issues and the fact it was within the Paddington Heritage Conservation Area. “The community has objected at every stage of this development,” said Edgecliff Residents Organisation manager Charlene Batson. Among those against the development is the Henroth Group, headed by prominent developer John Roth, because of the building’s height increase of 279 per cent on local current limits and removal of 152 trees. Other locals have raised concerns about traffic, overshadowing and the loss of so many homes in an area where cheap rents are challenging to find. Tavakoli’s patience with council looked to be wearing out by September 2023, when he turned to the Iemma Patterson Premier Advisory for assistance. Emails between Iemma and the planning minister’s deputy chief of staff Gino Mandarino seeking guidance over “the most appropriate pathway for assessment” make special mention of “how council delays, indecisiveness and obstruction is preventing serious analysis or proposals to provide urgently needed housing”.



Iemma’s email describes Cameron Court as “highly dilapidated and at the end of its building lifecycle, being over 60 years old now and in need of redevelopment”. In the ensuing months, there was a flurry of emails exchanged between Iemma’s office and the planning minister’s office. Among the issues was not only the “abrasive and ignorant” council, but also a condition by the Sydney Eastern City Planning Panel of an external independent design process for the site. The block of 106 apartments on New McLean Street, Edgecliff, is approved to be demolished to be redeveloped. Sitthixay Ditthavong It wasn’t a welcome condition. Iemma described it as “overreach on part of the panel” and instead requested an urgent meeting with the premier and planning minister’s office to discuss the issue. It is unknown if any such meeting took place.



But a few months later, Minns was on hand beside Tavakoli to officially open Landmark’s Victoria and George development at Kogarah, with Iemma in tow. Landmark’s break came in late 2024, when the state government announced the creation of the Housing Delivery Authority (HDA) as a fast-tracked approval process for land rezoning and major housing developments that bypassed council. Within a week or so, Landmark had withdrawn the proposal from council. Arash Tavakoli and Premier Chris Minns officially opening Landmark Group’s Kogarah development Victoria and George. Instagram Among the first proposals in line before the newly formed HDA was Landmark’s Edgecliff tower, and in February last year, the authority recommended it for state significant development status. Having secured the imprimatur of the HDA, there are now questions over whether the development will deliver an increase in housing after Landmark reworked the proposal into a two-stage project in which the site would be subdivided to allow for a 10-storey building of 65 luxury apartments on one block and an as yet unspecified development to make up stage two.



A spokesperson for the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure said the minister’s approval would require no net loss in the number of dwellings across the site once it was full developed. Related Article Exclusive

City life The premier, the developer and the string of defective Sydney buildings Woollahra councillor Mark Silcocks dismissed stage two as just an empty promise. “There is no definitive plan, no lodged application, no approved plans and no consent,” he said. “There is no legal obligation on the proponent to build stage two, no time frame for doing so, and no mechanism to enforce compliance with the no net loss requirement if stage two is never built.” Of the 45 submissions to Landmark’s most recent two-stage proposal, only four were supporting it, and three of those were from out of the area.



Woollahra councillor Harriet Price questioned why the project was eligible as a state significant development given its $63 million cost fell short of the HDA’s $75 million threshold. The HDA threshold is $60 million. Critics have also noted that the initial HDA recommendation for state significance incorrectly referred to the Edgecliff site adjoining Trumper Park as “an isolated piece of industrial land”. It was later corrected. The Rose Bay residence often features in the Instagram posts of Samira Jeihooni’s celebrity sister Sara Jeihooni. Instagram Tavakoli’s issues with Woollahra Council go beyond his Edgecliff proposal and include a dispute over his usage of the public land next to his waterfront home in Rose Bay that resulted in a damning Land and Environment Court judgment against him. The waterfront residence was purchased for $30 million after a protracted settlement in 2018 in the name of Tavakoli’s wife, Samira Jeihooni, sister of US singer-songwriter Sara Jeihooni, who starred in the 2020 season of reality TV show Shahs of Sunset.



It was later demolished and rebuilt, to a design by Burley Katon Halliday at a cost of $5.85 million, into a four-level residence with a signature skylight dome above its central staircase. In completing the look, Tavakoli took to the adjoining block, an unused roadway, and organised to have the parcel landscaped and three retaining walls built around it. The unauthorised work included a sandstone wall that allowed the land to be levelled in line with his harbour front wall. A low picket fence on the boundary was movable. The retaining wall fronting the public land and Arash Tavakoli’s Rose Bay home. Woollahra Council The Land and Environment judgment details how Tavakoli told council officers he was doing them a favour: “I need to improve my frontage verge. This area was overgrown and neglected. Why is council complaining, I have done a favour to you.” Justice Nicola Pain was unimpressed. “This is a case where a picture paints a thousand words,” she said in her judgment. “The additional area of fill placed on the land was grassed and presents as a continuous extension of the frontage of the residence.”



Despite pleading not guilty to what were originally 10 offences, a week later Tavakoli took the matter to the state’s planning department and commenced negotiations over an enforced undertaking in which Tavakoli admitted organising to have his company occupy and carry out the work without consent. It was a fortuitous move. “Mr Tavakoli obtained a substantial benefit as a result of entering into the [enforced undertaking], which was that five criminal charges against him personally were discontinued on the basis of the agreement reached,” Pain said in her judgment. Tavakoli’s costs totalled more than $1.54 million, including remediation works of $491,000 and $375,000 in ongoing maintenance costs. Tavakoli, who was recently celebrating his upcoming 50th birthday with family and friends on the French Riviera, was approached for comment. CLARIFICATION This story has been updated to clarify that the HDA threshold for a development is $60 million.

World.title: Unreleased report cites police complaints on domestic violence
World.content:
NationalQueenslandDomestic violence Unreleased report cites police complaints on domestic violence Julius Dennis July 22, 2026 — 9:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A report to the Queensland government from a group of domestic violence survivors calling for a civilian review system for complaints about poor police responses has been kept under wraps. The Lived Experience Working Group was convened by Prevention of Domestic and Family Violence Minister Amanda Camm in February 2025, tasked with meeting three times before providing a report on how victims were falling through the gaps. Initially reported by The Guardian, the report did not see light of day, despite consistent messaging from the government about putting victims first. Previously police would have had to call interstate offices to clarify information around protection orders. Police Media A summary of the final report, which found a fragmented system full of procedural and cultural barriers, was distributed to government bodies and key stakeholders, but not made public.



A footnote on the summary report, seen by this masthead, noted the confidentiality of working group members as a reason the report would not be made public. “Key challenges identified include inconsistent police and legal responses, lack of culturally safe and trauma-informed practices, weaponisation of service systems against victim-survivors by persons using violence, housing and financial insecurity, and inadequate support,” the summary’s executive summary reads. The most in-depth section of the report took aim at the Queensland Police Service, which it claimed reacted inconsistently to domestic violence complaints. These responses led to a “perception that outcomes depended on the officer that attended”, the author said, adding group members were discouraged from escalating complaints about police they felt did not take their concerns seriously. The group recommended a “civilian review mechanism” oversee the escalation of these concerns.



Victim-survivors involved in the group were frustrated by delays in charges being laid over DVO breaches when perpetrators had regular and predictable routines causing a lack of trust in the police service’s ability to make them safe. The roles of child protection, mental health supports, housing and financial security, the legal system, and specialist DVF services were also analysed by the group. The group found victims “overwhelmingly described experiences of being disregarded, not being taken seriously and being sent around in circles” and found the onus was on them to find the support they needed. Since the group was convened, Queensland police have disbanded their specialist domestic violence unit, deeming case management not “core business”. That decision came after a 100-day review of police operations found significant “mission creep” within the service.



Related Article Domestic violence Queensland police defend scrapping specialist domestic violence team In response to questions about the group’s report, Camm said the government was tackling the issue through record investment and the delivery of shelters, affordable housing, and more police. “The Crisafulli government has given a voice to victims of domestic and family violence and has prioritised turning around the deteriorating services we inherited from the former government,” she said. “For example, our government has increased DV Connect’s answer rate from 41.9 per cent under Labor to 84 per cent.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Trump to bomb Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site ‘soon’, appears to blame Jordan for US deaths
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war Trump to bomb Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site ‘soon’, appears to blame Jordan for US deaths Michael Koziol Updated July 22, 2026 — 9:52am ,first published 5:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: President Donald Trump declared he will bomb Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site “pretty soon”, while appearing to blame US partner Jordan for the deaths of at least two American troops when an Iranian missile hit a Jordanian air base last week. The US military has now released the identities of four service members killed in the renewed fighting, including 19-year-old Isabella Gonzales and Tyler Feehan, 25, who died at the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan. First Lieutenant Tyler Feehan and Private Isabella Gonzales were killed by an Iranian attack in Jordan. US Army Space and Missile Defence Command via AP Sergeant Michael Swinton was killed in Iraq. U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command via AP On Wednesday (AEST), the military confirmed that a third soldier believed killed in the Jordan attack was Sergeant Angel S. Rampersad, 28, of Ozone Park, New York.



Another soldier – now identified as 30-year-old Michael Swinton – died during the disposal of an Iranian drone in Iraq. Eighteen US service members have now been killed since the war began. Trump on Tuesday (Washington time) appeared to blame the Jordanian military for failing to stop the missile reaching its target. Loading “[The Iranians] did slip something through in Jordan, and if we had other operators, it would not have happened, unfortunately,” he said. “We have the best equipment in the world, we’ve stopped almost everything. But when you let other people do your job – with the United States, we let other people do the job – and sometimes it doesn’t work out so well.”



Trump also gave his strongest signal to date that he intends to authorise a strike on Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a key nuclear site buried deep underground near the Natanz facility that was bombed by the US last year. “We’ll be hitting that area probably pretty soon and there’s not a thing they can do about it,” he told reporters in the Oval Office. “Normally, I wouldn’t say that. If I thought they could do something about it, I would never say that. But we’ll be hitting that area pretty soon, and very heavily.” Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike Pickaxe Mountain since the conflict in Iran roared back to life two weeks ago after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps resumed firing at ships in the Strait of Hormuz.



So far, US forces have mostly targeted coastal surveillance assets, missile and drone launch sites, command centres and air defence systems along the Iranian coastline, and in some other areas. Mystery surrounds the exact purpose of Pickaxe Mountain. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Israeli intelligence believes Iran relocated thousands of centrifuges – used to enrich uranium – into tunnels deep inside the mountain, and had relayed this to the US. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the mouth of the Red Sea is another crucial global shipping passage. Graphic: Nathan Perri Trump was unfazed when asked about the report, saying he was focused on tracking any Iranian stockpiles of enriched uranium. “That’s where the action is.” Meanwhile, the risk of the conflict further infringing upon global shipping escalated, with at least two tankers turning around in the Red Sea after Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen threatened to attack ships in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.



Ship tracking data from LSEG showed a crude carrier, the Xin Long Yang, made a U-turn and headed back towards the Suez Canal, rather than trying to cross the strait bound for China, Reuters reported. It was carrying 2 million barrels of Saudi Arabian crude oil. Related Article Middle East at war Trump sets sights on Iran’s hidden nuclear fortress Aframax tanker Rodos, which loaded about 700,000 barrels of Saudi crude for India, also made a U-turn for Suez on Tuesday, according to the data. Gregory Brew, an Iran and oil analyst at the Eurasia Group consultancy, said the data showed at least five tankers carrying Saudi oil or bound for Saudi ports had stopped or turned around near the strait. “Non-Saudi traffic continues apace,” he said. The Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen largely sat out the conflict over the past five months, but on Monday declared a blockade on Saudi Arabia and warned shipping companies that vessels using Saudi ports could be targeted.



Trump was nonplussed about the potential escalation. “If something like that happens, we’ll take care of it. We’ve done that with the Houthis before,” he said. Meanwhile, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told a hearing of the Senate Appropriations Committee in Washington that the war against Iran had now cost $US37.5 billion ($53.16 billion), an increase of $US8 billion since the last public estimate. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing on Tuesday. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin General Dan Caine, chairman of the joint chiefs and the president’s top military adviser, faced questions about whether the US deliberately targeted desalination plants inside Iran, possibly violating international law. Iranian state media reported that the Bonji desalination plant – which provided water to more than 10,000 people in 20 villages – was destroyed by a US missile.



“I’m not aware of those being particular targets, nor I am aware of those reports,” Caine said. He undertook to find out what had happened, but maintained confidence in US forces to always act ethically. With Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: The luxury watches, the 20 flights to China and the Sydney international student
World.content:
NationalCrime The luxury watches, the 20 flights to China and the Sydney international student Sally Rawsthorne July 22, 2026 — 9:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Sydney international student is behind bars after allegations he fraudulently claimed more than $5 million worth of GST refunds on luxury watches. Mingyi Chi, a 28-year-old Chinese national living in Haymarket while studying in Sydney, was arrested in May by police probing suspicions of a transnational criminal syndicate using Australia’s tourist refund scheme to falsely claim GST refunds on luxury watches. A Patek Phillipe watch, one of several seized by police. AFP Chi was, police said in a media release on Wednesday, one of several individuals “engaged in rapid international travel, structured cash deposits and the circulation of high-value goods”. Investigators say Chi allegedly lodged more than $5 million in fraudulent refund claims for luxury watches at Sydney Airport.



Police say they seized $270,000 from a drawer inside the Haymarket unit. AFP In Australia, international visitors can claim GST refunds for goods worth more than $300 that are being permanently taken out of the country. Detectives further allege that he flew to Chengdu more than 20 times between November 2025 and May 2026, often staying in his native China for less than 24 hours at a time. Chi also allegedly deposited $1.1 million into Australian bank accounts via ATMs in the Sydney CBD between February 2025 and his arrest. The police raid on his Sydney apartment also resulted in investigators seizing $270,000 in cash, a Richard Mille watch worth about $170,000, three Patek Phillipe watches, one Van Cleef watch, two counterfeit luxury watches, mobile phones, a cash counting machine and multiple receipts and invoices. Chi was charged with dishonestly intending to obtain a gain, which carries a maximum of a decade behind bars. He was refused bail and remains inside Silverwater’s Metropolitan Reception and Remand Centre until at least the end of this month when he will apply for bail in the Supreme Court.



AFP Detective Superintendent Peter Fogarty said the arrest was a warning for others who would abuse the GST refund system. “Everyday Australians suffer when the taxation system is exploited and money goes into the pockets of criminals, which bankrolls future criminal ventures,” he said. “Anyone who abuses the taxation system is warned – your actions and transactions are always traceable, and you are in the AFP’s sights.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Madeleine McCann vanished in 2007. Her brother will swim at the Commonwealth Games
World.content:
SportSwimmingCommonwealth Games Madeleine McCann vanished in 2007. Her brother will swim at the Commonwealth Games Steve Bird July 22, 2026 — 9:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Madeleine McCann’s brother has been selected to represent Scotland in swimming at the Commonwealth Games. Sean McCann is expected to compete in a number of longer-distance freestyle swimming events when the Games start in Glasgow on Thursday. Scotland’s Sean McCann will compete at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games. Getty Images The 21-year-old student hopes success at the Games will improve his chances of securing a place to represent Great Britain at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles. McCann was two years old when Madeleine disappeared shortly before her fourth birthday during a holiday in Praia da Luz, Portugal, in 2007.



Their parents, Kate and Gerry McCann, fought tirelessly to try to find her. Madeleine, who is thought to have been abducted, has never been found. McCann’s family is expected to watch him compete at Tollcross International Centre during the 11-day competition. His twin sister, Amelia, is a high-level swimmer and triathlete. Madeleine McCann went missing while on holiday in Portugal in 2007. She has never been found. AP In 2023, McCann – whose father is Scottish – represented Scotland at the Youth Commonwealth Games in Trinidad and Tobago. He finished fifth in the 400m freestyle event. He has also represented Britain at the European junior open-water championship in Corfu.



The Loughborough University student trains in a pool nine times a week, completing 20 hours of training alongside his academic studies in chemical engineering. Writing on the website of the Joe Humphries Memorial Trust, an organisation set up to raise awareness of sudden arrhythmic death syndrome, McCann said he took up swimming when he was eight. Loading “In order to have achieved this, I have had to remain extremely dedicated, getting up at 4am multiple mornings each week to train, since the age of 11,” he wrote. “I train nine times a week in the pool, as well as three gym sessions, totalling over 20 hours of training per week. I’m aiming to compete at the 2026 Commonwealth Games and also the 2028 Olympics in LA.”



He is also a keen open-water swimmer, and is part of Britain’s national open water development squad. Although he has not spoken publicly about his sister’s disappearance, he has supported his parents and twin sister at vigils for Madeleine, most recently in May to mark the 19th anniversary of her disappearance. Kate and Gerry McCann hold a missing poster depicting an age progression computer generated image of their still missing daughter Madeleine, in 2012. AP His mother has previously suggested that the family had kept busy to cope with Madeleine being missing, as well as the intense glare of publicity that surrounded the search for her. “As a family, 98 per cent of the time we’re busy. I don’t know if that’s a conscious thing, but it helps. The urge to look for Madeleine absolutely hasn’t changed at all,” she said.



Related Article Exclusive

Commonwealth Games After four years, this swim star is ready to speak about ‘the worst thing that ever happened to me’ She also said that her youngest two children love to be active. “They have their own friends, and they keep busy and they’re really sporty. But their only wish is for their big sister to come home. We miss our complete family of five.” The former GP now works as a medical worker, while her husband is a British Heart Foundation professor of cardiology at the University of Leicester and an honorary consultant cardiologist at Glenfield Hospital. The family live in Leicestershire. Telegraph, London News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: ‘My wife didn’t deserve that’: Family devastated after two lives lost in blaze
World.content:
NationalQueenslandFire ‘My wife didn’t deserve that’: Family devastated after two lives lost in blaze Julius Dennis July 22, 2026 — 10:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Just four of the six people who tried to escape a devastating fire south of Brisbane managed to get out, leaving a family to mourn the loss of a mother and a friend who perished inside. Leanne Laver, 63, and 73-year-old Phillip Gordon were trapped inside the timber house in Kingston when it burst into flames at about 3pm Tuesday. Police declared an exclusion zone in the Logan suburb while seven crews of firefighters doused the flames, which had quickly taken over the entire building. Leanne Laver had lived in the house for 35 years. Facebook Leanne’s husband Sean Laver, who goes by Ari, escaped unharmed, along with the couples’ daughter, Chloe, their son Jay, and housemate Lucas Kirby.



Neighbours described hearing screams and yells of panic as flames took hold, destroying the house and burning five vehicles parked outside. Laver had lived in the house for 35 years, and the family told reporters at the scene they had done everything they could to save the now deceased pair. Phillip Gordon was a longstanding friend of the Lavers. Sean Laver told Today on Wednesday morning that he and his wife had been together for 40 years, describing her as “the most faithful, loving and selfless person”. He said he believed an electrical fault on the ground floor sparked the blaze, and the house went up in about three minutes.



“I’m not feeling anything except, I should have died with my wife, and what am I going to do for my kids? That’s all that’s going through my head,” he said. “My wife didn’t deserve that, she’d been battling stage four lymphoma, we’d just had good reports, we thought we were on the right route.” He said he thought Gordon may have gone back to try and save the family’s pet cats. Police were still investigating the cause of the blaze on Wednesday morning, and a report will be compiled for the coroner. NationalWACourts Teenager charged with murder over alleged stabbing attack on mum, sister Rebecca Peppiatt and Cameron Myles July 22, 2026 — 10:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A 16-year-old Perth boy has been charged with murder over an alleged stabbing attack that killed his mother and left his 12-year-old sister with serious injuries in hospital. Police were called to the scene of the attack in Bentley, in Perth’s south-east, early on Tuesday morning after the young girl fled to a nearby highway to raise the alarm. Police at the scene of a fatal stabbing in Bentley on Tuesday. 9News Perth Bystanders provided the girl with life-saving first aid. She remained in hospital recovering from her injuries on Wednesday. At the home, officers found the body of a 35-year-old woman, and the teenage boy was arrested at the scene.



Speaking to media on Tuesday, WA Police Major Crime Acting Inspector Jessica Securo said the incident was being treated as a suspected family violence homicide. “This incident will have a significant impact on the family, friends and loved ones of all those involved ... our thoughts are with them all, particularly the 12-year-old girl,” she said. The boy’s sister ran to the nearby Albany Highway, where bystanders provided live-saving first aid. 9News Perth Securo said the boy was known to police, and detectives were examining previous interactions the family and boy had with authorities. A source close to the family told this masthead the boy had been before the justice system on a number of occasions.



And the source said the family, who were allegedly known to the state’s child protection system, had reached out for support that never came. “He was failed by the courts,” the source said, after explaining that the boy had lived “a transient lifestyle” since he was 10 or 11 years old. “They reached out for support and got nothing,” the source said. “His family loved him. It’s a sad tragedy.” On Wednesday morning, police revealed the boy had been charged with murder over his mother’s death, and had also been charged with attempted unlawfully to kill over the injuries inflicted on his sister.



He is set to face Perth Children’s Court the same day. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: How a Sydney developer bypassed council to gain approval for 250 homes
World.content:
Eastern suburbs developer Arash Tavakoli has for the past four years been hatching plans for one of his Landmark Group’s most prominent projects yet: demolition of 106 low-rent apartments in Edgecliff to make way for a 25-storey tower overlooking Trumper Park. There have been more than a few hurdles along the way, not least of which were the half a dozen owners who didn’t want to sell, Woollahra Council’s rejection of the proposal, strong community opposition, and its location in Paddington’s Heritage Conservation Area. The 1970s complex Cameron Court in Edgecliff has 106 low-rent apartments. Sitthixay Ditthavong Despite that, the state planning minister Paul Scully has delivered good news for Tavakoli, giving the go-ahead for about 250 new homes on the site. It’s a win not only for Tavakoli, but also for former premier-turned-lobbyist Morris Iemma, given his work in recent years shepherding the development through the state’s planning approval processes.



Tavakoli is one of a growing number of developers to turn up on the books of Iemma’s registered lobby firm Iemma Patterson Premier Advisory since Labor won the state election in 2023. For Tavakoli, his association with Iemma not only brought the planning minister’s full attention to his Edgecliff development, but coincided with Tavakoli’s negotiations with the planning department over an enforced undertaking over unauthorised works he carried out on the waterfront site adjoining his Rose Bay home. Premier Chris Minns, Arash Tavakoli and Morris Iemma at the opening of Landmark Group’s Victoria and George development at Kogarah. Instagram Neither Tavakoli nor Iemma responded to requests for comment, but a tranche of documents obtained by the Herald via freedom of information requests and through parliament offer an inside look at the wizardry and influence of one of Sydney’s best-placed lobbyist in navigating the state’s planning approval process. The Cameron Court complex behind Edgecliff train station has long been a tempting acquisition for developers given it sits on a sprawling 7200 square metres in one of the most expensive locales in the country.



The 106 apartments, all separately owned, made the 1970-built complex an expensive acquisition process. Tavakoli, brother of high-profile plastic surgeon Dr Kourosh Tavakoli, who calls himself the “king of boobs”, had started doing just that by early 2022, buying up the majority of studio and one-bedroom apartments. Rents average between $500 and $700 a week. Arash Tavakoli heads up property developer Landmark Group. Landmark Group Despite snapping up the requisite 75 per cent of apartments to force a collective sale of the block, half a dozen owners held out, forcing Landmark to resort to legal proceedings to secure a new strata renewal plan. The last hold-out owners agreed to sell to Landmark’s acquisition company in 2024, by which time the developer was already in discussions with Woollahra Council to have it rezoned and included in its draft Edgecliff Commercial Centre Planning and Urban Design Strategy aimed at boosting building heights and floor space, among other things.



Landmark was not successful, and council raised further objections over the project’s excessive bulk and scale, traffic issues and the fact it was within the Paddington Heritage Conservation Area. “The community has objected at every stage of this development,” said Edgecliff Residents Organisation manager Charlene Batson. Among those against the development is the Henroth Group, headed by prominent developer John Roth, because of the building’s height increase of 279 per cent on local current limits and removal of 152 trees. Other locals have raised concerns about traffic, overshadowing and the loss of so many homes in an area where cheap rents are challenging to find. Tavakoli’s patience with council looked to be wearing out by September 2023, when he turned to the Iemma Patterson Premier Advisory for assistance. Emails between Iemma and the planning minister’s deputy chief of staff Gino Mandarino seeking guidance over “the most appropriate pathway for assessment” make special mention of “how council delays, indecisiveness and obstruction is preventing serious analysis or proposals to provide urgently needed housing”.



Iemma’s email describes Cameron Court as “highly dilapidated and at the end of its building lifecycle, being over 60 years old now and in need of redevelopment”. In the ensuing months, there was a flurry of emails exchanged between Iemma’s office and the planning minister’s office. Among the issues was not only the “abrasive and ignorant” council, but also a condition by the Sydney Eastern City Planning Panel of an external independent design process for the site. The block of 106 apartments on New McLean Street, Edgecliff, is approved to be demolished to be redeveloped. Sitthixay Ditthavong It wasn’t a welcome condition. Iemma described it as “overreach on part of the panel” and instead requested an urgent meeting with the premier and planning minister’s office to discuss the issue. It is unknown if any such meeting took place.



But a few months later, Minns was on hand beside Tavakoli to officially open Landmark’s Victoria and George development at Kogarah, with Iemma in tow. Landmark’s break came in late 2024, when the state government announced the creation of the Housing Delivery Authority (HDA) as a fast-tracked approval process for land rezoning and major housing developments that bypassed council. Within a week or so, Landmark had withdrawn the proposal from council. Arash Tavakoli and Premier Chris Minns officially opening Landmark Group’s Kogarah development Victoria and George. Instagram Among the first proposals in line before the newly formed HDA was Landmark’s Edgecliff tower, and in February last year, the authority recommended it for state significant development status. Having secured the imprimatur of the HDA, there are now questions over whether the development will deliver an increase in housing after Landmark reworked the proposal into a two-stage project in which the site would be subdivided to allow for a 10-storey building of 65 luxury apartments on one block and an as yet unspecified development to make up stage two.



A spokesperson for the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure said the minister’s approval would require no net loss in the number of dwellings across the site once it was full developed. Related Article Exclusive

City life The premier, the developer and the string of defective Sydney buildings Woollahra councillor Mark Silcocks dismissed stage two as just an empty promise. “There is no definitive plan, no lodged application, no approved plans and no consent,” he said. “There is no legal obligation on the proponent to build stage two, no time frame for doing so, and no mechanism to enforce compliance with the no net loss requirement if stage two is never built.” Of the 45 submissions to Landmark’s most recent two-stage proposal, only four were supporting it, and three of those were from out of the area.



Woollahra councillor Harriet Price questioned why the project was eligible as a state significant development given its $63 million cost fell short of the HDA’s $75 million threshold. The HDA threshold is $60 million. Critics have also noted that the initial HDA recommendation for state significance incorrectly referred to the Edgecliff site adjoining Trumper Park as “an isolated piece of industrial land”. It was later corrected. The Rose Bay residence often features in the Instagram posts of Samira Jeihooni’s celebrity sister Sara Jeihooni. Instagram Tavakoli’s issues with Woollahra Council go beyond his Edgecliff proposal and include a dispute over his usage of the public land next to his waterfront home in Rose Bay that resulted in a damning Land and Environment Court judgment against him. The waterfront residence was purchased for $30 million after a protracted settlement in 2018 in the name of Tavakoli’s wife, Samira Jeihooni, sister of US singer-songwriter Sara Jeihooni, who starred in the 2020 season of reality TV show Shahs of Sunset.



It was later demolished and rebuilt, to a design by Burley Katon Halliday at a cost of $5.85 million, into a four-level residence with a signature skylight dome above its central staircase. In completing the look, Tavakoli took to the adjoining block, an unused roadway, and organised to have the parcel landscaped and three retaining walls built around it. The unauthorised work included a sandstone wall that allowed the land to be levelled in line with his harbour front wall. A low picket fence on the boundary was movable. The retaining wall fronting the public land and Arash Tavakoli’s Rose Bay home. Woollahra Council The Land and Environment judgment details how Tavakoli told council officers he was doing them a favour: “I need to improve my frontage verge. This area was overgrown and neglected. Why is council complaining, I have done a favour to you.” Justice Nicola Pain was unimpressed. “This is a case where a picture paints a thousand words,” she said in her judgment. “The additional area of fill placed on the land was grassed and presents as a continuous extension of the frontage of the residence.”



Despite pleading not guilty to what were originally 10 offences, a week later Tavakoli took the matter to the state’s planning department and commenced negotiations over an enforced undertaking in which Tavakoli admitted organising to have his company occupy and carry out the work without consent. It was a fortuitous move. “Mr Tavakoli obtained a substantial benefit as a result of entering into the [enforced undertaking], which was that five criminal charges against him personally were discontinued on the basis of the agreement reached,” Pain said in her judgment. Tavakoli’s costs totalled more than $1.54 million, including remediation works of $491,000 and $375,000 in ongoing maintenance costs. Tavakoli, who was recently celebrating his upcoming 50th birthday with family and friends on the French Riviera, was approached for comment. CLARIFICATION This story has been updated to clarify that the HDA threshold for a development is $60 million.

World.title: Unreleased report cites police complaints on domestic violence
World.content:
NationalQueenslandDomestic violence Unreleased report cites police complaints on domestic violence Julius Dennis July 22, 2026 — 9:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A report to the Queensland government from a group of domestic violence survivors calling for a civilian review system for complaints about poor police responses has been kept under wraps. The Lived Experience Working Group was convened by Prevention of Domestic and Family Violence Minister Amanda Camm in February 2025, tasked with meeting three times before providing a report on how victims were falling through the gaps. Initially reported by The Guardian, the report did not see light of day, despite consistent messaging from the government about putting victims first. Previously police would have had to call interstate offices to clarify information around protection orders. Police Media A summary of the final report, which found a fragmented system full of procedural and cultural barriers, was distributed to government bodies and key stakeholders, but not made public.



A footnote on the summary report, seen by this masthead, noted the confidentiality of working group members as a reason the report would not be made public. “Key challenges identified include inconsistent police and legal responses, lack of culturally safe and trauma-informed practices, weaponisation of service systems against victim-survivors by persons using violence, housing and financial insecurity, and inadequate support,” the summary’s executive summary reads. The most in-depth section of the report took aim at the Queensland Police Service, which it claimed reacted inconsistently to domestic violence complaints. These responses led to a “perception that outcomes depended on the officer that attended”, the author said, adding group members were discouraged from escalating complaints about police they felt did not take their concerns seriously. The group recommended a “civilian review mechanism” oversee the escalation of these concerns.



Victim-survivors involved in the group were frustrated by delays in charges being laid over DVO breaches when perpetrators had regular and predictable routines causing a lack of trust in the police service’s ability to make them safe. The roles of child protection, mental health supports, housing and financial security, the legal system, and specialist DVF services were also analysed by the group. The group found victims “overwhelmingly described experiences of being disregarded, not being taken seriously and being sent around in circles” and found the onus was on them to find the support they needed. Since the group was convened, Queensland police have disbanded their specialist domestic violence unit, deeming case management not “core business”. That decision came after a 100-day review of police operations found significant “mission creep” within the service.



Related Article Domestic violence Queensland police defend scrapping specialist domestic violence team In response to questions about the group’s report, Camm said the government was tackling the issue through record investment and the delivery of shelters, affordable housing, and more police. “The Crisafulli government has given a voice to victims of domestic and family violence and has prioritised turning around the deteriorating services we inherited from the former government,” she said. “For example, our government has increased DV Connect’s answer rate from 41.9 per cent under Labor to 84 per cent.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Trump to bomb Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site ‘soon’, appears to blame Jordan for US deaths
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war Trump to bomb Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site ‘soon’, appears to blame Jordan for US deaths Michael Koziol Updated July 22, 2026 — 9:52am ,first published 5:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: President Donald Trump declared he will bomb Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site “pretty soon”, while appearing to blame US partner Jordan for the deaths of at least two American troops when an Iranian missile hit a Jordanian air base last week. The US military has now released the identities of four service members killed in the renewed fighting, including 19-year-old Isabella Gonzales and Tyler Feehan, 25, who died at the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan. First Lieutenant Tyler Feehan and Private Isabella Gonzales were killed by an Iranian attack in Jordan. US Army Space and Missile Defence Command via AP Sergeant Michael Swinton was killed in Iraq. U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command via AP On Wednesday (AEST), the military confirmed that a third soldier believed killed in the Jordan attack was Sergeant Angel S. Rampersad, 28, of Ozone Park, New York.



Another soldier – now identified as 30-year-old Michael Swinton – died during the disposal of an Iranian drone in Iraq. Eighteen US service members have now been killed since the war began. Trump on Tuesday (Washington time) appeared to blame the Jordanian military for failing to stop the missile reaching its target. Loading “[The Iranians] did slip something through in Jordan, and if we had other operators, it would not have happened, unfortunately,” he said. “We have the best equipment in the world, we’ve stopped almost everything. But when you let other people do your job – with the United States, we let other people do the job – and sometimes it doesn’t work out so well.”



Trump also gave his strongest signal to date that he intends to authorise a strike on Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a key nuclear site buried deep underground near the Natanz facility that was bombed by the US last year. “We’ll be hitting that area probably pretty soon and there’s not a thing they can do about it,” he told reporters in the Oval Office. “Normally, I wouldn’t say that. If I thought they could do something about it, I would never say that. But we’ll be hitting that area pretty soon, and very heavily.” Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike Pickaxe Mountain since the conflict in Iran roared back to life two weeks ago after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps resumed firing at ships in the Strait of Hormuz.



So far, US forces have mostly targeted coastal surveillance assets, missile and drone launch sites, command centres and air defence systems along the Iranian coastline, and in some other areas. Mystery surrounds the exact purpose of Pickaxe Mountain. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Israeli intelligence believes Iran relocated thousands of centrifuges – used to enrich uranium – into tunnels deep inside the mountain, and had relayed this to the US. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the mouth of the Red Sea is another crucial global shipping passage. Graphic: Nathan Perri Trump was unfazed when asked about the report, saying he was focused on tracking any Iranian stockpiles of enriched uranium. “That’s where the action is.” Meanwhile, the risk of the conflict further infringing upon global shipping escalated, with at least two tankers turning around in the Red Sea after Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen threatened to attack ships in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.



Ship tracking data from LSEG showed a crude carrier, the Xin Long Yang, made a U-turn and headed back towards the Suez Canal, rather than trying to cross the strait bound for China, Reuters reported. It was carrying 2 million barrels of Saudi Arabian crude oil. Related Article Middle East at war Trump sets sights on Iran’s hidden nuclear fortress Aframax tanker Rodos, which loaded about 700,000 barrels of Saudi crude for India, also made a U-turn for Suez on Tuesday, according to the data. Gregory Brew, an Iran and oil analyst at the Eurasia Group consultancy, said the data showed at least five tankers carrying Saudi oil or bound for Saudi ports had stopped or turned around near the strait. “Non-Saudi traffic continues apace,” he said. The Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen largely sat out the conflict over the past five months, but on Monday declared a blockade on Saudi Arabia and warned shipping companies that vessels using Saudi ports could be targeted.



Trump was nonplussed about the potential escalation. “If something like that happens, we’ll take care of it. We’ve done that with the Houthis before,” he said. Meanwhile, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told a hearing of the Senate Appropriations Committee in Washington that the war against Iran had now cost $US37.5 billion ($53.16 billion), an increase of $US8 billion since the last public estimate. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing on Tuesday. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin General Dan Caine, chairman of the joint chiefs and the president’s top military adviser, faced questions about whether the US deliberately targeted desalination plants inside Iran, possibly violating international law. Iranian state media reported that the Bonji desalination plant – which provided water to more than 10,000 people in 20 villages – was destroyed by a US missile.



“I’m not aware of those being particular targets, nor I am aware of those reports,” Caine said. He undertook to find out what had happened, but maintained confidence in US forces to always act ethically.
