World.title: The luxury watches, the 20 flights to China and the Sydney international student
World.content:
NationalCrime The luxury watches, the 20 flights to China and the Sydney international student Sally Rawsthorne July 22, 2026 — 9:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Sydney international student is behind bars after allegations he fraudulently claimed more than $5 million worth of GST refunds on luxury watches. Mingyi Chi, a 28-year-old Chinese national living in Haymarket while studying in Sydney, was arrested in May by police probing suspicions of a transnational criminal syndicate using Australia’s tourist refund scheme to falsely claim GST refunds on luxury watches. A Patek Phillipe watch, one of several seized by police. AFP Chi was, police said in a media release on Wednesday, one of several individuals “engaged in rapid international travel, structured cash deposits and the circulation of high-value goods”. Investigators say Chi allegedly lodged more than $5 million in fraudulent refund claims for luxury watches at Sydney Airport.



Police say they seized $270,000 from a drawer inside the Haymarket unit. AFP In Australia, international visitors can claim GST refunds for goods worth more than $300 that are being permanently taken out of the country. Detectives further allege that he flew to Chengdu more than 20 times between November 2025 and May 2026, often staying in his native China for less than 24 hours at a time. Chi also allegedly deposited $1.1 million into Australian bank accounts via ATMs in the Sydney CBD between February 2025 and his arrest. The police raid on his Sydney apartment also resulted in investigators seizing $270,000 in cash, a Richard Mille watch worth about $170,000, three Patek Phillipe watches, one Van Cleef watch, two counterfeit luxury watches, mobile phones, a cash counting machine and multiple receipts and invoices. Chi was charged with dishonestly intending to obtain a gain, which carries a maximum of a decade behind bars. He was refused bail and remains inside Silverwater’s Metropolitan Reception and Remand Centre until at least the end of this month when he will apply for bail in the Supreme Court.



AFP Detective Superintendent Peter Fogarty said the arrest was a warning for others who would abuse the GST refund system. “Everyday Australians suffer when the taxation system is exploited and money goes into the pockets of criminals, which bankrolls future criminal ventures,” he said. “Anyone who abuses the taxation system is warned – your actions and transactions are always traceable, and you are in the AFP’s sights.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Madeleine McCann vanished in 2007. Her brother will swim at the Commonwealth Games
World.content:
SportSwimmingCommonwealth Games Madeleine McCann vanished in 2007. Her brother will swim at the Commonwealth Games Steve Bird July 22, 2026 — 9:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Madeleine McCann’s brother has been selected to represent Scotland in swimming at the Commonwealth Games. Sean McCann is expected to compete in a number of longer-distance freestyle swimming events when the Games start in Glasgow on Thursday. Scotland’s Sean McCann will compete at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games. Getty Images The 21-year-old student hopes success at the Games will improve his chances of securing a place to represent Great Britain at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles. McCann was two years old when Madeleine disappeared shortly before her fourth birthday during a holiday in Praia da Luz, Portugal, in 2007.



Their parents, Kate and Gerry McCann, fought tirelessly to try to find her. Madeleine, who is thought to have been abducted, has never been found. McCann’s family is expected to watch him compete at Tollcross International Centre during the 11-day competition. His twin sister, Amelia, is a high-level swimmer and triathlete. Madeleine McCann went missing while on holiday in Portugal in 2007. She has never been found. AP In 2023, McCann – whose father is Scottish – represented Scotland at the Youth Commonwealth Games in Trinidad and Tobago. He finished fifth in the 400m freestyle event. He has also represented Britain at the European junior open-water championship in Corfu.



The Loughborough University student trains in a pool nine times a week, completing 20 hours of training alongside his academic studies in chemical engineering. Writing on the website of the Joe Humphries Memorial Trust, an organisation set up to raise awareness of sudden arrhythmic death syndrome, McCann said he took up swimming when he was eight. Loading “In order to have achieved this, I have had to remain extremely dedicated, getting up at 4am multiple mornings each week to train, since the age of 11,” he wrote. “I train nine times a week in the pool, as well as three gym sessions, totalling over 20 hours of training per week. I’m aiming to compete at the 2026 Commonwealth Games and also the 2028 Olympics in LA.”



He is also a keen open-water swimmer, and is part of Britain’s national open water development squad. Although he has not spoken publicly about his sister’s disappearance, he has supported his parents and twin sister at vigils for Madeleine, most recently in May to mark the 19th anniversary of her disappearance. Kate and Gerry McCann hold a missing poster depicting an age progression computer generated image of their still missing daughter Madeleine, in 2012. AP His mother has previously suggested that the family had kept busy to cope with Madeleine being missing, as well as the intense glare of publicity that surrounded the search for her. “As a family, 98 per cent of the time we’re busy. I don’t know if that’s a conscious thing, but it helps. The urge to look for Madeleine absolutely hasn’t changed at all,” she said.



Related Article Exclusive

Commonwealth Games After four years, this swim star is ready to speak about ‘the worst thing that ever happened to me’ She also said that her youngest two children love to be active. “They have their own friends, and they keep busy and they’re really sporty. But their only wish is for their big sister to come home. We miss our complete family of five.” The former GP now works as a medical worker, while her husband is a British Heart Foundation professor of cardiology at the University of Leicester and an honorary consultant cardiologist at Glenfield Hospital. The family live in Leicestershire. Telegraph, London News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: CNMI pushes back against US birthright citizenship bill
World.content:
Opposition is growing in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) to a United States congressional proposal that would end automatic citizenship for many children born in American territories from 2027.

CNMI delegate to the US Congres Kimberlyn King-Hinds, delegate candidate Galvin Guerrero, Saipan-born author Kelvin Rodeo and several community advocates say the measure could undermine the Covenant between the CNMI and the US and leave future generations in legal uncertainty.

Rodeo, the author of Shadows in Paradise: The Dark History of the CNMI Guest Worker Program, said the issue was deeply personal because he was born and raised on Saipan as the child of two overseas Filipino workers.

"As a child of two OFWs (Overseas Filipino Worker) who was born and raised on Saipan during the CNMI Guest Worker Program, my first thought is that this feels very personal to me," Rodeo said.

He said the bill would directly challenge the Covenant, which defines the political relationship between the CNMI and the United States and contains citizenship guarantees for people born in the Commonwealth.

"The Covenant is not merely a policy preference. It is the foundational agreement governing the political relationship between the CNMI and the United States," Rodeo said.

"Congress should not be casually discarding one of its core guarantees by amending it to eliminate birthright citizenship."

Rodeo also said the proposal would be disrespectful to residents of US territories who have served in the American military.

"I believe this would be a tremendous slap in the face to every active duty service member from the US territories currently serving in our Armed Forces, every veteran who has already served, and especially the thousands of sons and daughters of the territories who never came home after being sent to fight America's forever wars," he said.

He warned that ending birthright citizenship could have particularly serious consequences for the CNMI, which has relied heavily on foreign labour since the establishment of its Guest Worker Program in 1983 and continues to do so under the federal CW programme.

Creating 'second-class citizens'

Many foreign workers have lived in the Commonwealth for decades, contributed to its economy and raised families without gaining a realistic pathway to permanent residency or citizenship.

Rodeo said children born to such families could grow up without permanent legal status despite spending their entire lives in the CNMI.

"In effect, we would be creating a second generation of second-class residents, children whose entire lives begin with institutional exclusion," he said.

He said the measure could accelerate the CNMI's long-term population and economic decline.

"I genuinely believe that if legislation like this were enacted, it would accelerate the CNMI's long-term decline unless our local government, alongside the other US territories, aggressively pushed for its repeal," Rodeo said.

King-Hinds said she supported stronger enforcement against immigration fraud but argued the legislation targeted the wrong people.

"I support securing our borders and stopping anyone who tries to abuse America's immigration laws," she said.

"If someone is exploiting our immigration system, they should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. I have zero tolerance for fraud or abuse."

"But this bill targets the wrong people."

Federalisation

King-Hinds said the CNMI had not controlled its immigration system since federalisation in 2009, with visa processing, border security, inspections and enforcement all under federal authority.

"If there are vulnerabilities in our immigration system, Congress should strengthen federal enforcement, not single out Americans living in the territories," she said.

She also warned against applying one citizenship standard to people born in the 50 states and another to those born in US territories.

"The people of the CNMI have disproportionately and proudly served in our Armed Forces, contributed to this nation, and lived as loyal Americans for generations," King-Hinds said.

"They should not become the testing ground for policies that Congress cannot or will not apply elsewhere."

Deleon Guerrero said citizenship under the Covenant was more than a legal designation.

"Under the Covenant, citizenship is more than legal status-it is a promise that every child born in our islands fully belongs to the American family," he said.

"That promise should never be threatened."

He said any proposal weakening citizenship rights in the territories should concern CNMI families, even if it applied only to future births.

"We have one of the highest rates of military service in the nation, and our sons and daughters should never have to question whether their citizenship will be fully protected for future generations," Deleon Guerrero said.

Foreign worker advocate Irene Holl questioned why Congress was targeting the territories.

"Why target CNMI and Guam? I understand they have concerns about birth tourism but it's going to hurt more than help," Holl said.

"What about the children of US citizens and legal foreign workers? I'm not in support of this idea."

Advocate Carlito Marquez said the federal government should use immigration safeguards rather than remove birthright citizenship.

"If the issue is security concern, they should put a safeguard for the people entering CNMI or other US territories," Marquez said.

"Limit the stay to avoid birthright citizenship."

Businessman Bong Malasarte said future generations should not be placed in legal uncertainty.

"Any change affecting such a fundamental right should be carefully considered, consistent with the US Constitution, existing federal law, and, in the CNMI's case, the Covenant with the United States," he said.

'Assault on rights'

Former CNMI lawmaker Edwin Propst called the proposal "an assault on our rights" and described it as "deplorable", "selective" and "racist".

The End Birthright Citizenship for Territories Act was introduced by Republican congressman Morgan Griffith of Virginia.

Supporters say the bill is intended to curb so-called birth tourism and would preserve automatic citizenship when at least one parent is a US citizen or lawful permanent resident.

It would apply to children born in Puerto Rico, Guam, the US Virgin Islands, and the CNMI on or after 1 January 2027.

Griffith said Congress had authority to change statutory citizenship rights in the territories.

"Just like Congress possesses the power to grant the territories Constitutional rights in statute, we have the power to take them away in statute," he said.

Territorial rights organisation Right to Democracy disputes the claim that the measure is narrowly limited to birth tourism.

Its co-directors say the bill's wording could deny citizenship more broadly and may conflict with Covenant provisions that they argue require mutual consent before they can be changed.

World.title: Thousands of MBIE workers stop work over pay offers 'well below' inflation
World.content:
About 2700 workers at the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment are downing tools on Wednesday morning.

The Public Service Association (PSA) said negotiations were underway for more than 10,000 public servants, including staff at MBIE, the Department of Internal Affairs, Corrections, and the Ministry of Social Development.

National secretary Fleur Fitzsimons said all were currently facing pay offers well below inflation.

"The current offer includes changes to pay that mean it will take staff longer to reach higher pay bands, at the same time as the cost of living keeps rising. Public servants are being asked to accept going backwards in a cost-of-living crisis."

The union said the largest group of MBIE staff involved in the bargaining were immigration officers, most of whom earned around $70,000 a year.

"MBIE workers help run New Zealand's economy, from employment and immigration services to consumer protection and business support. They deserve to be treated with respect and not presented with a deal that takes them backwards and told to accept it," Fitzsimons said.

MBIE chief people officer Jennifer Nathan said the ministry was engaged in collective bargaining with the Public Service Association (PSA) and would continue to engage with the union in good faith through the process.

"The meeting taking place today is a paid union meeting, which unions are entitled to hold under the Employment Relations Act. It is not strike action.

"PSA members work across MBIE, and MBIE makes appropriate operational adjustments to ensure members can attend meetings while maintaining services."

World.title: Waikato town chemical incident believed to be petroleum or oil-based
World.content:
It's thought an "extremely frustrating" chemical incident in a small Waikato town was petroleum or oil-based and came from a commercial or industrial property.

Emergency services were called to the Kowhai St and Matipo Dr area in Tuakau on Tuesday afternoon when the chemical was detected in water, causing a strong fuel or LPG smell.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) said firefighters responded to the "hazardous substances incident" at 4pm and evacuated 10 homes, with a further two self evacuated. They said firefighters flushed out drains and returned the atmosphere to safe levels, residents allowed to return home around 10.30pm last night.

IAWAI's chief executive Peter Winder said the exact nature of the substance had not yet been identified but indications were it was a petroleum or oil-based product.

The odour was initially noticed at the Pukekohe Wastewater Treatment Plant earlier in the day, he said, and investigations started by water services company IAWAI and its contractor Watercare.

These investigations tracked the substance back to a wastewater pump station in Tuakau, which channelled waste from a number of properties. Investigations were at an early stage but indicated a potential source could be a commercial or industrial property in the town.

Winder said this incident was a stark reminder that the rules around wastewater networks were there for a reason.

"It is extremely frustrating that this entire event was needless and appears to have been completely avoidable.

"Our wastewater networks operate under strict bylaws, with the Local Government Act providing for penalties of up to $200,000 for allowing non-compliant substances into our systems. Costs for dealing with damage to our system can be recovered from people or businesses responsible.

"This sort of incident poses significant risks to individuals and families, as well as potential damage to our network and plant operations."

Waikato district mayor Aksel Bech said when staff first detected the LPG or fuel smell in the internal drainage system of the stormwater system, all incoming water was separated into a different pond so that it wouldn't contaminate drinking water.

"Straight away that was acted on and it actually happened over a period of some hours where there was a buildup of odour and at a point where it became clear that it wasn't just a small amount, but it was continuing to come through, FENZ were also alerted and became involved."

Bech said there was a precautionary evacuation while they tried to work out what that smell was.

"Clearly, there's something in the stormwater that shouldn't be there. It could be hazardous substance, could be an underground tank, perhaps which has given way or some sort of spillage.

"Whether it was an accidental spill or some sort of failure of perhaps an underground fuel storage tank at a service station or something, we're not sure. Could be an industrial site that maybe has a larger quantity of fuel on site. So we're still investigating what it is. But for now, everything is contained and there is no new smells or odours. Everyone's returned to their homes."

He said they were having it tested and expected to have some more information on Wednesday afternoon.

World.title: One dead after Central Otago collision
World.content:
One person has died following a two-vehicle collision near the Central Otago town of Springvale.

Emergency services were called to Springvale Road, near Letts Gully Road, just after 9am.

Police said one person died at the scene.

Hato Hone St John said it responded with two ambulances and treated two people before one was transported to Dunstan Hospital in a moderate condition.

Springvale Road runs between Clyde and State Highway 85, and police advised at 11.19am that it was closed while the Serious Crash Unit conducts a scene examination.

Motorists are advised to follow diversions and expect delays.

World.title: Pass rate in critical NCEA numeracy test fall
World.content:
Barely half the teens who attempted the critical NCEA numeracy exam earlier this year passed.

The result, a pass rate of 52 percent, was down from 57 percent for the corresponding testing period last year.

The Qualifications Authority said 82,900 students sat at least one of the three online tests offered in May and each test had about 60,000 candidates.

The pass rate for reading was 61 percent, the same as for the corresponding test last year, and for writing it was 57 percent, up from 55 percent for the same time last year.

The tests are the main way students meet compulsory NCEA literacy and numeracy requirements.

Those who failed could try again in September, or, if they were still at school, next year.

Qualifications Authority figures showed students from poor communities had the worst pass rates in the May round of tests.

Just a quarter passed the numeracy assessment and a little over a third succeeded in reading and writing.

In contrast, students facing the fewest socioeconomic barriers as measured by the Education Ministry's equity index had pass rates of 73 percent in reading, 68 percent in writing, and 70 percent in numeracy.

European students had pass rates of 72 percent in reading, 66 percent in writing, and 60 percent in numeracy.

Asian students' pass rates were 58 percent for reading, 55 percent for writing and 61 in numeracy.

Māori students' rates were 49 percent reading, 46 percent writing, and 36 percent numeracy.

Pacific students' pass rates were 41 percent reading, 43 percent writing, and 27 percent numeracy.

Year 10 students were the largest group of students, accounting for more than half the students who sat the reading and numeracy tests and nearly half the writing candidates.

They had higher pass rates across all three tests than other year groups.

World.title: KMD to divest SE Asia facility and phase down operations
World.content:
Outdoor goods retail company KMD Brands is divesting its Southeast Asia manufacturing facility and will phase down operations over the next 12 months as it looks to improve its capital position.

The NZX and ASX-listed owner of Kathmandu, Rip Curl and Oboz footwear said the divestment was expected to unlock working capital of about $6 million.

The net proceeds of property was expected to be between $5m and $7m, and used to further strengthen the group's balance sheet, after it reported a first half net loss of $13.1m earlier this year.

Trading update

Kathmandu sales continued to improve in the fourth quarter (Q4) ending July, led by a strong performance in the rainwear, fleece and base layer categories, with New Zealand outperforming Australia.

Full year underlying group profit was expected to be in the range of $38m to $41m for the year ending July, which compared with $17.7m the year earlier.

Total full year group sales were expected to be in a range of $1.04b to $1.044b, which compared with 2025's $989m.

Kathmandu's same store sales, including online, were up 4.8 percent for the first full 24 weeks of the second half, though Rip Curl's sales were 2.8 percent down on the year earlier.

However, it said the winter sale period had seen weaker consumer demand associated with unseasonably warm weather on the east coast of Australia.

On the plus side, it said Oboz sales had returned to growth in Q4, as anticipated, driven by continued strong online performance and flow of new product launches.

The group's net debt was expected to be in the range of $63m to $66m at the end of July, which compared with $52.8m in the year earlier.

World.title: New Zealand now at risk of missing all its climate targets, Climate Commission warns
World.content:
New Zealand is at risk of missing all of its climate targets, and time to get back on track is running out, the Climate Change Commission says.

The commission says lagging progress on switching to low-emissions technology is no longer just a climate change problem: it's preventing households from saving money on energy costs.

Its annual emissions monitoring report said New Zealand's climate pollution had gradually decreased over time.

However, progress stalled in 2024, and the pace of reductions now needed to double to get back on track, it said.

If the government did not come up with new ways to save emissions within the next year or two, the country would not be able to meet some of its targets at all, the commission warned.

"The time available to correct course is now short," the report said.

"Many emissions reductions depend on decisions made well before the reductions are realised, and some options ... are no longer available."

That included planting more forestry, which would not mature quickly enough to meet the nearest targets.

The risks were across nearly every sector, the report said.

Agricultural emission pricing had been axed, and current government policies and industry incentive schemes were insufficient to bring methane emissions down.

Confidence in the emissions trading scheme - which the government has said is its main tool to drive down greenhouse gases - was "fragile".

And almost all the emissions reductions in industry to date were from projects funded by the previous government's GIDI scheme, which the current government scrapped.

'Current policy settings not delivering at pace needed'

"This is a clear warning sign," commission chief executive Jo Hendy said.

"Current policy settings are not delivering at the pace needed. Government choices in the next 12 to 24 months will be critical to getting the country back on track."

Climate Change Commission chief executive Jo Hendy says government choices in the next year or two will be critical. RNZ / Dom Thomas

Climate disruption was already affecting households through severe weather events - but inaction was also adding to everyday cost of living.

Low-emissions technology like solar panels and EVs were cheaper to run than fossil fuel equivalents, but the upfront costs to households meant roll-out was lagging, Hendy said.

"This isn't just a missed opportunity to reduce emissions, it means that households and businesses may be paying higher energy costs than they need to."

The government had low-cost opportunities to fix that, through targeted funding and financing and better information for households about their choices.

"It's not just about what the government spends money on, but also the signals it gives," Hendy said.

"Clear and stable policy settings help households, businesses and investors make decisions with confidence."

Unsplash

National has said it will campaign on a home energy scheme to make low-cost loans available to help households shift to solar.

At the moment, the country's flagship net-zero target for 2050 - which is enshrined in law - would not be met, the commission said.

The government must also meet emissions 'budgets' - the maximum amount of emissions the country can produce in a five-year time period - in order to keep it on track for 2050.

The current emissions budget was at significant risk, and the subsequent one would not be met with current plans and policies, the commission said.

That was despite climate accounting changes that had actually made the budgets easier to achieve.

The country was now also off-track to meet a 2030 target of reducing methane emissions by 10 percent.

The government had announced some actions to reduce emissions, but these were likely to be outweighed by other decisions it had made that could increase emissions.

The report also took aim at the government's emissions projections - saying in some cases they "do not appear to be driven by a realistic assessment of current policy".

Earlier this year, Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment Simon Upton said the government's assumptions about uptake of a methane vaccine for livestock were "heroic".

The government's baseline emissions projections rely on at least 37 percent of dairy cattle receiving a vaccine by 2030 - but the vaccines are still only at 'proof-of-concept' stage.

"Not only do we not yet have such a vaccine, but the government's decision to abandon a price on methane removes the incentive to use one should it materialise," Upton said.

Some of the actions that could increase emissions include:

Excluding agriculture from emissions pricing

Changes to the Clean Car Standard (including an option to scrap it)

Increasing the mandatory climate reporting threshold for listed companies

Delays implementing a regulated product stewardship scheme for refrigerants

Committing to a liquefied natural gas (LNG) import facility

Potential actions that could decrease emissions include:

Improved energy regulatory measures

Extending the road user charges exemption for electric heavy vehicles

Passing legislation to enable time-of-use charging for transport systems

The new Gas Transition Loan Guarantee Scheme, which was announced after the commission's assessment period ended.

Since the assessment period ended on March 31, the government had also announced a $51 million investment fund to help roll out methane-busting technology on farms.

Agricultural methane accounts for half of New Zealand's total greenhouse gas emissions and the country's plan to meet its climate targets relies heavily on farmers cutting emissions.

World.title: Cameron McEvoy has lived a life between trips to Glasgow
World.content:
When Cameron McEvoy travelled to Glasgow in 2014, he was a 19-year-old "kid".

Twelve years later, he returns to the site of his Commonwealth Games debut as a completely different man with a completely different outlook on a sport that is almost unrecognisable.

McEvoy emerged as part of the ill-fated batch of sprint stars at the 2012 Olympics — the so-called "weapons of mass destruction" who returned from London without a gold medal from any male swimmer.

Two years later, McEvoy won six medals, including two relay golds, at the Commonwealth Games despite still trying to find his place in the squad.

"I still felt like a new person on the team back in 2014," he told reporters at Glasgow airport on Wednesday morning (AEST).

Cam McEvoy says his 50m freestyle world record is just the beginning When Cameron McEvoy broke the long-standing 50m freestyle world record in March, he was at great pains to note that he believes he can go even faster.

"I was super shy; I wasn't really outspoken. I'm in the same sport but the way I'm conducting training on a day-to-day basis, the way being on the team feels now compared to as a rookie, almost feels like it's a new sport.

"It's going to be almost nostalgic being back at the Tollcross pool, seeing the set-up and going through the same thing I did as a teenager."

As he and the Dolphins touched down in the Scottish capital once again, McEvoy is a brand new man and one of only two Australian swimmers, along with Lakeisha Patterson, back for another go.

"A lot has changed," he said.

"I was basically a kid [in 2014], and now I've got my own kid. Things are very different now.

A baby-faced McEvoy won three individual silvers as part of a six-medal haul in Glasgow 12 years ago. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"There's actually a member on the swim team who's 14 [Mia Hogan], so she was only two when I was back here competing last time.

"A lot has happened; basically, my entire international career has unfolded."

Do you know an athlete competing at the Commonwealth Games? Share with us Whether you are you a family member, a friend, a colleague or a coach, share your connection with us and how you will be supporting them.

McEvoy missed out on individual medals at his first three Olympic Games and is surprisingly still hunting his first individual Commonwealth gold.

At Glasgow 2014 he finished second in the 50m, 100m and 200m. At his home Games on the Gold Coast in 2018, the pain was amplified when he picked up bronze in the 50m but missed the medals in the 100m despite entering as the Commonwealth record holder and fastest qualifier for the final.

McEvoy struggled to bounce back from those setbacks, particularly at Rio 2016 and Gold Coast 2018, to the point that when the last Commonwealth Games were on, he was at home considering his future in the sport.

He said he was "in the wilderness", unsure if he wanted to continue swimming after so many painful disappointments, but teammate Elijah Winnington's mental resilience got him back in the pool.

"Elijah had just won the 400m freestyle world title on the back of falling short in Tokyo [2021 Olympics]. For me, I saw that as a massive inspiration," he said.

"I fell short in Rio and couldn't bounce back that following year, but seeing Elijah go from Tokyo seventh in the 400m final to world champion, that was definitely a factor in motivating me to want to take that next step and come back."

ABC Sport will be live blogging every day of the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

World.title: US rider hit by car in road rage incident before Tour de France time trial
World.content:
American rider Brandon McNulty was apparently involved in a road rage incident before the time trial stage of the Tour de France.

McNulty, a teammate of overall race leader Tadej Pogačar, was confronted by an angry motorist who overtook him on his way to the start of stage 16, Mauro Gianetti, the CEO of UAE Emirates XRG, told broadcaster Eurosport.

Gianetti said the driver of the car was furious and that he stopped his vehicle after overtaking McNulty, who then collided with the vehicle.

"He was just coming to the start with the bike. One car was a little bit upset behind him; we don't know why, and then he overtook Brandon, and he stopped the car. Unfortunately, of course, Brandon crashed into the car," he said.

"Apparently it's nothing so big and all good, but it was not nice. Yes, it was a car from the public, and we don't know."

Time-trial champ wins back-to-back stages

Time trial world champion Remco Evenepoel was fastest as he won the 16th stage of the Tour de France to shave 28 seconds off Tadej Pogačar's commanding lead.

Evenepoel completed the 26.1-kilometre individual time trial in 32 minutes, 19 seconds, more than a minute faster than Mattias Skjelmose, the previous quickest, before the Belgian rider waited to see Pogačar cross the line with the second-best effort of the day.

It is the third year straight that Evenepoel has won a time trial at the Tour. His parents and family members were present on Belgium's national holiday to see him take back-to-back stage victories after winning the 15th stage on Sunday. Monday was a rest day.

His teammate Florian Lipowitz crashed out, however. The German rider slipped going around a sharp bend toward the finish and slid across the road into the sidewalk kerb. He was unable to continue with what looked like a shoulder injury.

"It's a bittersweet pill to swallow with this victory. I wish him all the best, and I hope he's not too bad," Evenepoel said of his Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe teammate. "I will really miss him for the whole week."

Paxti Vila, director sportif of the Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe team, had mixed feelings after the stage.

"On one side, you're happy because we won, but on the other side, you are kind of sad because Florian had that crash at kilometre 19.8 on that right turn," Vila said. "He's still on the way to the hospital. Let's see when the medical update arrives."

Pogačar survives scare

Pogačar had a wobble going around the same corner where Lipowitz crashed but recovered to continue.

The four-time Tour champion leads second-place Evenepoel by 4 minutes, 32 seconds with five stages remaining.

"Tadej is on his way to win a fifth Tour de France," Evenepoel said of a feat that would move the Slovenian rider level with Belgium's Eddy Merckx, Spain's Miguel Indurain and French riders Jacques Anquetil and Bernard Hinault.

"I think it's just amazing that I can be a bit close to him," he said of Pogačar. "It's an honour to race with him … so, for me, it's a big step forward that I can at least be a bit around him, and I try to learn from him."

AP

World.title: Players and fans made the World Cup a success, but the politics shouldn't be forgotten
World.content:
The past six weeks across the USA, Canada and Mexico have been so full of life, colour, controversy, and chaos that the longest men's World Cup in history feels like it has zipped past all too fleetingly.

The 'sad Pablo Escobar' memes are now in overdrive in social media algorithms that have been contorted into a daily World Cup newsfeed delivered in a very 2026 way.

Loading Instagram content

It is very likely that even if you were not a fan beforehand, you at least know about the Viking row, the Tartan Army, that Cabo Verde is a country and one that is quite good at football, and basically everything and anything about Erling Haaland.

Whether consumed through meme form, subtle second screening while at work, watch parties, or attending live, this tournament has delivered on its promise of capturing the world's attention.

But mega sporting events always do that, so how was this one any different, and what sort of legacy will it come away with?

Bringing people together

FIFA President Gianni Infantino is a hype master and summed it up in spectacularly hyperbolic terms.

"This World Cup has not just broken all possible records, it has smashed them. It has destroyed every record," he said after Spain's victory in the final.

Spain celebrates winning its second men's World Cup trophy. (Getty Images: Alex Livesey-Danehouse)

"The official figures will come out soon, but probably over 6 billion people watching it from home. The world was standing still.

"I think we have to invent a new vocabulary, new words to define the success of this World Cup."

For now, we will go with the words we have.

Infantino is right about the omnipresence of this World Cup in powerful and unexpected ways.

It is no surprise that competing countries and diaspora communities were entranced by following their nation, with emotive scenes playing out all around the world as they lived and breathed their teams' campaigns, including in Australia.

Many Socceroos fans travelled to North America to follow the team. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

What was more evocative was the people who, on face value, had no real connection to the participating teams but felt drawn to them for their own varying reasons.

Like the pictures from Gaza of Palestinians supporting Egypt against Argentina in the round of 16, whilst sitting on the rubble of destroyed buildings.

Palestinians gathered among buildings destroyed by Israeli strikes to cheer on Egypt against Argentina. (Getty Images: Saeed M. M. T. Jaras)

Or the way the small Midwest town of Lawrence, Kansas, wholeheartedly embraced hosting the Algerian team who set up base camp there.

Dr Lindsay Sarah Krasnoff, from New York University's Tisch Institute for Global Sport, is an expert in sports diplomacy, and said connections between fans and communities would provide an important legacy.

"Small acts of sports diplomacy, particularly on a citizen-to-citizen level, add up and move mountains," she said.

Mexico fans were ubiquitous throughout North America. (ABC Sport: Amanda Shalala)

"However, I think it's important to note that it is not a magic wand. Sports diplomacy by itself cannot instantly fix things. It's not going to create world peace overnight. It's not going to resolve terse political, financial or other policy differences.

"But it does have that ability — once you interact with someone through sport — you understand a little bit more about them.

"And you'll also realise that there's a lot more that binds us together … than what sets us apart.

Dr Krasnoff added that players and national teams could help create change through their presence on the global stage.

Iraq played in its first World Cup since 1986. (Getty Images/FIFA: Maddie Meyer)

"Up until this summer's tournament, most of the Western and particularly the Anglophone press, whenever we've heard about Iraq over the last 20, 30 years, it's usually been in a very negative connotation," she said.

"Related to civil war, religious fundamentalism, bombing. However, by being part of the select 48 who were able to qualify for the tournament, they showed that they are just like everyone else in the world."

But as this tournament unfolded, two more people were shot and killed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in separate incidents in Maine and Houston.

A phone call, making money, and going big

The biggest controversy of the tournament centred on the US President Donald Trump and a phone call to his friend.

The leader of one of the host countries freely admitted to calling FIFA president Infantino to ask for a favour for star American player Folarin Balogun to have his suspension wiped out.

US President Donald Trump presented Spain with the trophy after its victory. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

FIFA insisted it was an above-board process undertaken by its independent disciplinary committee, but this is an issue which will not wash away in the positive afterglow of this tournament, and is still being probed.

It would be fair to say the hosting across three countries and expanded 48-team format was broadly a success.

There were no excessive blowouts, some all-time classics, stirring underdog tales and new heroes emerged.

On the flip side, there were some rather forgettable clashes thrown in, and the days with six games felt like too much, even for the most passionate fans.

But with broadcast deals its biggest source of revenue, there is no way FIFA will turn back to 32 teams now, although it could expand even further in four years' time.

Argentina's Lionel Messi had a brilliant tournament. (Getty Images: Tom Weller)

"The next one is at home! In 2030, the World Cup is coming to Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay," CONMEBOL President Alejandro Dominguez wrote on social media.

"It will ‌be ⁠a great opportunity for football, to celebrate the World Cup's centenary with a 64-team tournament."

FIFA has not confirmed the format for 2030, although it runs the risk of having too much of a good thing should it go down that path.

The ticket prices were another hot topic; ultimately, the market justified the inflated prices, as most stadiums were filled across the 104 matches.

But it is also worth pointing out that many of the atmospheres inside were not always the frenzied fever pitch that might be experienced in top domestic leagues.

At times the venues were more akin to the Super Bowl, where the diehards could not make it in, only those with the deepest wallets.

Whether or not you think that matters, all comes down to perspective.

The excessive heat was dangerous for players and fans at times, not helped by most marquee games kicking off in the afternoon, to accommodate European TV viewing schedules.

And the mandatory hydration breaks, while needed on a 40-degree day in Miami or Philadelphia, were laughable in an air-conditioned Atlanta or Dallas Stadium.

The match between France and Paraguay in Philadelphia was played in stifling heat. (Getty Images: FIFA/Maddie Meyer)

"I think we've seen up close and from the front row, FIFA diplomacy at work, in a wide variety of different ways, the good, the bad and everything in between," Dr Krasnoff said.

"And there's also likely a lot going on beneath the surface that hasn't yet made its way into the public spotlight.

"I think this was perhaps a rapid-fire immersion in the world of FIFA and how FIFA is its own entity. And sometimes things are not necessarily always as logical as one would think."

The greatest successes and positives of this tournament came from the players and the football being played on the pitch, and the fans who embraced it so wholeheartedly.

Curaçao Livano Comenencia celebrated scoring his country's first ever World Cup goal. (Getty Images: Alexander Hassenstein)

From the smallest nation to ever qualify, Curaçao, scoring its first World Cup goal, to 40-year-old Cabo Verde goalkeeper Vozinha becoming an international treasure, to the phenomenal feats of current greats like Lionel Messi, Kylian Mbappé, Haaland, Harry Kane, and the Spanish team.

And the scenes of the Dutch Oranje walk taking over Texas, Mexicans in literally every single North American city outnumbering any other fan in huge numbers, or Egyptians celebrating a loss as if it was one of their greatest victories.

Thousands of Dutch fans took part in the Oranje Fanwalk ahead of all their games. (Reuters: Joseph Buvid)

But this does not automatically absolve the key powerbrokers or negate the legitimate concerns and issues that were raised in the lead-up and throughout.

It just means the football did the talking for the most part as it usually does, and now the rest will come back into play.

Soccer converts

The bigger question of the legacy in North America, particularly in Canada and the USA where 'soccer' is not number one, is more difficult to answer in the immediate aftermath.

The conversation is different in Mexico, where football's status as number one has never been questioned, although its legacy will be tangled up in the immense cost to co-host, and whether it was worth it as it continues to deal with serious social issues.

Canadians watched and attended in record numbers, as the team had its best result, making it to the round of 16.

This was Canada's most successful men's World Cup campaign. (Getty Images: Fran Santiago)

Their engagement with the tournament is not overly surprising in a country where ice hockey is linked to its identity, but football is the number one participation sport.

"When you start seeing these top-level performances, say making it to the top 16 or coming top four or [the women's team] winning gold at the Olympics, in a sport so competitive as soccer, it has a different reckoning, I think for the audience and certainly for Canada," Dr Nicole Forrester from Toronto Metropolitan University said.

"If we're talking about the emotional impact and the intangible piece to it, I think it would be interesting to track how our athletes, our male athletes in particular, fare in future major international competitions.

"And with our audience in terms of how much we get behind, not just supporting, but perhaps there might be a shift where there's [more] expectation."

Major League Soccer (MLS) is already in overdrive trying to capitalise on the commercial success of the tournament and convert it to eyeballs on the domestic product.

The organisation has said it wants to become one of the best leagues in the world, alongside Europe's top five.

That is a big, bold ambition, and would need a lot more Messi/Inter Miami partnerships to bring that to fruition.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

And while travelling fans and immigrant communities were always going to be swept up in the game here, the non-traditional football fans are the ones that now need to be converted.

Of the three co-hosts, the USA was always going to be the most scrutinised as a world superpower and hosting the most games.

Throughout the US, I spoke to countless locals who did not consider themselves football fans but were excited by the energy and buzz around their city hosting a World Cup.

They now need to hold onto that feeling and watch more games on TV and attend MLS and National Women's Soccer League matches.

Right now, there is still a high, a palpable buzz from having pulled off the most ambitious staging of the biggest standalone sporting event in the world.

But it is what comes next that will be most telling.

World.title: McRae sends special message to Hill before Pies head west
World.content:
Coach Craig McRae says Bobby Hill will always be welcome at Collingwood despite the troubled star looking to cut short his contract.

Hill was the hero of the Magpies' 2023 premiership under McRae, winning the Norm Smith Medal after a four-goal grand final showing against Brisbane.

But taking stretches of personal leave, the 26-year-old small forward has not played for almost a year and is unlikely to wear Collingwood colours again.

With the club and Hill's management dealing with the issue of a contract that runs until the end of 2030, McRae said he was more concerned for Hill's wellbeing, and sent a message of support.

Magpies admit Hill is 'a long way away from playing footy' Bobby Hill returns to Collingwood training, but coach Craig McRae says it will be some time before the 2023 Norm Smith medallist is ready to play in the AFL again.

"I haven't seen Bobby in the building for a while … if you're out there, Bobby, we've got a lot of love and care for you, we'll never waver in our love and support for the young man," McRae said.

"And then the other part is completely out of my hands, conversations around management and other things, so I'll leave others to do those things.

"He's a premiership player, and Norm Smith medallist, and he'll forever be welcome in our four walls."

McRae was speaking ahead of the Magpies' clash with Adelaide on Thursday night, which he expected to have a finals-like atmosphere.

The teams squared off in a qualifying final at Adelaide Oval last year, with Collingwood triumphant by 24 points.

"We've got some good memories, that game last year, the final, a big crowd there, it was a highlight of the year for me and the team. It was a huge game, and we played the ground well," he said.

"We anticipate this game to be like a final; big crowd and we're anticipating a big game."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The Magpies had only a five-day turnaround between games but surprised McRae with their training intensity, which meant he was unlikely to rest any veteran players, including Scott Pendlebury.

Gun midfielder Josh Daicos skipped training with an ankle injury but is expected to be available, while defender Jeremy Howe is also set to be named after overcoming a calf injury.

"We trained today, and we played Saturday night, and if you watch training you go, 'No way that group just played three days ago,'" he said.

"There's a huge energy in the building right now … at this stage, I don't think we've got a reason to rest too many players or manage players."

World.title: How this Champions League winner aims to ignite Stingers
World.content:
Australia's women's water polo team, the Stingers, are no strangers to success.

Winning a silver medal at the Paris Olympics, the best performance by any Australian team at those Games, put the Stingers right in the upper echelons of their field.

It's what makes the World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup finals, being hosted in Australia from July 22-26 at the Sydney Aquatics Centre at Homebush, so exciting.

But the fact the Stingers are challenging at the top of the world rankings is no accident.

The entire team is packed with genuine superstars, playing in some of Europe's biggest clubs in the biggest competitions in the world.

Abby Andrews has proven herself to be one of the very best.

Abby Andrews's first major trophy was the biggest in club water polo. (Supplied: Instagram)

The 25-year-old left-handed shooter won the LEN European Champions League title with Greek giants Olympiacos earlier this year.

Not only that, but the Brisbane native was named the most valuable player in the Final Four tournament, scoring four goals in the semifinal and a fabulous five in the final.

"It was definitely an out-of-body experience," the 25-year-old told ABC Sport ahead of this week's World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup event in Sydney.

"I mean, as an Australian, we always look and we watch the Champions League finals every year and we always think, 'Oh, how cool would it be to be in that, let alone win?'

"I said to some of my [Stingers] teammates here in Australia when I got back, I don't think I've ever won anything.

"Actually being able to lift a cup and just the feeling of euphoria with that, and the celebrations and our massive fan base in Europe is insane …

"That was probably one of the coolest moments of my life. It was awesome."

Abby Andrews scored nine goals across the semifinal and final. (Supplied: LEN European Aquatics)

Andrews's Olympiacos side beat Barcelona-based CN Mataró, featuring Stingers teammate Tilly Kearns, 14-12 in the semifinal, before downing Hungarian giants Ferencvárosi TC in the final by a score of 17-14.

"As the season went on, our team was really gaining strength," Andrews said.

"The semifinal was tough, but I think it was a great stepping stone for us.

"And then the final was brutal. We had lots of momentum swings but honestly, until the very end, we just completely stuck together."

The Final Four, held on the Mediterranean island of Malta, was an enormous occasion, the first time the men's and women's competitions were held at the same venue at the same time.

That allowed the women's teams to truly benefit from the enormous and fanatical support of their ultras.

Loading Instagram content

"It's insane," Andrews admitted of the enormous support.

"I mean, certain games that we play will have flares. They'll have this massive police presence and you just never know like what the crowd's going to do; when they're going to start chanting, if they'll go quiet for a bit.

"It's just something we don't experience here.

"I think what's so cool about the European multi-sport organisations is that they're just fanatics, like, they are absolutely mad, but ultimately their presence is so lifting and we love playing in front of them.

"It's just such a different experience.

"And for women's water polo to get that kind of attention as well, both our men's and women's teams were in the Final Four and the men unfortunately lost the semi, so all the attention shifted to us and the fans just went, 'you know what, let's give [the support] to the women'."

Abby Andrews has been a mainstay in the Stingers team. (Getty Images: James Worsfold)

Andrews joined Olympiacos, the enormous multi-sport club based in the Piraeus region of Athens better known for its football team, soon after winning Olympic silver in 2024.

Having already played overseas in the American college system and in Italy, Andrews has been exposed to the very best of the best for her entire career.

Being able to cap her second season by winning the biggest prize in club water polo underlines the fact that she is on the right track personally.

"I think each experience teaches you something different," Andrews said.

"Having that exposure against the European powerhouses and just playing them regularly, having camps with them is honestly so invaluable and it's been a huge addition to my game.

"I love bringing the new techniques that they have, because obviously some Europeans are different in size, strength, skill and you kind of just adopt new methods as you see them. So it's really fun.

"I think my latest one in Olympiacos, it being my second year, I was able to establish myself more in the systems that the Greek teams play and really settle into that, as well as just realising that I can also step up and have a really big attacking presence.

"It's just such a cool environment to be in and I love like learning about myself in those environments and how I can step up."

Abby Andrews is expecting pressure at her first-ever home World Cup finals. (Getty Images: DeFodi Images/Marcel ter Bals)

Andrews did accept that playing at such a huge club comes with enormous pressure, but that it was "kind of a good extra pressure to have".

Extra pressure is something that Andrews is hoping to embrace over the next week, as the Stingers look to show off their status as genuine world challengers in the World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup, starting in Sydney on Wednesday.

The world's top eight men's and women's national water polo teams will all compete at the event at the Sydney Aquatic Centre, the first time the city has hosted a major global water polo competition since the 2000 Olympics.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Sydney has twice hosted the World Cup finals before: the men's edition in 1999, won by Hungary; and the women's in 1995, won by the Aussies.

The Women's World Cup has also been hosted in Brisbane (1981) and Perth (2002).

But as much as the overall goal is to win the title in Sydney, emulating the Australian women's water polo team that won gold in the same Sydney Olympic Pool at the Sydney Games of 2000, filling the stands and inspiring others to follow in the Stingers' wake is just as important.

"I think this new generation coming through is so eager, I've never seen this kind of excitement from the younger kids coming through," Andrews said.

"I think it's already got such a good momentum and I think if we can really build on that and just fill the stands, get everyone there.

"You're going to be seeing some high-quality water polo from every team around the world, and being able to have this at home, who knows when we'll have this again, maybe not until Brisbane [2032].

"So while we've got this, let's use it. Everyone come down. I just think it's going to be such a spectacle."

World.title: Vaughters says night tests would have saved cycling '25 years of drama'
World.content:
Former professional cyclist and Cannondale-EF team boss Jonathan Vaughters has weighed in on the row over pre-dawn doping tests at the Tour de France, arguing such controls ​could have exposed cycling's blood-doping era decades earlier had they existed at the time.

Riders including race leader Tadej Pogačar and Jonas Vingegaard were woken in the early hours of Sunday for unannounced doping checks ahead of ​the 15th stage, prompting ‌complaints that the disruption to sleep was unfair and potentially dangerous.

Vaughters, who rode professionally through the late 1990s and early 2000s, defended the practice.

"2am testing is one of the very effective ways ‌to prevent peptide (EPO, hGH) and testosterone micro dosing," Vaughters wrote on social media.

"If ⁠UCI [Union Cycliste Inter]ationale) had tested us in 2001 at 2am? We'd all have ‌been suspended and saved the sport ​25 years of drama."

His comments ‌carry particular weight given his own history with doping.

Jonathan Vaughters (right) was teammates with Lance Armstrong (left) on the US Postal team. (Getty Images: Graham Watson)

Vaughters was a teammate of Lance Armstrong on the US Postal Service team and later admitted using performance-enhancing drugs, including EPO, during his career.

When Lance met Oprah Lance Armstrong had successfully doped for years. But when the evidence backed him into a corner, he took control of the narrative and confessed live on Oprah's couch, martyring himself to cycling's EPO era.

He subsequently testified in the US Anti-Doping Agency's (USADA) investigation into ​Armstrong, ‌who was stripped of his seven Tour titles in 2012 after the agency concluded he ran what it called the most sophisticated doping program the sport had seen.

Vaughters ⁠went on to found the team now ‌known as Cannondale-EF, positioning it as ‌an advocate for clean racing.

His remarks come as riders pushed back on the timing of ‌Sunday's tests.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Vingegaard, tested at 2 am, said the visit cost him about 40 minutes of sleep before a mountain stage on which he later ‌crashed ​and broke his collarbone.

Pogačar, ⁠tested at 5 am, said he managed only four hours of sleep. Stage winner Remco Evenepoel called the practice "inhuman".

The International Testing Agency, which oversees doping controls for the UCI, said it was "conscious that night-time testing may be disruptive ⁠to riders' rest and recovery" but that effective testing must, "in limited and justified circumstances," occur outside daytime hours.

Micro-dosing of substances ‌such as EPO ‌and human growth hormone, which can clear the body within ​hours, has long concerned anti-doping authorities, who say predictable daytime-only testing makes such practices easier to evade.

Reuters

World.title: Weatherald retains Australian Test spot despite middling Ashes returns
World.content:
Opening batsman Jake Weatherald has retained his spot in Australia's Test squad for the looming series against Bangladesh.

Despite a middling Ashes campaign last summer, Weatherald is among a 13-man squad bolstered by the return of a trio of big guns.

Captain Pat Cummins, paceman Josh Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon all return after recovering from injury.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"They have worked extremely hard, individually and with the [fitness] teams, over the past few months to return from their respective injuries," Australia's chairman of selectors George Bailey said.

"While this is a 13-player squad, we have players prepared and available should any adjustments be required in the lead-up to these matches.

"The volume of cricket and schedule across the next 12 months are likely to present further opportunities across all formats for many players."

Missing from Australia's squad for the final Test against England last January are Usman Khawaja (retired), Michael Neser, Todd Murphy and Brendan Doggett.

The Australians host Bangladesh in Darwin from August 13-17 and Mackay from August 22-26, the start of a gruelling 12 months featuring 20 Test matches.

Weatherald will resume his opening batting partnership with Travis Head after playing all five Tests last summer against England.

The Darwin-born left-hander made only 201 runs at an average of 22.33 but has been given another chance to enhance his Test credentials.

World.title: Buckley opts out of Dons, Blues coaching races after Tasmania snub
World.content:
A disappointed Nathan Buckley is ruling out bidding for other vacant AFL head coaching jobs after being overlooked by the Tasmania Devils.

While Buckley, who openly coveted the Tasmanian post that went to Ken Hinkley, says he wants to be a head coach again, he is unlikely to pitch for the vacant positions at Essendon and Carlton.

"I haven't really reflected on where those roles sit, and I don't think I would enter those processes," Buckley told Fox Footy on Monday night.

Loading...

Buckley said his most likely outcome next year was to remain at Geelong, where he is an assistant to Chris Scott.

"I am absolutely focused on the next six to 10 weeks with Geelong and how that plays out," he said.

"I will take some time to reassess what is after that."

Buckley was committed to winning the Devils job that instead was given to former Port Adelaide boss Hinkley.

"I went home, kicked the dog, threw the toys out of the cot … because I was really keen on it," he said.

"If you're going to go for a job, you have got to decide if you're absolutely all in on it — and I was.

"And I absolutely respect the process that the Devils have run, and I respect their decision with Ken as well. I am glad they have found their man, and they're really clear that Kenny is the guy for them."

However, the former Collingwood boss said the Devils' decision was a personal "fork in the road".

"I was really deliberate in getting back into Geelong, and that was as much to give myself the very best chance to be ready to go for the Tasmania role," he said.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"Now that is off the table, so I will be absolutely committed to what is going on at Geelong. I have got an option for next year there and that is probably the most likely outcome.

"There are no guarantees in this, and you have got to put yourself out there, and you have got to have a crack.

"So there's disappointment."

Asked if he remained steadfast in wanting to be a head coach again, Buckley replied: "Yeah. I determined that about 12 months ago.

"That is what I believe I am capable of doing. It's what I want to do."

Tech.title: Neill Blomkamp’s new zombie AI ‘film’ is just slop warmed over
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

On Monday, District 9 and Gran Turismo director Neill Blomkamp unveiled his latest project: a 13-minute sci-fi short titled Nightborne that’s loosely based on Peter Watts’ 2014 novel Echopraxia. The short comes from Blomkamp’s new AI startup / production company, Barley Studios, and features characters whose voices and faces are modeled after human actors. But every single one of Nightborne’s shots was made with ByteDance’s Seedance 2.0 text-to-video generator.

In an X post about the short, Blomkamp described it as a “test start” meant to demonstrate what generative AI is capable of, and he said that he wants “to tackle a full feature in this format” at some point in the future. Blomkamp seems to think that Nightborne is a strong proof of concept that might get people intrigued to see what he prompts next. But as polished as the “film” might be compared to most of the AI-generated videos floating around the internet today, it still bears many of the hallmarks we associate with slop. And even though a team of real people was involved in the project’s production, Nightborne is such a terrible watch that one would be hard-pressed to call it the future of moviemaking.

Set against the backdrop of a military conflict between the US and Syria, Nightborne tells the story of an American pilot who sustains life-threatening injuries when her helicopter is shot down. Though most of the pilot’s body is badly injured, she’s still technically alive and her head is intact. Those things make her the ideal candidate for Project Nightborne — a governmental program that turns brain-dead soldiers into remote controlled, weaponized zombies. And because the military has an endless supply of bodies at its disposal, the pilot is one of many uniformed ghouls being trained for war in secret.

Like basically every other AI-generated film that has come before it, Nightborne is really a collection of very short video clips that have been edited together to tell a simple story. Nightborne frequently cuts from shots of its zombified main character to documentary-style interviews with people involved in Project Nightborne. These cuts give the film — which was edited by Austyn Daines — a way to obfuscate the fact that Seedance 2.0 is only capable of generating a few seconds of video footage at a time. And the way the film’s dialogue is mixed almost (but not quite) makes it seem like you’re listening to real people speaking.

Blomkamp’s creative voice feels almost nonexistent

When you really take a good look at Nightborne’s visuals and listen closely to its audio, it’s easy to pick up on how much gen AI is in the mix. Signs in the background are often written in complete gibberish, and characters deliver their lines with unusual emphases that make them come across like people who don’t actually know what they’re saying. According to Blomkamp, “real concept artists” contributed work to the project, and 32 human actors agreed to have their likenesses used on-screen. But that human input doesn’t seem like it’s anywhere near enough to keep Nightborne from feeling more like machine-made content than a piece of art.

Aside from it coming from the same director who dreamt up Alive in Joburg — an imaginative exercise in using VFX to explore ideas about apartheid-era bigotry — there’s nothing remarkable about Nightborne. Blomkamp’s creative voice feels almost nonexistent as the short’s story unfolds, and if Seedance 2.0 wasn’t part of the equation, people probably wouldn’t be talking about it.

Though Seedance 2.0 can clearly churn out videos of people emoting, Nightborne highlights how the model still doesn’t have any sort of real understanding of the minute details that make human performances feel organic and truly alive. Whatever emotive nuance you might see in the short is really just a reflection of the videos Seedance 2.0 has been trained on, and not exactly something that it can take credit for.

Aside from zombies, Nightborne doesn’t have all that much in common with its source material. But it’s a lot like Jia Zhangke’s Jia Zhangke’s Dance short and Ruairí Robinson’s viral AI video depicting Tom Cruise and Brad Pitt fighting — both of which were created with Seedance 2.0. Each of these projects has demonstrated that traditional filmmakers tend to know how to downplay gen AI’s technical limitations, but their skills can only do so much to offset the technology’s innate weaknesses.

Though text-to-video models may be getting more sophisticated, they haven’t advanced enough to produce finished works that audiences are excited to see. Nightborne’s announcement was almost immediately met with a wave of backlash from people who saw the film as a sign of Blomkamp being washed. And while Blomkamp might have thought that Nightborne would generate some positive buzz for himself, it seems much more like he’s wandered into an unfortunate situation similar to the one Darren Aronofsky created with his terrible AI series about the Revolutionary War.

The most interesting thing about Nightborne is the way its story can be interpreted as commentary on the technology that was used to make it. Project Nightborne is all about individuals in positions of power repurposing dead people’s bodies without their consent in order to generate labor on the cheap. Generative AI isn’t as (immediately or obviously) destructive as killer zombie soldiers, but those pushing for the technology’s use are driven by a desire that’s similar to the one motivating Nightborne’s villains.

Tech.title: OpenAI says it accidentally hacked Hugging Face with a new AI system
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI says its AI models mistakenly breached open-source AI platform Hugging Face during internal testing. In a blog post on Tuesday, OpenAI writes that GPT-5.6 Sol and “an even more capable pre-release model” discovered vulnerabilities within their sandboxed testing environment, allowing them to gain access to the internet and target Hugging Face.

On July 16th, Hugging Face disclosed a security incident that it says was driven by “an autonomous AI agent system.” Hugging Face’s AI agents detected and stopped the breach, which OpenAI has now admitted occurred during an evaluation of its models’ cybersecurity capabilities. OpenAI says “all evidence suggests that the models were hyperfocused on finding a solution for ExploitGym,” a benchmark system that measures whether AI models can turn security vulnerabilities into exploits.

As part of efforts to complete the evaluation, the AI models gained access to the internet by exploiting a zero-day vulnerability in the sandboxed environment. From there, OpenAI says its models “inferred that Hugging Face potentially hosted models, datasets and solutions for ExploitGym,” and then “searched for and successfully found ways to gain access to secret information that it could use to cheat the evaluation:”

In one example, the model chained together multiple attack vectors, including using stolen credentials and zero-day vulnerabilities to find a remote code execution path on the Hugging Face servers.

But as serious as this incident is, OpenAI appears to be using the “unprecedented” attack as an opportunity to make its AI systems look good — especially as it competes with cybersecurity rivals, like Anthropic’s Mythos and Gemini Flash 3.5 Cyber. OpenAI’s blog post has a chart showing how GPT-5.6 Sol is getting better at sustaining multi-step cyber operations, and also encourages enterprise customers to sign up to access its “Cyber” security model.

OpenAI adds that it’s now working with Hugging Face to investigate the security incident, and will implement new controls within its research environment.

Tech.title: Substack adds an AI detector to help spot blogs written by no one
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Substack will now help users determine whether what they’re reading may have been written by AI. A new tool coming to the platform can scan posts, notes, replies, and comments to provide an estimate of how much text could be AI-generated or written with AI assistance, according to a blog post published on Tuesday.

The tool is powered by an AI detection company called Pangram and is rolling out across the web and the iOS app, with an Android launch coming “soon.” Readers can analyze content longer than 100 words by choosing the “Scan for AI text” option from the three-dot menu in the top-right corner of a post.

Image: Substack

Substack co-founder and CEO Chris Best says the Pangram integration is meant to increase transparency on the platform as AI becomes more prevalent on social media. “The core problem is not people using AI, or the quality of its output,” Best writes. “The problem is when there is a mismatch between a reader’s expectation and reality, especially when they unwittingly invest their attention in something with no human thought on the other end. That’s Claudefishing.”

In line with this change, Substack will also allow creators to explain their writing process to readers with a new “How I make this” statement. Writers can scan their drafts with Pangram, too, and will have an option to report inaccurate results.

Best notes that “Pangram can only detect whether AI was used to make the text, not whether great human care went into creating it, nor whether AI tools were used as a source.” But the goal, according to Best, is to make it easier for someone to choose to invest their time reading a blog post. “When readers have to wonder if what they’re reading is real, it undermines trust in authorship and threatens the livelihood of writers — including those who use AI tools thoughtfully to produce work they believe in,” Best writes. “Platforms that reward fakeness will create a race to the bottom.”

Tech.title: Peak Design’s modular Field Bracket has a finder tag built-in
Tech.content:
is a technology reporter who has been covering the industry since 2007. He co-hosts the Waveform podcast with MKBHD. A former engineer, he now specializes in topics like computational photography and social media protocols.

I am a very clumsy man. So clumsy, that I have AirTags hanging off practically every camera I own. Have I left my camera in an Uber? Yes. Have I left it on an airplane? Also yes. For me, finder tags are essential for my cameras.

The problem is, strapping a finder tag to a camera is always cumbersome. I currently have them hanging off my camera straps like a phone charm circa 2001. They’re ugly, and very much get in the way when I’m trying to focus on shooting. But Peak Design thinks it has a solution in its new Field Bracket system, which it launched today on Kickstarter, starting at $150 for early birds.

Image Credit: Peak Design

The Peak Design Field Bracket is part L-Bracket, part hand grip, part cheese plate. It’s made for photographers and videographers who want to quickly switch between landscape and portrait orientation on their tripod, or sometimes want to mount a light or mic to their camera when there isn’t a dedicated place to do so. But possibly the most enticing thing, to me at least, is that the bracket comes with a slot for a dedicated Finder Tag.

Peak’s Beacon Finder Tag is a Peak Design-branded finder that works with Apple Find My and Google Find Hub. That means it’ll work with both Apple and Android phones, so you don’t have to worry about losing access to your camera finder if you switch ecosystems. The tag uses a standard CR2025 battery, and Peak says it’s rated to last up to 6 months. It’s also rated for IP67 water and dust resistance, and it fits flush inside the base plate of the L-bracket.

The Beacon Finder Tag is just one of the accessories Peak Design is selling alongside the Field Bracket. The base product you’ll be buying is in fact an L-bracket, but once that’s on your camera, you’ll have access to other add-on accessories like a hand grip, finger grip, and cheese plate. Peak says the Field Bracket will work with most ARCA-compatible tripods, and won’t get in the way if you use it with its own capture clip or camera straps. In fact, the bracket itself has dedicated slots to attach your Peak Design camera strap, so you won’t have to sacrifice the strap you own to use the bracket.

Peak calls the vertical attachment to the L-bracket the Field Latch, and it uses the company’s new locking system to quickly attach and detach it without any tools. This is the same place you attach the optional cheese plate, which pulls out in adjustable stops in case you need to access ports or run cables from the camera.

Image Credit: Peak Design

Of course, you’ll have to choose the exact bracket you want for the camera you own, considering it’s molded specifically to that body. At launch, most cameras supported are the newest, or near-newest models of each camera line. You can see a compatibility list here. And if you want to see your camera supported, Peak has a dedicated feedback page to submit the camera you own.

The bracket itself will MSRP at $149.95, and if you want a bundle of all the accessories currently offered, you can get everything for $269.80. As usual, though, Peak Design is offering a Kickstarter discount, which puts the bracket at $125 and the bundle at $199, while supplies last at least.
